lessons.title: What Pattern Recognition Is
lessons.content:
Walk into the fish market at Karwan Bazar early in the morning. A boy of twelve, the fish seller's son, glances at a pile of silver fish and in two seconds says "these are ilish, those are sardines." Nobody gave him a rulebook. He has seen thousands of fish, and his brain quietly learned which shapes, sizes and shines belong to which kind. This course is about giving a computer that same skill: look at something, measure it, and decide which group it belongs to. That skill is called pattern recognition.

What a pattern is: a pattern is any object, event or signal that we want to describe and put into a group. A photo of a face is a pattern. A handwritten digit is a pattern. A two-second recording of someone saying "haan" is a pattern. A list of bKash transactions from one account in one day is a pattern. The word does not mean "something that repeats nicely like a tile floor"; in this subject it simply means "a thing we want to recognise".

Class, sample and label: a class (also called a category) is a group of patterns that belong together, like "ilish", "sardine", "digit 7" or "fraud". A sample is one actual pattern we have measured, like one particular fish on one particular morning. A label is the name of the correct class for a sample, given by a human expert or by some trusted source. Recognition means: given a new sample with no label, guess its class.

Why we need it: humans recognise patterns effortlessly, but humans are slow, get tired, cost money and cannot look at a million transactions per minute. A post office in Dhaka receives huge piles of envelopes; a bank must check every card payment in a fraction of a second; a hospital has thousands of X-ray images. Before pattern recognition, all of this was done by people, by hand, one item at a time. Pattern recognition lets a machine do the boring, repeated recognising, so humans can handle the hard and unusual cases.

Where you already meet it: face unlock on a phone, the fingerprint scanner at an office gate, the NID and passport photo checks, voice assistants, number-plate cameras on the expressway, the spam folder in your email, Google Lens reading a signboard written in Bangla, and the fraud alert when someone tries to use your card from another country. Each of these is a pattern recognition system with the same basic skeleton.

The pipeline, step by step: almost every pattern recognition system is built as a chain of stages. Sensing captures the raw data: a camera, microphone, scanner or a log of transactions. Preprocessing cleans it: removing noise, fixing brightness, resizing. Segmentation cuts out the object of interest from the background, like separating each fish on the conveyor belt or each digit in a postcode. Feature extraction turns the object into a short list of numbers, such as length, weight and colour. Classification uses those numbers to pick a class. Post-processing uses context to fix or act on the decision, for example checking that a recognised postcode actually exists.

The fish factory story: imagine a small factory in Chattogram that wants to sort ilish and sardines on a conveyor belt. A camera takes a picture of each fish (sensing). Software evens out the lighting (preprocessing) and finds the outline of the fish (segmentation). It measures length in centimetres and how bright the scales are (features). A rule like "if length is more than 30 cm, call it ilish" makes the decision (classification). Finally, if the belt sends that fish to the ilish bin but the next machine weighs it at only 80 grams, it is flagged for a human to check (post-processing).

Why one feature is rarely enough: suppose ilish are usually 30 to 45 cm long and sardines 12 to 20 cm. Length alone works well. But young ilish (jatka) can be 20 cm too, and then length alone confuses them. Add a second feature, such as body depth or scale brightness, and the two groups separate much better. Choosing features that really separate the classes is often the most important design decision in the whole system, more important than the cleverness of the classifier.

A tiny classifier by hand: suppose the factory measured eight fish. Ilish lengths: 34, 38, 41 and 22 cm (the last one a jatka). Sardine lengths: 14, 17, 19 and 21 cm. Try the rule "length above 30 means ilish". It gets all four sardines right and three of the four ilish right, so 7 out of 8 correct, an accuracy of 87.5 percent. Can we move the threshold to fix the jatka? If we use "above 21.5 cm" the jatka at 22 becomes ilish and the 21 cm sardine stays sardine, so 8 out of 8. But that threshold sits right on the edge of the data; the very next 22 cm sardine will be called ilish. This little exercise already shows the three big questions of the course: where to put the boundary, how to judge it, and whether it will still work on fish we have not seen yet.

Feature vector and feature space: if we measure two features, length and brightness, every fish becomes a point (length, brightness) on a 2D graph. That list of numbers is called a feature vector, and the graph is the feature space. Ilish points tend to gather in one region and sardine points in another. The classifier's job is to draw a decision boundary, a line or curve, that splits the space into decision regions. With three features we get a 3D space, and with fifty features a 50-dimensional space that we cannot draw but the maths works the same.

The design cycle: building a recogniser is not a straight road, it is a loop. First collect data, many labelled samples. Then choose features. Then choose a model, such as a Bayes classifier, nearest neighbour or a linear discriminant. Then train it, meaning fit its numbers to the data. Then evaluate it on samples it has never seen. If the results are poor, go back: maybe you need more data, better features or a different model. Real projects go round this loop many times.

Supervised learning: when every training sample comes with a label, we do supervised learning. The fish factory has a person label 500 fish, and the system learns from those pairs of (features, label). Most of this course is about supervised classification, because it is the classic core of pattern recognition.

Unsupervised learning: sometimes nobody has labels. A shop has records of 10,000 customers but no one has said "this is a big buyer". Unsupervised learning, mainly clustering, finds natural groups in the data by itself. Later in the course we do clustering, fuzzy c-means and Gaussian mixtures.

Semi-supervised and reinforcement: semi-supervised learning uses a few labelled samples plus many unlabelled ones, which is common because labelling is expensive; a doctor may label 200 X-rays but the hospital has 50,000. Reinforcement learning, where an agent learns by reward, is a different area covered in its own course (deep-cse-8-4); we only mention it.

Three approaches: the statistical approach treats features as random numbers and uses probability to decide; this is the main road of the course (Bayes decision theory, density estimation, linear discriminants). The structural or syntactic approach describes a pattern by its parts and how they connect, like describing the digit 4 as "a vertical stroke, a slanted stroke and a horizontal cross bar"; we meet it in lesson 23. The neural approach uses networks of simple units that learn features and boundaries together; it is the root of today's deep learning and has its own courses (deep-cse-7-8 and deep-cse-8-1).

Pattern recognition vs machine learning: the two fields overlap heavily. Pattern recognition grew from engineering problems like reading characters and recognising speech, and it cares a lot about the whole pipeline: sensors, features, decisions and error rates. Machine learning grew from computer science and statistics and cares about learning algorithms in general. You already met k-NN, naive Bayes, SVM, k-means and PCA in the Machine Learning course (deep-cse-6-1). Here we revisit them only briefly and go deeper into the theory behind good decisions: why Bayes is optimal, how to estimate densities, how to design linear boundaries, how to handle sequences and structure.

Errors are unavoidable: even a perfect system will sometimes be wrong, because the classes truly overlap. A big jatka and a small adult ilish can have exactly the same length. If two classes share the same feature values, no rule can always be right. The smallest possible error rate for given features is called the Bayes error, and much of this course is about getting close to it. The only way to beat it is to add better features, not a cleverer classifier.

Real-life example 1, Bangla postcodes: Bangladesh Post wants to read handwritten postcodes like 1205 in Bangla digits. Sensing: a scanner photographs the envelope. Preprocessing: convert to black and white and remove smudges. Segmentation: find the postcode box and cut out four separate digits. Feature extraction: shrink each digit to a small grid and count dark pixels in each cell. Classification: decide which of the ten Bangla digits each one is. Post-processing: check that the four-digit code exists in the list of real postcodes; if "1295" does not exist but "1205" does, and the third digit was uncertain, choose 1205.

Real-life example 2, fraud on a mobile wallet: a mobile-wallet company watches every cash-out. Sensing: the transaction log. Preprocessing: fix time zones and remove test accounts. Features: amount, time of day, how many cash-outs in the last hour, whether the device is new. Classification: normal or suspicious. Post-processing: a suspicious decision does not block the user at once; it sends a one-time code or calls the customer. Here there is no picture at all, which shows that patterns do not have to be images.

Common mistakes: students often think pattern recognition is only about images; it is equally about sound, text, signals and tables. Another mistake is jumping straight to a fancy classifier before thinking about features; bad features cannot be rescued. A third is forgetting that some error is natural when classes overlap. Exam questions at this stage usually ask you to draw and explain the pipeline, define pattern, class and feature, and contrast supervised and unsupervised learning, or statistical and structural approaches.

Course map: lessons 02 and 03 build the language of features and probability. Lessons 04 to 06 are Bayesian decision theory, the heart of the subject. Lessons 07 to 11 show how to estimate probabilities from data, with and without assumed formulas. Lessons 12 to 15 build linear and kernel classifiers. Lessons 16 and 17 handle features. Lessons 18 to 20 deal with sequences. Lessons 21 and 22 are clustering, 23 is structural recognition, 24 and 25 are evaluation and combining, and 26 puts everything together.

Recap: a pattern is a thing to be recognised, a class is a group, a feature vector is the list of numbers that describes a sample, and a classifier draws boundaries in feature space. Real systems are pipelines from sensor to decision, and their quality depends first on good features and data, then on a sound decision rule.
key_points: A pattern is any object or signal to be recognised; a class is a group; a label is the correct class of a sample.
Pipeline: sensing, preprocessing, segmentation, feature extraction, classification, post-processing.
A feature vector is a point in feature space; a classifier draws decision boundaries that split it into regions.
Design is a loop: data, features, model, training, evaluation, then improve.
Supervised uses labels, unsupervised (clustering) finds groups, semi-supervised mixes a few labels with many unlabelled samples.
Statistical, structural and neural are the three main approaches.
When classes overlap, some error (the Bayes error) is unavoidable; only better features can lower it.
lessons.tip: For every system you use today (face unlock, spam folder, number-plate camera), say the six pipeline stages out loud. After three or four systems the pipeline becomes second nature.
lessons.task: Collect 10 coins or 10 leaves. Pick two features you can measure with a ruler or your eyes, write them in a table, and plot each item as a point on graph paper. Can you draw one line that separates two kinds? Which feature helped more?

quiz.q: In pattern recognition, what is a feature vector?
options: The final class decided by the system
A list of numbers that describes one sample
The camera or sensor used to collect data
A table of all the labels
quiz.explain: Each sample is turned into a list of measured numbers, such as length and brightness; that list is its feature vector.

quiz.q: Which pipeline stage cuts each digit out of a scanned postcode?
quiz.explain: Segmentation separates the objects of interest, here each digit, from the background and from each other.

quiz.q: A shop has 10,000 customer records with no labels and wants to find natural groups. Which kind of learning is this?
quiz.explain: With no labels, the system has to find groups by itself, which is unsupervised learning (clustering).

quiz.q: Big jatka and small adult ilish have exactly the same length. What is the best way to reduce mistakes?
options: Use a more complicated classifier on length only
Add a new feature that differs between the two
quiz.explain: If classes overlap on the features you have, no classifier can separate them; only a better feature can lower the error.

quiz.q: Describing the digit 4 as "a vertical stroke, a slanted stroke and a cross bar" is an example of which approach?
quiz.explain: The structural approach describes a pattern by its parts and how they are connected.

lessons.title: Features, Feature Space and Distances
lessons.content:
A doctor in a village clinic cannot see inside your body, so she measures what she can: temperature 38.5, pulse 96, blood pressure 120 over 80. Three numbers, and already she can tell a cold from dengue far better than by guessing. A computer is in the same position as that doctor. It cannot "see" a fish or "hear" a word the way we do; it only gets numbers. Choosing which numbers to measure, and how to compare them, is the subject of this lesson.

What a feature is: a feature is one measurable property of a sample. Length of a fish, number of loops in a handwritten digit, average pitch of a voice, number of cash-outs in the last hour. A feature should be something you can compute the same way for every sample, automatically, without a human deciding each time.

Why features matter so much: raw data is huge and messy. A small 28 by 28 grey image already has 784 numbers, and most of them say nothing useful about which digit it is. A good set of features squeezes out the useful part and throws away the rest. With good features even a simple classifier works; with poor features even the cleverest classifier fails. Experienced engineers often say that the features decide most of the final accuracy.

Four types of feature: features are not all the same kind of number, and the kind decides what maths you may do with them. Nominal features are just names: colour of a rickshaw (red, blue, green), blood group. You can only check equal or not equal; "red minus blue" means nothing. Ordinal features have an order but no fixed gaps: exam grade A, B, C, or a pain level "mild, medium, severe". You can say A is better than B, but not that the gap A to B equals the gap B to C. Interval features have equal gaps but no true zero: temperature in Celsius. 30 degrees minus 20 degrees is a real 10 degree difference, but 20 degrees is not "twice as hot" as 10. Ratio features have a true zero: length, weight, money, count. A 40 cm fish really is twice as long as a 20 cm one.

Why the type matters in practice: if you code blood groups as A = 1, B = 2, AB = 3, O = 4, a distance-based method will think O is "closer" to AB than to A, which is nonsense. Nominal features are usually turned into separate yes/no features (one-hot coding, covered in deep-cse-6-1-03). Ordinal features can be coded as 1, 2, 3 if you accept that the gaps are only approximate.

The feature vector: we collect d features of a sample into a column of numbers x = (x1, x2, ..., xd). For a fish with length 34 cm and brightness 0.7, x = (34, 0.7). Every sample becomes one point in a d-dimensional space called the feature space. A data set of n samples is a table with n rows and d columns, or a cloud of n points.

Decision regions and boundaries: a classifier splits the feature space into regions, one region per class (a region can have several separate pieces). Any new point falling in the "ilish" region is called ilish. The border between regions is the decision boundary. In 2D it is a line or curve, in 3D a surface, and in higher dimensions we call it a hypersurface (or a hyperplane if it is flat). Much of this course is about where to put these boundaries.

What makes a good feature: first, it must be discriminative, meaning its values differ clearly between classes. Second, it should be invariant to changes that do not matter: a digit should give the same features whether it is written big or small, slightly rotated, or shifted on the page. Third, it should be robust to noise, so a little dust on the scanner does not change it much. Fourth, it should be cheap to compute, because a system may run millions of times a day. Finally, features should not all repeat the same information; length in cm and length in inches together add nothing new.

Checking a feature quickly: a simple way to judge one feature is to draw a histogram of its values for each class on the same axis. If the two humps are far apart with little overlap, the feature is useful. If they sit on top of each other, it is nearly useless on its own. For a numeric score, compare the gap between class means with the spread inside each class; lesson 17 turns this idea into the Fisher score.

The scale problem: features come in different units. Length in cm might range 10 to 50, while weight in grams ranges 50 to 1500. Any method that measures distance will be dominated by the feature with the bigger numbers, simply because its numbers are bigger, not because it is more important. That is why we usually normalise features first.

Min-max normalisation: rescale each feature to the range 0 to 1 using x' = (x - min) / (max - min). Worked: fish lengths are 14, 22 and 38 cm. Min is 14, max is 38, so the range is 24. The 22 cm fish becomes (22 - 14) / 24 = 0.333, the 14 cm fish becomes 0 and the 38 cm fish becomes 1. Simple, but one extreme value (a 90 cm fish entered by mistake) squashes everything else near 0.

Z-score standardisation: subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation, z = (x - mean) / sd. Worked: values 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 have mean 30 and (population) standard deviation about 14.14. So 10 becomes (10 - 30) / 14.14 = -1.41, 30 becomes 0 and 50 becomes 1.41. After this every feature has mean 0 and spread 1, so they compete fairly. Important rule: compute min, max, mean and sd on the training data only, then apply the same numbers to test data.

Distance: to say two samples are "similar" we need a distance. A distance d(a, b) should be zero only when a = b, never negative, symmetric (d(a, b) = d(b, a)) and should obey the triangle inequality, d(a, c) <= d(a, b) + d(b, c), meaning a detour is never shorter than the direct road.

Euclidean distance: the everyday straight-line distance. For a = (1, 2) and b = (4, 6), the differences are 3 and 4, so d = square root of (9 + 16) = 5. In d dimensions you add up all the squared differences and take the square root. It is the default choice for continuous features on similar scales.

Manhattan distance: add the absolute differences: |1 - 4| + |2 - 6| = 3 + 4 = 7. The name comes from city blocks: in a grid of streets you cannot walk diagonally through buildings, you walk along streets. It is less affected by one huge difference in a single feature.

Chebyshev distance: take only the biggest single difference: max(3, 4) = 4. Useful when the worst feature matters most, for example in quality control where any one measurement out of range is a reject. Euclidean, Manhattan and Chebyshev are all members of one family called the Minkowski distance with power p = 2, 1 and infinity.

Cosine similarity: sometimes direction matters more than size. Cosine similarity is the dot product divided by the product of lengths. For a = (3, 4) and b = (4, 3): dot = 12 + 12 = 24, both lengths are 5, so cosine = 24 / 25 = 0.96, very similar. For text, a long news article and a short one about the same cricket match point in a similar direction in word-count space even though their sizes differ, so cosine is the usual choice for documents. Cosine distance is 1 minus the similarity.

Worked example, why scale matters: three fish as (length cm, weight g): X = (30, 500), Y = (40, 520), Z = (31, 560). Raw Euclidean: X to Y is the square root of (100 + 400) = 22.4, X to Z is the square root of (1 + 3600) = 60.0. So Y looks closer. Now scale length by dividing by 10 and weight by dividing by 100, so that a typical spread is about 1 in both: X = (3, 5), Y = (4, 5.2), Z = (3.1, 5.6). Now X to Y = 1.02 and X to Z = 0.61, so Z is closer. The answer flipped only because of units. That is the whole argument for normalising.

Mahalanobis distance, a preview: Euclidean distance treats every direction the same, but real classes are often stretched and tilted ovals, because features are correlated (long fish are also heavy). The Mahalanobis distance measures distance in units of the class's own spread and correlation, using its covariance matrix. We build it properly in lessons 03 and 06; for now, remember it is "Euclidean distance after undoing the stretch and tilt of the data".

Real-life example 1, sorting tomatoes in Jessore: a vegetable packer wants to grade tomatoes into export, local and reject. Features: diameter in mm (ratio), redness score from a camera from 0 to 1 (ratio), and "has a crack" yes or no (nominal, coded 0 or 1). Diameter ranges 40 to 90 while redness is 0 to 1, so without z-scoring, diameter would swamp redness. After standardising, a simple nearest-centre rule (compare each tomato with the average export, local and reject tomato) works well, and the crack flag alone sends a tomato to reject whatever its other features say.

Real-life example 2, matching news articles: a Bangla news portal wants to show "related stories". Each article becomes a vector of word counts for, say, 5,000 common words. A short 200-word report on a Mirpur test match and a 2,000-word analysis of the same match have very different lengths, so their Euclidean distance is large. Their cosine similarity is high because they use the same words in similar proportions. The portal uses cosine and gets sensible recommendations.

Common mistakes: doing arithmetic on nominal codes; forgetting to normalise before using distances; computing normalisation statistics on all the data including the test set (a small leak that makes results look better than they are); and adding many weak features hoping more is always better, which lesson 17 shows can hurt. Exams often ask you to classify feature types, compute Euclidean, Manhattan and cosine values for two vectors, normalise a small list, and explain invariance.

Recap: features turn samples into points in feature space; classifiers carve that space into decision regions. Know the four feature types and what each allows, make features discriminative, invariant, robust and cheap, normalise them, and pick a distance that fits the data: Euclidean for general numbers, Manhattan for robustness, Chebyshev for worst-case checks and cosine for direction.
key_points: A feature is one measurable property; d features form a feature vector, a point in d-dimensional feature space.
Feature types: nominal (names), ordinal (order only), interval (equal gaps, no true zero), ratio (true zero).
Good features are discriminative, invariant, robust to noise, cheap and not redundant.
Normalise: min-max x' = (x - min)/(max - min), or z-score z = (x - mean)/sd, fitted on training data only.
Euclidean (3,4 gives 5), Manhattan (gives 7), Chebyshev (gives 4) are Minkowski distances with p = 2, 1, infinity.
Cosine similarity compares direction: (3,4) and (4,3) give 24/25 = 0.96.
Units can flip which sample is nearest, so scale features before using distances.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see a distance-based method, ask two questions before anything else: what are the units of each feature, and have they been put on the same scale? Most surprising results come from forgetting this.
lessons.task: Write down height (cm) and shoe size for five family members or friends. Compute the Euclidean distance between two people using raw numbers, then z-score both features and compute it again. Did the "closest pair" change?

quiz.q: Blood group (A, B, AB, O) is which type of feature?
quiz.explain: Blood groups are only names with no order or gaps, so the feature is nominal.

quiz.q: What is the Manhattan distance between (1, 2) and (4, 6)?
Using min-max normalisation with min 14 and max 38, what does 22 become?
Why is cosine similarity popular for comparing documents?
options: It is always smaller than Euclidean distance
It compares the direction of word-count vectors, so long and short articles on the same topic still match
It ignores which words are used
It only works on nominal features
quiz.explain: Cosine depends on direction, not length, so documents of different sizes with similar word proportions score high.

quiz.q: Where should the mean and standard deviation for z-scoring be computed?
options: On the training data only, then applied to test data
On all data together, including test
quiz.explain: Using test data to compute normalisation leaks information and makes results look better than they really are.

lessons.title: Probability Refresher for Pattern Recognition
lessons.content:
Before a long bus trip from Dhaka to Sylhet you check the sky. Dark clouds, and it is July: you pack an umbrella. You did not know for sure it would rain; you weighed how likely rain is. Pattern recognition makes decisions in exactly this way, under uncertainty, and the language for that is probability. This lesson refreshes the probability you met in deep-cse-2-6 and sharpens the pieces that the rest of the course uses every day: Bayes' rule, densities, the Gaussian, the mean vector and the covariance matrix.

Why probability at all: the same feature value can come from different classes. A 22 cm silver fish could be a jatka or a sardine. A transaction of 5,000 taka at midnight could be normal or fraud. Because of this overlap we cannot give a sure answer; we can only say how likely each class is, and then choose wisely. Probability is the tool that turns "it might be this or that" into numbers we can compare.

Random variable: a random variable is a quantity whose value depends on chance. The class of the next fish on the belt, call it w, is a random variable taking values like ilish or sardine. Its length x is another random variable, taking real numbers. Discrete random variables (class, number of loops) have probabilities for each value; continuous ones (length, weight) are described by densities, which we come to shortly.

Joint, marginal and conditional, with a table: suppose a phone company looked at 100 SMS messages. 40 are spam and 60 are normal (ham). Of the spam, 30 contain the word "offer"; of the ham, 5 contain "offer". The joint probability P(spam and offer) = 30 / 100 = 0.30. The marginal probability P(spam) = 40 / 100 = 0.40, found by adding across the row; P(offer) = 35 / 100 = 0.35. The conditional probability P(offer | spam), read "offer given spam", = 30 / 40 = 0.75: among spam, three quarters say offer. And P(spam | offer) = 30 / 35 = 0.857: among messages saying offer, about 86 percent are spam.

The product rule: joint = conditional x marginal. P(spam and offer) = P(offer | spam) x P(spam) = 0.75 x 0.40 = 0.30, matching the table. It also equals P(spam | offer) x P(offer) = 0.857 x 0.35 = 0.30. Writing both versions and setting them equal is all Bayes' rule is.

Independence: two events are independent if knowing one tells you nothing about the other, which means P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B). Check: P(spam) x P(offer) = 0.40 x 0.35 = 0.14, but the real joint is 0.30. Not independent: seeing "offer" really changes the chance of spam. That is exactly why "offer" is a useful feature. A feature independent of the class would be useless.

Bayes' rule: P(w | x) = P(x | w) P(w) / P(x). Each piece has a name you must know. P(w) is the prior: how common the class is before you look at the sample. P(x | w) is the likelihood: how typical this feature value is for that class. P(x) is the evidence: how common the feature value is overall, a normalising number that is the same for every class. P(w | x) is the posterior: the updated belief after seeing the feature. In words: posterior = likelihood x prior / evidence.

Computing the evidence: P(x) is found by the law of total probability, adding over all classes: P(x) = sum over j of P(x | wj) P(wj). Because it is the same for every class, when we only want to know which class wins we can compare likelihood x prior and skip dividing. We need the division only when we want the actual posterior numbers.

Worked Bayes example, fraud and new devices: in a mobile wallet, 1 percent of cash-outs are fraud. Of fraud cases, 70 percent come from a device the account has never used; of normal cases only 5 percent do. A cash-out arrives from a new device. Likelihood x prior for fraud = 0.70 x 0.01 = 0.007. For normal = 0.05 x 0.99 = 0.0495. Evidence = 0.007 + 0.0495 = 0.0565. Posterior P(fraud | new device) = 0.007 / 0.0565 = 0.124, about 12 percent. The new device made fraud 12 times more likely than the 1 percent prior, yet most new-device cash-outs are still normal. The small prior keeps the posterior modest; forgetting the prior is one of the most common reasoning errors, called base-rate neglect.

Probability mass vs probability density: for a discrete variable, P(x = 3 loops) is a real probability between 0 and 1. For a continuous variable like length, the chance of exactly 34.000... cm is zero. Instead we use a probability density function p(x): the probability of falling in a small interval is about p(x) times the interval width, and the total area under p(x) is 1. A density value can be bigger than 1 (a very narrow hump), because it is "probability per centimetre", not a probability. Bayes' rule works the same with densities: P(w | x) = p(x | w) P(w) / p(x).

The 1D Gaussian: the most used density is the normal or Gaussian bell curve, p(x) = 1 / (sigma times square root of 2 pi) times exp(-(x - mu) squared / (2 sigma squared)). It has two parameters: the mean mu (centre) and the standard deviation sigma (width). About 68 percent of values lie within one sigma of the mean, about 95 percent within two, and about 99.7 percent within three.

Gaussian worked: suppose ilish lengths follow a Gaussian with mu = 35 cm and sigma = 4 cm. The density at 35 cm is 1 / (4 x 2.5066) = 0.0997. At 39 cm, one sigma away, it is 0.0997 x exp(-0.5) = 0.0605. At 43 cm, two sigma away, it is 0.0997 x exp(-2) = 0.0135. So a 39 cm fish is fairly typical for ilish, and a 43 cm fish is unusual but possible. These density values are exactly the likelihoods p(x | ilish) that we will plug into Bayes' rule in the next lesson.

Why the Gaussian is everywhere: when a measurement is the sum of many small independent effects (genes, food, water temperature, measurement error), the central limit theorem says it tends to look Gaussian. It is also mathematically convenient: it is fully described by its mean and variance, and its logarithm is a simple quadratic, which makes classifiers built on it neat. But real data is not always Gaussian: incomes are skewed, and some features have two humps. Lesson 10 shows how to manage without assuming a shape.

Many features: the mean vector: with d features each sample is a vector, and its average is the mean vector, the average of each feature separately. Take four samples (1, 2), (3, 3), (5, 7), (7, 8). The mean of the first feature is (1 + 3 + 5 + 7) / 4 = 4, and of the second (2 + 3 + 7 + 8) / 4 = 5. The mean vector is (4, 5), the centre of the cloud.

Covariance: variance tells how spread one feature is; covariance tells whether two features move together. Subtract the mean from each sample: (-3, -3), (-1, -2), (1, 2), (3, 3). Variance of feature 1 = (9 + 1 + 1 + 9) / 4 = 5. Variance of feature 2 = (9 + 4 + 4 + 9) / 4 = 6.5. Covariance = average of the products = (9 + 2 + 2 + 9) / 4 = 5.5. Positive covariance means that when feature 1 is above its mean, feature 2 tends to be above its mean too.

The covariance matrix: put these into a d by d table, Sigma = [[5, 5.5], [5.5, 6.5]]. Variances sit on the diagonal, covariances off the diagonal, and the matrix is symmetric. (We divided by n = 4; many books divide by n - 1 = 3 for an unbiased estimate, giving [[6.67, 7.33], [7.33, 8.67]]. Lesson 07 explains the difference.) The correlation, covariance divided by the product of standard deviations, is 5.5 / square root of (5 x 6.5) = 0.96, a very strong positive link.

Reading the shape: the multivariate Gaussian in d dimensions has a mean vector mu and a covariance matrix Sigma. Its contours of equal density are ellipses (ellipsoids in more dimensions). If Sigma is a multiple of the identity, the contours are circles. If the diagonal entries differ but the off-diagonals are zero, the ellipses are stretched along the axes. If the off-diagonals are non-zero, the ellipses are tilted, like our data where both features rise together. The eigenvectors of Sigma point along the ellipse axes and the eigenvalues give the squared lengths of spread along them; PCA in lesson 16 uses exactly this.

The multivariate formula in words: the d-dimensional Gaussian is p(x) = 1 / ((2 pi) to the power d/2 times the square root of the determinant of Sigma) times exp(-0.5 (x - mu)^T Sigma^-1 (x - mu)). Do not panic at the symbols. The part inside exp is minus half of a squared distance from x to the mean, measured in the units of the data's own spread; that squared distance is the Mahalanobis distance of lesson 06. The determinant in front measures the volume of the cloud: a more spread-out cloud has a lower peak so that the total probability still adds to 1. With d = 1 and Sigma = sigma squared, the formula collapses back to the familiar bell curve.

Real-life example 1, a cricket batting check: a coach records two features for each ball a batter faces in the nets: ball speed in km per hour and the batter's reaction time in milliseconds. Over 200 balls the mean vector might be (130, 240). A positive covariance between speed and reaction time would be surprising (faster balls should give less time, so the link is likely negative), and seeing its sign in the covariance matrix tells the coach immediately how the two move together without drawing anything.

Real-life example 2, a dengue season at a clinic: in a normal month 2 percent of fever patients at a Dhaka clinic have dengue, but in August it rises to 20 percent. A test with the same likelihoods gives very different posteriors in the two months because the prior changed. Doctors know this instinctively: the same positive result is far more convincing in peak season. Pattern recognition systems must also update priors when the world changes, or their decisions slowly go wrong.

Common mistakes: mixing up P(x | w) and P(w | x) (the chance that a spam says offer is not the chance that an offer message is spam); ignoring the prior; treating a density value as a probability and being shocked when it is above 1; forgetting that covariance depends on units; and assuming features are independent without checking. Exams typically give a small table and ask for joint, marginal and conditional probabilities, a Bayes posterior, a Gaussian density value, or a mean vector and covariance matrix from four or five points.

Recap: probability measures uncertainty. Bayes' rule, posterior = likelihood x prior / evidence, is the engine of statistical pattern recognition. Continuous features use densities, most often the Gaussian with mean and standard deviation, or in many dimensions the multivariate Gaussian with a mean vector and covariance matrix whose shape tells you how features spread and move together.
key_points: Joint, marginal and conditional are linked by the product rule: P(A and B) = P(A | B) P(B).
Independence means P(A and B) = P(A) P(B); a feature independent of the class is useless.
Bayes' rule: posterior = likelihood x prior / evidence, with evidence = sum of likelihood x prior over classes.
Worked: 1 percent fraud prior, 70 vs 5 percent likelihoods give a posterior of 0.124.
A density is probability per unit and can exceed 1; the Gaussian has mean mu and standard deviation sigma.
Mean vector and covariance matrix describe a cloud: for (1,2),(3,3),(5,7),(7,8), mean (4,5), Sigma [[5,5.5],[5.5,6.5]].
Covariance shape: identity gives circles, diagonal gives axis-aligned ellipses, off-diagonals tilt them.
lessons.tip: Always write Bayes' rule with the four names under each term (posterior, likelihood, prior, evidence). Saying the names aloud stops you from swapping P(x | w) and P(w | x), the most common slip.
lessons.task: Look at your last 30 SMS messages. Count how many are promotional and how many contain a word like "offer", "free" or "cashback". Fill a 2 by 2 table and compute P(promo), P(word | promo) and P(promo | word).

quiz.q: In Bayes' rule, what is the prior P(w)?
options: How common the class is before looking at the sample
How typical the feature value is for the class
The updated belief after seeing the feature
The total probability of the feature value
quiz.explain: The prior is the class probability before any measurement; the likelihood is P(x | w) and the posterior is P(w | x).

quiz.q: With a 1 percent fraud prior, P(new device | fraud) = 0.7 and P(new device | normal) = 0.05, what is P(fraud | new device)?
A density value p(x) = 2.5 is computed for a very narrow Gaussian. What does this mean?
options: There is a mistake, probabilities cannot exceed 1
It is probability per unit length, which can exceed 1
quiz.explain: Densities are not probabilities; a narrow hump can have height above 1 while the total area stays 1.

quiz.q: For samples (1,2), (3,3), (5,7), (7,8), what is the covariance of the two features (dividing by n)?
quiz.explain: Deviations multiply to 9, 2, 2, 9; their average is 22 / 4 = 5.5.

quiz.q: A covariance matrix has non-zero off-diagonal entries. What do the Gaussian contours look like?
options: Ellipses tilted away from the axes
Ellipses always aligned with the axes
quiz.explain: Non-zero covariance means the features move together, which tilts the equal-density ellipses.

lessons.title: Bayesian Decision Theory I: Minimum Error Decisions
lessons.content:
You are blindfolded at the fish market and someone hands you a fish. Before you touch it, what do you guess? If the stall is full of sardines and has only a few ilish, you guess sardine, and you are right most of the time. Now the blindfold comes off and you see it is 27 cm long. Your guess may change. Bayesian decision theory is the exact, mathematical version of this everyday reasoning, and it is the foundation of statistical pattern recognition. It tells us the best possible decision rule when we know the probabilities, and every later classifier is in some sense an attempt to copy it from data.

The problem it solves: before Bayes decision theory, a designer picked a threshold by eye, like "above 30 cm is ilish". Such a rule might be fine or awful; nobody could say whether a better rule existed. Bayesian decision theory answers a sharper question: if we know how likely each class is and how its features are distributed, which rule makes the fewest mistakes on average? The answer turns out to be beautifully simple.

The setting: there are c classes w1, ..., wc (for us, w1 = ilish and w2 = sardine). Each has a prior P(wj). Each has a class-conditional density p(x | wj), describing how the feature x is spread inside that class. For this lesson assume we know all of these exactly; lessons 07 to 10 handle learning them from data.

Deciding with priors only: with no measurement, the best you can do is always choose the class with the larger prior. Say 70 percent of fish on the belt are sardines and 30 percent ilish. Always saying sardine is right 70 percent of the time, so the error rate is 0.30. Any other rule that ignores the fish, even a random coin flip weighted 50-50, does worse. This is the baseline any real classifier must beat.

Deciding with likelihoods only: the opposite naive idea is to look only at p(x | wj) and pick the class for which the observed x is most typical. This is called the maximum likelihood decision. It is right when the classes are equally common, but it ignores priors, so when one class is rare it calls too many samples that rare class. It is like a new doctor who sees fever and headache and declares malaria in Dhaka, where it is far less common than in some hill districts.

The Bayes decision rule: combine both. Compute the posterior P(wj | x) = p(x | wj) P(wj) / p(x) for each class and choose the class with the largest posterior. Because p(x) is the same for all classes, an equivalent rule is: choose the class with the largest p(x | wj) P(wj). This is called the minimum error rate rule, or simply the Bayes classifier.

Why it is optimal: for any particular x, if we decide w1, the probability we are wrong is P(w2 | x); if we decide w2, it is P(w1 | x). So the error at that x is the posterior of the class we did not choose. Picking the larger posterior makes this as small as possible at every x. The average error over all x, P(error) = integral of P(error | x) p(x) dx, is then also as small as possible, because we made every piece of the integral as small as we could. No rule using the same feature can do better.

Worked example, the setup: let ilish length be Gaussian with mean 35 cm and standard deviation 4, sardine length Gaussian with mean 18 cm and standard deviation 3. Priors: P(ilish) = 0.3, P(sardine) = 0.7. A fish of x = 25 cm arrives.

Worked example, the numbers: the density of 25 cm under ilish is 0.00438 (it is 2.5 standard deviations below the mean). Under sardine it is 0.00874 (2.33 standard deviations above the mean). Multiply by priors: ilish 0.00438 x 0.3 = 0.00131; sardine 0.00874 x 0.7 = 0.00612. Sum = 0.00743. Posterior P(ilish | 25) = 0.00131 / 0.00743 = 0.177 and P(sardine | 25) = 0.823. Decide sardine, and the chance this decision is wrong is 0.177.

Moving along the length: at 26 cm the posterior of ilish becomes 0.472, still just below half, so we still say sardine. At 27 cm it jumps to 0.797, so we say ilish. The decision boundary is where the two posteriors are equal, near 26.1 cm. With equal priors (50-50) the boundary would sit at about 25.5 cm; the higher prior for sardine pushes the boundary towards the ilish side, giving sardine a wider region. This is a key lesson: priors move boundaries.

The likelihood ratio test: rewrite the rule as: decide ilish if p(x | ilish) / p(x | sardine) > P(sardine) / P(ilish). The left side is the likelihood ratio, which depends only on the measurement. The right side is a fixed threshold, here 0.7 / 0.3 = 2.33. At 26 cm the ratio is 2.09, below 2.33, so sardine. At 27 cm it is 9.14, far above, so ilish. This form is popular in signal detection, radar and biometrics because the threshold can be changed without touching the models.

Probability of error: at each x, P(error | x) = min of the two posteriors. At 25 cm it is 0.177, at 27 cm it is 1 - 0.797 = 0.203, and far from the boundary it drops to almost zero. Errors pile up near the boundary where the classes overlap. The total error rate is the overlapping area under the two curves p(x | wj) P(wj) on the wrong side of the boundary.

Worked total error, Bayes vs a hand-picked rule: with the boundary at 26.1 cm, ilish fall on the wrong side when they are shorter than 26.1 cm, which is about 1.3 percent of ilish; weighted by the prior 0.3 that is 0.0039. Sardines fall on the wrong side when longer than 26.1 cm, about 0.36 percent of sardines; weighted by 0.7 that is 0.0025. Total Bayes error = 0.0063, roughly 6 mistakes per 1,000 fish. Now try the "obvious" hand rule, ilish if longer than 30 cm. Almost no sardines are wrong, but about 10.6 percent of ilish are shorter than 30 cm, giving 0.3 x 0.106 = 0.032, about 32 mistakes per 1,000 fish, five times worse. Even the equal-prior boundary at 25.5 cm gives 0.0070, slightly worse than 0.0063. The Bayes boundary is not just one reasonable choice among many; it is the best one.

Being honest about uncertainty: a posterior of 0.82 and a posterior of 0.99 both lead to "sardine", but they are very different situations. A good system keeps the posterior, not just the label, so that later stages can act on it: send uncertain fish to a human, ask for a second measurement, or combine with other classifiers (lesson 25). The next lesson adds costs and a formal reject option.

The Bayes error: the error of the Bayes classifier is called the Bayes error rate. It is the floor: the lowest error any classifier using these features can achieve. Example: two classes with Gaussians of mean 0 and mean 2, both with standard deviation 1, and equal priors. The boundary is at 1, halfway. Each class has the part of its curve beyond 1 standard deviation on the wrong side, which is 15.9 percent. So the Bayes error is 0.159. If someone claims 2 percent error on this problem with these features, they are measuring wrongly (often testing on training data).

Decision regions: a decision rule divides the feature line into regions R1 (say ilish) and R2 (sardine). With different variances, as in our fish, the regions are not just "left of the boundary, right of the boundary". Mathematically the wider ilish curve also wins again very far on the left, at impossible negative lengths, so the ilish region R1 here is really two pieces. In real problems such extra pieces can appear at sensible values too, which is why Bayes regions are not always one simple interval.

Many classes: nothing changes with c classes. Compute p(x | wj) P(wj) for each and take the largest. For Bangla digit recognition c = 10, and the classifier picks the digit with the biggest posterior. With many features the densities become multivariate, as lesson 06 shows, but the rule is the same.

When Bayes is the target, not the tool: in reality we rarely know the true densities. So why study a rule we cannot apply directly? Because it tells us what to aim for. Every practical classifier, k-NN, linear discriminants, SVMs, neural networks, is trying to approximate the Bayes rule from finite data. And it tells us when to stop: if your error is already close to the Bayes error (estimated somehow), more model tuning will not help; you need better features.

Real-life example 1, sorting jute fibre: a jute mill in Narayanganj grades fibre as "top" or "standard" by a brightness reading. Last season 20 percent of bales were top grade. A new bale gives a brightness reading of 0.72; from records, p(0.72 | top) = 2.0 and p(0.72 | standard) = 0.4 (densities per unit brightness). Likelihood x prior: top 2.0 x 0.2 = 0.40, standard 0.4 x 0.8 = 0.32. Posterior of top = 0.40 / 0.72 = 0.56. Decide top, but with only 56 percent confidence; a sensible mill might also check by hand when the posterior is close to half.

Real-life example 2, rain or no rain for a cricket match: a forecaster at Sylhet stadium uses humidity as a feature. In October, the prior chance of afternoon rain is 0.2. If p(humidity 90 | rain) is 4 times p(humidity 90 | no rain), the likelihood ratio is 4, while the threshold is 0.8 / 0.2 = 4. Exactly on the boundary: a coin-flip day. If the season were July with a prior of 0.5, the threshold would be 1, and a ratio of 4 would clearly say rain. Same measurement, different decision, because the prior changed.

Common mistakes: forgetting priors and using maximum likelihood when classes are unbalanced; thinking the Bayes classifier has zero error (it has the least error, not none); dividing by evidence when comparing classes and then making arithmetic slips (you do not need it to decide); and drawing the boundary at the crossing of the plain densities p(x | wj) instead of the weighted ones p(x | wj) P(wj). Exams love: compute posteriors from given likelihoods and priors, find a boundary for two Gaussians with equal variance, write the likelihood ratio test, and explain why the Bayes rule minimises error.

Recap: Bayes decision theory chooses the class with the largest posterior, or equivalently the largest likelihood x prior. This rule minimises the probability of error, which is the Bayes error, the floor for given features. Priors shift boundaries, the likelihood ratio test is the same rule in another dress, and real classifiers are attempts to approximate this ideal from data.
key_points: Bayes rule: choose the class with the largest posterior P(wj | x), or equivalently largest p(x | wj) P(wj).
It minimises the probability of error because at each x the error is the posterior of the class not chosen.
With priors only, always choose the most common class; error = 1 - largest prior (0.30 in the fish example).
Worked: at 25 cm, P(ilish | x) = 0.177, so sardine; boundary near 26.1 cm with priors 0.3 and 0.7.
Likelihood ratio test: decide w1 if p(x|w1)/p(x|w2) > P(w2)/P(w1).
The Bayes error is the floor for given features; for N(0,1) vs N(2,1) with equal priors it is 0.159.
Bigger prior for a class widens its decision region.
lessons.tip: Draw the two curves p(x | w1) P(w1) and p(x | w2) P(w2) on the same axis every time. The boundary is where they cross, and the shaded overlap on the wrong sides is the error. One sketch answers half the questions.
lessons.task: Using a calculator or phone, redo the fish example at x = 24, 26 and 28 cm (means 35 and 18, standard deviations 4 and 3, priors 0.3 and 0.7). Then change the priors to 0.5 and 0.5 and see how the decision at 26 cm changes.

quiz.q: The Bayes minimum error rule chooses the class with the largest...
options: Posterior, or equivalently likelihood times prior
quiz.explain: Picking the largest posterior makes the error at each x as small as possible, and p(x) is the same for all classes.

quiz.q: If 70 percent of fish are sardines and you must decide without measuring, what is the lowest possible error rate?
quiz.explain: Always choose sardine; you are wrong only on the 30 percent that are ilish.

quiz.q: In the likelihood ratio test with P(w1) = 0.3 and P(w2) = 0.7, the threshold on p(x|w1)/p(x|w2) for deciding w1 is...
quiz.explain: The threshold is P(w2)/P(w1) = 0.7/0.3 = 2.33.

quiz.q: What does the Bayes error rate represent?
options: The error of the worst classifier
The lowest possible error for the given features and probabilities
Always zero when there is enough data
The error of maximum likelihood decisions
quiz.explain: No classifier using the same features can beat the Bayes error; only better features can lower it.

quiz.q: The prior of class w2 increases. What happens to its decision region?
options: It grows, the boundary moves towards w1
quiz.explain: A larger prior makes w2 win more often, so its region widens and the boundary shifts towards the other class.

lessons.title: Bayesian Decision Theory II: Risk, Loss and the Reject Option
lessons.content:
A security guard at a bank gate in Motijheel sees a man with a bulging bag. If the guard stops an innocent customer, the cost is a few minutes and an annoyed face. If he lets a robber through, the cost is enormous. So the guard stops people even when he thinks they are probably innocent. He is not trying to make the fewest mistakes; he is trying to make the cheapest mistakes. Last lesson's Bayes rule minimised the number of errors, treating every error as equally bad. Real life is rarely like that, and this lesson extends Bayes decision theory to unequal costs.

The problem with counting errors: in medicine, missing a dengue patient can lead to dangerous bleeding, while a false alarm costs an extra blood test. In fraud detection, blocking a real customer is annoying, letting fraud through loses money. In airport security, missing a weapon is far worse than an extra bag check. A rule that minimises error count treats all of these as equal, which is plainly wrong. We need a way to put costs into the decision.

Actions and states: in this more general theory we separate what is true from what we do. The true state is the class wj. The action ai is what we decide to do: "treat as dengue", "send home", or even "do a second test". Usually actions match classes one to one, but not always; refusing to decide is also an action, as we will see.

The loss function: a loss lambda(ai | wj) says how much it costs to take action ai when the true class is wj. We write all losses in a table called the loss matrix, rows for actions and columns for classes. The diagonal (correct decisions) usually has zero loss. Losses can be in money, time, risk points or any agreed unit; only their ratios matter for the decision.

Worked loss matrix for dengue: two classes, w1 = dengue, w2 = not dengue. Two actions, a1 = keep for monitoring and a2 = send home. Losses: keep a dengue patient, 0; keep a healthy patient, 1 (a wasted bed and test); send home a dengue patient, 10 (serious danger); send home a healthy patient, 0. So the loss matrix is [[0, 1], [10, 0]].

Conditional risk: for a given measurement x, the expected loss of an action is R(ai | x) = sum over j of lambda(ai | wj) P(wj | x). It is the average cost of doing ai, weighted by how likely each true class is. The Bayes decision rule in its general form says: take the action with the smallest conditional risk.

Worked conditional risk: a patient's tests give P(dengue | x) = 0.2 and P(not dengue | x) = 0.8. Risk of keeping: 0 x 0.2 + 1 x 0.8 = 0.8. Risk of sending home: 10 x 0.2 + 0 x 0.8 = 2.0. Keeping has lower risk, so keep the patient, even though dengue is only 20 percent likely. A minimum-error rule would have sent this patient home, because 0.8 is bigger than 0.2. The costs changed the decision.

The threshold this creates: keep when 1 x P(not dengue | x) < 10 x P(dengue | x). Since the two posteriors add to 1, this means P(dengue | x) > 1 / 11 = 0.091. So with these costs, any patient with more than about 9 percent dengue probability is kept. Change the cost of a miss from 10 to 3 and the threshold rises to 1 / 4 = 0.25. The costs set the threshold, and the threshold sets how cautious the system is.

The general two-class rule: decide w1 if (lambda21 - lambda11) P(w1 | x) > (lambda12 - lambda22) P(w2 | x), where lambdaij means the loss of deciding wi when the truth is wj. In likelihood ratio form: decide w1 if p(x | w1) / p(x | w2) > [(lambda12 - lambda22) / (lambda21 - lambda11)] x [P(w2) / P(w1)]. Notice the threshold now has two factors: one from priors, one from costs. Both push the boundary in the same simple way.

More than two actions, worked: add a third action, a3 = order an NS1 antigen test, which costs 0.5 whatever the truth (the test fee and a day of waiting), and assume it then settles the case. Risks for a patient with posterior p = P(dengue | x): keep = 1 x (1 - p), send home = 10 x p, test = 0.5. At p = 0.2: keep 0.8, home 2.0, test 0.5, so order the test. At p = 0.6: keep 0.4, home 6.0, test 0.5, so keep without testing. At p = 0.03: keep 0.97, home 0.3, test 0.5, so send home. Solving the inequalities, testing wins when 0.05 < p < 0.5. The decision line is now cut into three bands: send home, test, keep. This is how real clinical guidelines look: clear cases are decided at once, and the middle band gets more evidence.

The operating point: changing costs slides the threshold, and each threshold gives one pair of numbers, the detection rate and the false alarm rate. A system's "operating point" is the threshold you finally choose. The full curve of all possible pairs is the ROC curve (recapped in lesson 24). Bayes theory tells you which point on that curve is best once the costs and priors are agreed; arguing about the threshold is really arguing about the costs, and it is healthier to argue about them openly.

Bayes risk: the overall risk of a decision rule is the average of its conditional risk over all x, R = integral of R(alpha(x) | x) p(x) dx. Choosing the minimum conditional risk at every x makes the overall risk as small as possible, by the same argument as last lesson. That smallest overall risk is called the Bayes risk, the best achievable performance under those costs.

Zero-one loss gives back the old rule: if every wrong decision costs 1 and every right one costs 0, then R(ai | x) = 1 - P(wi | x). Minimising risk then means maximising the posterior, which is exactly the minimum error rule from lesson 04. So minimum error is just the special case where all mistakes are equally bad.

The reject option: sometimes the best action is "I am not sure, ask a human". Add an action a_reject with a fixed cost lambda_r, smaller than the cost of a wrong decision (1 under zero-one loss). The rule becomes: choose the class with the largest posterior if that posterior is at least 1 - lambda_r; otherwise reject. Worked: with lambda_r = 0.1, reject whenever the largest posterior is below 0.9. A cheque digit with posteriors (0.85 for 7, 0.15 for 1) is rejected and shown to a bank officer; one with (0.95, 0.05) is accepted automatically.

The reject trade-off: a smaller lambda_r means more rejections and fewer errors on the accepted samples. If lambda_r is 0, everything is rejected; if lambda_r is 0.5 or more in a two-class problem, nothing is rejected, because the largest posterior is always at least 0.5. Banks reading cheque amounts and post offices reading addresses use exactly this: let the machine handle the easy 90 percent and send the hard 10 percent to people.

When priors or costs are unknown, Neyman-Pearson: in radar, sonar and some medical screening, assigning a cost to a miss is hard, but we can say "no more than 5 percent false alarms". The Neyman-Pearson criterion fixes the false alarm rate and maximises the detection rate. Its solution is again a likelihood ratio test; only the threshold is chosen to hit the false alarm target. Worked: noise readings follow a Gaussian with mean 0 and sd 1, signal readings mean 2 and sd 1. To allow 5 percent false alarms, the threshold must be at 1.645 (only 5 percent of noise exceeds it). The detection rate is then the share of signal above 1.645, which is 63.9 percent. Allow 10 percent false alarms and the threshold drops to 1.28, raising detection to 76.4 percent. You cannot improve both at once with the same feature.

When priors may change, minimax: if a factory's mix of fish changes month to month and you do not know the priors, you can choose the rule whose worst-case risk over all possible priors is smallest. This is the minimax rule. It is cautious, never the best for any specific prior, but never terrible. It is useful when a system is deployed in places with unknown class balance, for example a disease test used in both low and high prevalence districts.

Real-life example 1, mobile wallet fraud: a wallet company estimates that letting a fraud through costs on average 8,000 taka, while wrongly blocking a genuine cash-out costs about 200 taka in support calls and lost goodwill. With zero loss for correct decisions, block when 8,000 x P(fraud | x) > 200 x P(genuine | x), which is P(fraud | x) > 200 / 8,200 = 0.024. So any cash-out with more than about 2.4 percent fraud probability is held for an OTP check. A posterior of 12 percent, like the new-device case from lesson 03, is held immediately.

Real-life example 2, cheque processing at a bank: an automated reader recognises handwritten amounts. Wrong reading cost: a full reconciliation, say 50 units of effort. Manual check cost: 3 units. Treating a wrong read as loss 1, the reject cost is lambda_r = 3 / 50 = 0.06, so accept only when the top posterior is at least 0.94. The bank tracks two numbers: the reject rate (how many cheques go to staff) and the error rate on accepted cheques, and tunes lambda_r when staff numbers change.

Where the numbers in the loss matrix come from: engineers do not invent them alone. Costs come from accountants (money lost per fraud), doctors (harm of a missed case), lawyers (penalties) and users (how many false blocks they tolerate before leaving). Writing them down forces these people to agree on what matters, which is often the most valuable part of the exercise.

Common mistakes: forgetting that only cost ratios matter, so multiplying all losses by 100 changes nothing; putting losses in the wrong cell (row is action, column is truth); assuming the reject option is free; and using minimum-error thresholds in settings like medicine where misses are much costlier. Exams usually give a 2 by 2 loss matrix and posteriors, ask for both conditional risks and the decision, ask for the posterior threshold, or ask you to explain Neyman-Pearson and the reject rule with a small number.

Recap: generalised Bayes decision theory minimises expected loss, not error count. Conditional risk R(ai | x) = sum of lambda(ai | wj) P(wj | x); take the action with the smallest. Costs and priors together set the threshold, zero-one loss gives back the minimum-error rule, the reject option hands hard cases to humans when the top posterior is below 1 - lambda_r, Neyman-Pearson fixes the false alarm rate, and minimax protects against unknown priors.
key_points: Loss lambda(ai | wj) is the cost of action ai when the truth is wj; only cost ratios matter.
Conditional risk R(ai | x) = sum over j of lambda(ai | wj) P(wj | x); choose the action with the smallest risk.
Dengue worked: posterior 0.2 and losses 1 vs 10 give risks 0.8 (keep) and 2.0 (send home), so keep.
Two-class threshold: keep if P(dengue | x) > 1/11 = 0.091; costs and priors both set the threshold.
Zero-one loss turns minimum risk back into the minimum-error (maximum posterior) rule.
Reject option: decide only if the top posterior is at least 1 - lambda_r; otherwise hand to a human.
Neyman-Pearson fixes the false alarm rate (5 percent gives threshold 1.645 and 63.9 percent detection in the worked case); minimax guards against unknown priors.
lessons.tip: Before computing any risk, write the loss matrix with "action" labels on the rows and "truth" labels on the columns. Half of all mistakes in risk questions come from reading the matrix the wrong way round.
lessons.task: Pick a decision you make often, such as "take an umbrella or not". Write a 2 by 2 loss matrix with your own costs (for example, carrying an umbrella for nothing costs 1, getting soaked costs 6). Work out the rain probability above which you should carry the umbrella.

quiz.q: With losses keep-healthy = 1, send-home-dengue = 10 (correct decisions cost 0), and P(dengue | x) = 0.2, what is the conditional risk of sending the patient home?
Under zero-one loss, minimising conditional risk is the same as...
options: Choosing the class with the largest prior
Choosing the class with the largest posterior
Choosing the class with the largest loss
quiz.explain: Under zero-one loss R(ai | x) = 1 - P(wi | x), so the smallest risk is the largest posterior.

quiz.q: With reject cost lambda_r = 0.1 under zero-one loss, a sample has posteriors 0.85 and 0.15. What should the system do?
options: Reject and send to a human
quiz.explain: Reject when the top posterior is below 1 - 0.1 = 0.9; 0.85 is below that.

quiz.q: What does the Neyman-Pearson criterion do?
options: Minimises the worst-case risk over all priors
Fixes the false alarm rate and maximises detection
quiz.explain: Neyman-Pearson keeps false alarms at a chosen level and, subject to that, detects as much as possible using a likelihood ratio threshold.

quiz.q: Multiplying every entry of the loss matrix by 100 changes the decisions how?
options: Not at all, only ratios of costs matter
It makes the classifier more cautious
quiz.explain: Scaling all losses by the same factor scales every risk equally, so the action with the smallest risk stays the same.

lessons.title: Discriminant Functions and the Gaussian Case
lessons.content:
At a cricket selection camp, each player gets a score from each selector, and whoever has the highest total gets the place. The selectors do not need to agree on the exact numbers, only on who comes out on top. A classifier can work the same way: give every class a score for the sample, and pick the class with the highest score. Those score-giving functions are called discriminant functions. In this lesson we see how the Bayes rule becomes a set of discriminant functions, and what the decision boundaries look like when the classes are Gaussian. This is where lines, ellipses and the Mahalanobis distance appear, and it explains why some classifiers draw straight boundaries and others draw curves.

What a discriminant function is: for c classes we define c functions g1(x), ..., gc(x). The classifier assigns x to class wi if gi(x) > gj(x) for every other j. That is all. The functions can be anything; the classifier is just "compute all the scores, take the biggest". This is a very general way to describe almost every classifier, from Bayes to neural networks, whose output layer gives one score per class.

Bayes as discriminants: the Bayes rule fits this form with gi(x) = P(wi | x). But we may replace each gi by any increasing function of it, f(gi), without changing which is biggest. So these all give the same decisions: gi(x) = P(wi | x); gi(x) = p(x | wi) P(wi) (drop the shared evidence); and gi(x) = ln p(x | wi) + ln P(wi) (take logs). The log form is the favourite because Gaussian densities contain exp, and the log cancels it, leaving simple algebra.

Two classes, the dichotomizer: with two classes we can use a single function g(x) = g1(x) - g2(x) and decide w1 if g(x) > 0, w2 otherwise. A classifier for two classes is called a dichotomizer. The decision boundary is the set of points where g(x) = 0. A handy form is g(x) = ln [p(x | w1) / p(x | w2)] + ln [P(w1) / P(w2)], which is just the log of the likelihood ratio test from lesson 04.

The Gaussian discriminant: if p(x | wi) is a multivariate Gaussian with mean mu_i and covariance Sigma_i, the log discriminant is gi(x) = -1/2 (x - mu_i)^T Sigma_i^-1 (x - mu_i) - d/2 ln 2 pi - 1/2 ln |Sigma_i| + ln P(wi). Read it as four parts: a squared distance from x to the class mean measured in that class's own spread, a constant, a penalty for classes with large spread, and the log prior. The shape of the boundary depends entirely on what the covariance matrices look like, and the classic textbook splits this into three cases.

Case 1, Sigma_i = sigma^2 I for every class: all features are independent with the same variance, so every class is a round cloud of the same size. The discriminant simplifies to gi(x) = -||x - mu_i||^2 / (2 sigma^2) + ln P(wi). With equal priors this says: assign x to the class with the nearest mean in Euclidean distance. This is the minimum distance classifier, also called the nearest mean or template classifier.

Case 1 is linear: expand ||x - mu_i||^2 = x.x - 2 mu_i.x + mu_i.mu_i. The x.x term is the same for every class, so drop it. What remains is gi(x) = (mu_i / sigma^2).x - mu_i.mu_i / (2 sigma^2) + ln P(wi), which is a linear function of x: a weight vector times x plus a constant. So the boundary between two classes is a straight line (a hyperplane in higher dimensions). It is perpendicular to the line joining the two means.

Case 1 worked: class 1 has mean (0, 0), class 2 has mean (4, 0), sigma^2 = 1. With equal priors the boundary is the perpendicular bisector, the vertical line x1 = 2. A sample at (2.2, 1) is at distance 2.42 from mean 1 and 2.06 from mean 2, so it goes to class 2. Now set P(w1) = 0.8 and P(w2) = 0.2. The discriminants are g1 = ln 0.8 = -0.223 (the mean term is zero) and g2 = 4 x1 - 8 + ln 0.2 = 4 x1 - 9.609. At x1 = 2.2, g2 = -0.809, which is less than -0.223, so the sample now goes to class 1. Setting g1 = g2 gives the new boundary x1 = 2.35. The general formula moves the boundary along the line of means by sigma^2 / ||mu1 - mu2|| x ln(P1 / P2) = (1 / 4) x 1.386 = 0.35 units, away from the more likely class.

How priors and spread interact: the shift is proportional to sigma^2 and inversely proportional to the squared distance between the means. When classes are far apart compared with their spread, priors hardly move the boundary, because the measurement is decisive. When classes are close or very spread out, priors move it a lot, because the measurement says little and the prior has to do more of the work.

Case 2, all classes share the same Sigma: now clouds are ellipses, all with the same size, shape and tilt, but at different centres. The terms -1/2 ln |Sigma| and the quadratic part x^T Sigma^-1 x are the same for every class and drop out, so the discriminant is again linear: gi(x) = (Sigma^-1 mu_i).x - 1/2 mu_i^T Sigma^-1 mu_i + ln P(wi). The boundaries are still straight, but now they are generally not perpendicular to the line between the means; they tilt to follow the shape of the clouds. This is the model behind classical Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA).

The Mahalanobis distance: in case 2 with equal priors, assign x to the class whose mean is nearest in Mahalanobis distance, r^2 = (x - mu)^T Sigma^-1 (x - mu). It measures distance in units of the spread along each direction. If a cloud is wide in one direction, a step in that direction counts for less; if narrow, a step counts for more.

Mahalanobis worked, axis-aligned: let Sigma = [[4, 0], [0, 1]] and the mean (0, 0). The point (2, 0) is 2 units away in Euclidean terms, but along a direction with variance 4 (sd 2), so r^2 = 4 / 4 = 1 and r = 1. The point (0, 2) is also 2 units away, but along a direction with variance 1, so r = 2. Same Euclidean distance, but (0, 2) is twice as "unusual".

Mahalanobis worked, tilted: let Sigma = [[2, 1], [1, 2]], whose inverse is (1/3) [[2, -1], [-1, 2]]. For the point (1, 1): r^2 = (1/3)(2 - 1 - 1 + 2) = 2/3, r = 0.82. For (1, -1): r^2 = (1/3)(2 + 1 + 1 + 2) = 2, r = 1.41. Both are Euclidean distance 1.41 from the mean, yet (1, 1) lies along the direction in which the data naturally stretch (both features rising together), so it is much more typical.

Case 3, arbitrary Sigma_i: when each class has its own covariance, nothing cancels. The discriminant keeps the quadratic term x^T Sigma_i^-1 x, so gi is a quadratic function of x, and the boundaries are quadratic curves: ellipses, parabolas, hyperbolas, or pairs of lines in 2D, called hyperquadrics in general. This is Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA). It is more flexible, but each class needs its own covariance matrix estimated from data, which needs more samples.

Case 3 worked in 1D: class 1 is Gaussian with mean 0 and sd 1, class 2 has mean 0 and sd 2, equal priors. g1(x) = -x^2 / 2 - ln 1 and g2(x) = -x^2 / 8 - ln 2 (constants shared by both are dropped). Class 1 wins when -x^2 / 2 > -x^2 / 8 - 0.693, which simplifies to 3x^2 / 8 < 0.693, so x^2 < 1.85 and |x| < 1.36. Check: at x = 1.36 both densities equal 0.158. So class 1 owns the middle interval from -1.36 to 1.36 and class 2 owns both outer parts. Two boundaries from one quadratic, something no linear classifier can do.

Choosing the case in practice: case 1 has the fewest parameters (just the means and one variance) and is robust with little data, but ignores correlation and unequal spreads. Case 2 handles correlation with one shared covariance, d(d+1)/2 numbers. Case 3 needs one covariance per class, c x d(d+1)/2 numbers; with d = 50 features that is 1,275 numbers per class, far too many for a few hundred samples. A common compromise is to use case 2, or to shrink each class's covariance towards a shared one (regularised discriminant analysis).

From theory to a working classifier: in this lesson the means and covariances were simply given. In practice we estimate them from labelled samples, the sample mean of each class and its sample covariance, and then plug those estimates into the discriminant formulas. This is called a plug-in classifier. How to estimate well, and what goes wrong with little data, is the subject of the next two lessons.

Real-life example 1, sorting rice grains: a rice mill in Dinajpur grades grains as whole or broken using length and width from a camera. Whole and broken grains have similar width spread but very different length, and length and width are correlated in a similar way in both groups. A shared-covariance (case 2) classifier fits well and gives a straight, slightly tilted boundary in the length-width plane. It is fast enough to judge thousands of grains per minute on a cheap computer.

Real-life example 2, detecting a faulty transformer: a power company monitors temperature and vibration of transformers. Healthy ones sit in a tight cluster; faulty ones are scattered widely in many directions because they fail in different ways. The covariances are very different, so case 3 (QDA) is natural: the healthy region becomes a closed ellipse and everything outside it is flagged, just like the middle interval in the 1D example.

Common mistakes: thinking Gaussian classes always give curved boundaries (only with unequal covariances); forgetting the ln P(wi) term so the boundary sits exactly at the midpoint even with unequal priors; computing Mahalanobis distance with the covariance instead of its inverse; and using QDA with too little data, which gives wild, overfitted curves. Exams ask you to identify the case from given covariances, write the discriminant, find a boundary point for case 1 with unequal priors, compute a Mahalanobis distance, and explain why case 3 is quadratic.

Recap: a classifier can be written as a set of discriminant functions, one score per class. For Gaussian classes the log discriminant leads to three cases: equal round clouds give the minimum distance classifier with straight perpendicular boundaries; a shared covariance gives the Mahalanobis rule and straight tilted boundaries (LDA); class-specific covariances give quadratic boundaries (QDA). More flexibility needs more data.
key_points: A discriminant function gives each class a score; choose the class with the highest score.
Any increasing transform keeps decisions, so the log form gi = ln p(x|wi) + ln P(wi) is used for Gaussians.
Case Sigma = sigma^2 I: minimum (Euclidean) distance classifier, linear boundary perpendicular to the line of means.
Worked: means (0,0) and (4,0), sigma^2 = 1, priors 0.8 and 0.2 move the boundary from x1 = 2 to 2.35.
Shared Sigma: Mahalanobis distance r^2 = (x - mu)^T Sigma^-1 (x - mu) and linear, tilted boundaries (LDA).
Class-specific Sigma_i: quadratic boundaries (QDA); 1D worked sd 1 vs sd 2 gives class 1 for |x| < 1.36.
More flexible cases need many more parameters, so they need more data.
lessons.tip: When you meet a Gaussian classifier question, first look only at the covariance matrices: all equal and round, all equal, or all different. That single look tells you whether to expect nearest-mean, straight tilted lines, or curves.
lessons.task: On graph paper mark two class means, (0, 0) and (4, 0). Draw the equal-prior boundary. Then compute the shifted boundary for priors 0.8 and 0.2 and for 0.95 and 0.05 (use ln 19 = 2.94). How far does each move?

quiz.q: When all classes have covariance sigma^2 I and equal priors, the Bayes classifier becomes...
options: A minimum Euclidean distance (nearest mean) classifier
quiz.explain: With equal round clouds, the log discriminant reduces to minus the squared distance to each mean.

quiz.q: Which case gives quadratic decision boundaries?
options: Each class has its own covariance matrix
All classes share one covariance matrix
quiz.explain: When covariances differ, the quadratic term x^T Sigma_i^-1 x does not cancel, so boundaries are quadratic.

quiz.q: With Sigma = [[4, 0], [0, 1]] and mean (0, 0), what is the Mahalanobis distance of (2, 0)?
quiz.explain: r^2 = 2^2 / 4 = 1, so r = 1, because that direction has variance 4.

quiz.q: In case 1 with means (0,0) and (4,0), the prior of class 1 rises from 0.5 to 0.8. The boundary...
options: Moves away from class 1's mean, to about x1 = 2.35
quiz.explain: A larger prior gives class 1 a bigger region, so the boundary moves towards class 2.

quiz.q: Why is the log form of the discriminant popular for Gaussian classes?
options: The log cancels the exp in the Gaussian, leaving simple algebra
It removes the need for priors
quiz.explain: Log is increasing, so decisions stay the same, and it turns the exponential into a quadratic expression that is easy to analyse.

lessons.title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation
lessons.content:
Your friend says her coin is fair. You toss it 20 times and get 7 heads. Is the coin really fair, or does it land heads about 35 percent of the time? Your gut answer, "it looks like 7 out of 20, so 0.35", is the maximum likelihood estimate. This lesson explains why that gut answer is principled, how to get it for the Gaussian, and where it goes wrong. It matters because the Bayes classifier of lessons 04 to 06 needs priors, means and covariances, and in real life nobody hands them to us. We must estimate them from labelled samples.

The problem: Bayes decision theory assumes we know P(wj) and p(x | wj). In practice we have a training set: a few hundred fish with lengths and labels, a few thousand digits with pixels and labels. The design question becomes: from these samples, what are the best numbers to plug into the classifier? Priors are easy, just the class proportions (if the training set was sampled fairly). The class-conditional densities are harder.

The parametric approach: one strategy is to assume the shape of each density and estimate only a few numbers. For example, assume ilish lengths are Gaussian; then only the mean and variance are unknown. This turns an impossible problem (learn a whole curve) into an easy one (learn two numbers). The cost is that if the assumed shape is wrong, the estimates may be misleading. Lesson 10 shows the non-parametric alternative that makes no shape assumption.

Parameters and the likelihood: call the unknown numbers theta (for a Gaussian, theta = (mu, sigma^2)). Given samples x1, ..., xn drawn independently from the same density, the likelihood is L(theta) = p(x1 | theta) x p(x2 | theta) x ... x p(xn | theta). It answers: if the true parameters were theta, how probable (or how dense) would our observed data be? Maximum likelihood estimation picks the theta that makes the observed data most probable.

Likelihood vs probability: the formula looks like a probability, but we read it differently. A probability fixes theta and asks about data. A likelihood fixes the data (it has already happened) and asks how well each theta explains it. The likelihood is not a probability distribution over theta; it does not have to add up to 1 across thetas. That difference becomes important in the next lesson, where we do treat theta as random.

The log-likelihood: multiplying hundreds of small numbers produces values so tiny that computers round them to zero. So we take logs: ln L(theta) = sum of ln p(xk | theta). Because ln is increasing, the theta that maximises ln L also maximises L. Sums are also easier to differentiate than products.
