To find the maximum, set the derivative (or gradient) of ln L to zero and solve.

MLE for a coin, worked: let p be the probability of heads. With k heads in n tosses, L(p) = p^k (1 - p)^(n - k). With k = 7 and n = 20, compare: at p = 0.30, L = 2.12 x 10^-6; at p = 0.35, L = 2.38 x 10^-6; at p = 0.40, L = 2.14 x 10^-6; at p = 0.50, L = 0.95 x 10^-6. The peak is at 0.35. Calculus confirms it: ln L = k ln p + (n - k) ln(1 - p), derivative k/p - (n - k)/(1 - p) = 0, so p = k / n = 7 / 20 = 0.35. The fair coin p = 0.5 explains the data less than half as well as 0.35.

MLE for class priors: the same reasoning gives the prior estimate P(wj) = nj / n, the share of training samples in class j. If 300 of 1,000 labelled fish are ilish, P(ilish) = 0.3. This is only valid if the training set was collected in the same proportions as the real world. If the factory deliberately collected 500 ilish and 500 sardines to have balanced data, the 0.5 estimate is wrong for deployment and you must use the real-world rate instead.

MLE for the Gaussian mean: for samples from a Gaussian with unknown mu and known sigma, ln L = -sum (xk - mu)^2 / (2 sigma^2) + constant. Maximising means minimising the sum of squared differences, and the derivative gives mu = (1/n) sum xk: the sample mean. Worked: five ilish lengths 32, 36, 38, 34 and 40 cm give mu = 180 / 5 = 36 cm. The average you have used since school is the maximum likelihood estimate.

MLE for the Gaussian variance: with mu also unknown, the MLE of the variance is sigma^2 = (1/n) sum (xk - mu)^2, using the sample mean. Worked: deviations from 36 are -4, 0, 2, -2, 4; squares 16, 0, 4, 4, 16; sum 40; divided by 5 gives 8, so sigma is about 2.83 cm.

The bias of the variance estimate: on average, the MLE variance comes out slightly too small. The reason: the sample mean is computed from the same data, so it sits closer to the data points than the true mean would, making the squared deviations a bit smaller. The expected value of the MLE is (n - 1)/n times the true variance. The fix is to divide by n - 1 instead of n, giving the unbiased sample variance: 40 / 4 = 10 in our example. With 5 samples the gap is big (8 vs 10); with 1,000 samples it hardly matters. Both are "correct" answers to different questions: MLE maximises likelihood, the n - 1 version is unbiased.

Multivariate Gaussian: for d-dimensional samples the same results hold. The MLE of the mean vector is the average of the sample vectors, and the MLE of the covariance matrix is (1/n) sum (xk - mu)(xk - mu)^T, the average outer product of deviations. You computed exactly this in lesson 03 for four points, getting mean (4, 5) and covariance [[5, 5.5], [5.5, 6.5]]. That was MLE.

The plug-in classifier: estimate each class's prior, mean and covariance by MLE from its training samples, then plug them into the Gaussian discriminants of lesson 06. This is the classic way to build an LDA or QDA classifier. For LDA (shared covariance), pool the deviations of all classes, each from its own class mean, to estimate the one shared matrix.

Plug-in classifier worked: training data gives ilish lengths 32, 36, 38, 34, 40 (MLE mean 36, variance 8) and sardine lengths 17, 19, 18, 16, 20 (mean 18, variance 2). Use priors 0.3 and 0.7 from the belt. For a 24 cm fish: the ilish density is 0.0000174 and the sardine density 0.0000348; times priors, 0.0000052 vs 0.0000244, so the posterior of ilish is 0.18 and we say sardine. At 26 cm the ilish posterior is already above 0.999. The boundary lands near 24.3 cm. Notice how sharp the change is: with only five samples per class, the estimated sardine variance of 2 is tiny, so the model is very sure that a sardine is never longer than about 22 cm. Is that really true of sardines, or just of these five? With so few samples we cannot tell, which is the overconfidence problem described below.

Good properties of MLE: as n grows, the MLE converges to the true value (it is consistent). For large n, no other unbiased estimator has smaller variance (it is asymptotically efficient). And it is invariant: if the MLE of sigma^2 is 8, the MLE of sigma is the square root, 2.83. These properties are why MLE is the default method throughout statistics and machine learning; training a logistic regression or a neural network with cross-entropy loss is maximum likelihood in disguise.

MLE beyond the Gaussian: the recipe works for any assumed family. For waiting times modelled by an exponential density, the MLE of the rate is 1 divided by the average wait. For counts like "SMS per hour" modelled by a Poisson, the MLE of the rate is the average count. When no neat formula exists, as in mixture models (lesson 22) or neural networks, we maximise the log-likelihood numerically with gradient methods or with the EM algorithm.

Where MLE goes wrong, small data: with one sample, the MLE variance is 0: the model believes every future fish will be exactly that length, and the density becomes an infinitely tall spike. With 3 heads in 3 tosses, the MLE says the coin always lands heads, p = 1. With few samples and many features, a covariance matrix estimated by MLE may be singular (cannot be inverted), which breaks the Gaussian discriminant: you need at least d + 1 samples per class for a d-dimensional covariance to be invertible, and in practice many more. This overconfidence with little data is overfitting, and the next lesson shows how a prior tames it.

Where MLE goes wrong, wrong model: MLE finds the best parameters within the assumed family. If ilish lengths actually have two humps (jatka and adults), the best single Gaussian sits between the humps, where few fish really are. The fit is the "best" Gaussian, yet a poor description of reality. Always look at a histogram before trusting a parametric model.

Real-life example 1, estimating a shop's daily customers: a tea stall owner in Mirpur counts customers for five mornings: 42, 38, 45, 40, 35. Assuming a Gaussian, MLE gives a mean of 40 and a variance of (4 + 4 + 25 + 0 + 25) / 5 = 11.6, sd about 3.4. She now knows that about 95 percent of mornings should have between roughly 33 and 47 customers, and can buy enough milk and sugar without much waste.

Real-life example 2, a speech recogniser's vowel models: a speech system for Bangla models the sound "aa" by a Gaussian over a few acoustic features, estimated by MLE from thousands of recorded examples. With plenty of data the estimates are excellent. For a rare sound in a regional dialect with only 20 examples, the MLE covariance is unreliable, so engineers borrow strength from similar sounds, a practical version of the Bayesian ideas in the next lesson.

Common mistakes: confusing likelihood with probability of the parameter; forgetting to take logs and then getting zero from underflow; using the unbiased n - 1 formula and calling it the MLE (or vice versa) without saying which; estimating priors from a deliberately balanced training set; and trusting MLE with very little data. Exams usually ask you to derive the MLE of a Bernoulli or Gaussian parameter, compute the sample mean and both variance versions for five numbers, explain why the MLE variance is biased, and state when MLE overfits.

Recap: maximum likelihood chooses the parameters that make the observed data most probable. Take logs, differentiate, set to zero. For a coin it gives k/n, for priors class proportions, for a Gaussian the sample mean and the (1/n) variance, which is slightly biased. MLE is consistent and widely used, but it overfits with little data and cannot fix a wrong model shape.
key_points: Likelihood L(theta) = product of p(xk | theta); MLE picks theta that maximises it, usually via the log-likelihood.
Coin worked: 7 heads in 20 tosses gives p = 7/20 = 0.35, which beats p = 0.5 by more than double.
Priors by MLE are class proportions nj/n, valid only if the training set matches real-world proportions.
Gaussian MLE: mean = sample average (36 for 32, 36, 38, 34, 40); variance = (1/n) sum of squares (8).
The MLE variance is biased low by (n - 1)/n; dividing by n - 1 gives the unbiased value (10).
Plug-in classifier: estimate priors, means and covariances by MLE, then use lesson 06 discriminants.
MLE overfits with little data (zero variance, p = 1, singular covariance) and cannot fix a wrong model shape.
lessons.tip: For any MLE derivation, follow the same four steps every time: write the likelihood as a product, take the log to make a sum, differentiate with respect to the parameter, set to zero and solve. Once the steps are automatic, every MLE question looks the same.
lessons.task: Toss a coin (or a bottle cap) 20 times and record heads. Compute the MLE of p. Then compute p^k (1 - p)^(n - k) for p = 0.3, 0.5 and your MLE on a calculator and confirm that your MLE gives the biggest value.

quiz.q: You get 7 heads in 20 tosses. What is the maximum likelihood estimate of the probability of heads?
quiz.explain: The MLE for a Bernoulli parameter is k/n = 7/20 = 0.35.

quiz.q: Why do we usually maximise the log-likelihood instead of the likelihood?
options: It turns a product into a sum, avoids underflow, and has the same maximum
It gives a different and better answer
Logs remove the need for data
quiz.explain: The log is increasing, so the maximiser is the same, and sums are easier to handle than products of tiny numbers.

quiz.q: For lengths 32, 36, 38, 34, 40, what is the MLE of the variance?
quiz.explain: Squared deviations from 36 sum to 40; dividing by n = 5 gives 8. Dividing by 4 gives the unbiased 10.

quiz.q: A factory collected 500 ilish and 500 sardines for training, but on the belt only 30 percent are ilish. What prior should the deployed classifier use for ilish?
quiz.explain: Priors must reflect where the classifier will be used; the balanced training set does not represent the belt.

quiz.q: With only one training sample, what does the MLE of a Gaussian's variance become?
quiz.explain: With one sample the deviation from the sample mean is zero, so the MLE variance is 0, a clear case of overfitting.

lessons.title: Bayesian Parameter Estimation and MAP
lessons.content:
A new student joins your class and scores 100 in the first maths quiz. Do you now believe she will score 100 in every quiz forever? Of course not. You know most students score somewhere around 60 to 80, so you think "she is probably very good, maybe around 85 or 90, but one quiz is not enough to say 100". You blended what you already believed about students in general with the new evidence. That blend is Bayesian parameter estimation, and it is the cure for the overconfidence of maximum likelihood with small data that we saw in the last lesson.

The problem it solves: MLE uses only the data. With 3 heads in 3 tosses it says the coin always lands heads; with one fish it says the variance is zero. In pattern recognition we often have little data for some classes: a rare disease, a rare fraud type, a regional dialect. We need a principled way to say "the data suggest this, but let us not jump to extremes".

The key idea, parameters are random too: in MLE, the parameter theta is a fixed unknown number. In the Bayesian view, we describe our uncertainty about theta with a probability distribution. Before seeing data, this is the prior p(theta). After seeing data D, Bayes' rule gives the posterior p(theta | D) = p(D | theta) p(theta) / p(D). The same Bayes' rule we used for classes, now applied to parameters.

Reading the formula: p(D | theta) is the likelihood from the last lesson, how well theta explains the data. p(theta) is the prior, what we believed beforehand. Their product, normalised, is the posterior. Where the likelihood and the prior agree, the posterior is high. With little data the prior has a strong voice; with lots of data the likelihood dominates and the prior hardly matters.

A prior for a probability, the Beta distribution: for a coin's head probability p (between 0 and 1), the convenient prior is the Beta distribution, Beta(a, b), whose density is proportional to p^(a - 1) (1 - p)^(b - 1). Think of a - 1 and b - 1 as imaginary heads and tails you have "already seen" before the experiment. Beta(1, 1) is flat: no opinion at all. Beta(2, 2) gently prefers values near 0.5, like having seen one head and one tail. Beta(20, 20) strongly believes the coin is near fair.

Conjugacy, why Beta is convenient: multiply a Beta(a, b) prior by the Bernoulli likelihood p^k (1 - p)^(n - k) and you get p^(a + k - 1) (1 - p)^(b + n - k - 1), which is again a Beta: Beta(a + k, b + n - k). The posterior has the same form as the prior, with the counts simply added. A prior with this property is called conjugate to the likelihood. It makes Bayesian updating as easy as adding numbers.

Worked, 3 heads in 3 tosses: prior Beta(2, 2). Posterior Beta(2 + 3, 2 + 0) = Beta(5, 2). Its peak (the MAP estimate) is (a - 1) / (a + b - 2) = 4 / 5 = 0.8. Its mean is a / (a + b) = 5 / 7 = 0.71. Compare MLE = 3 / 3 = 1. The Bayesian answer says "probably biased towards heads, but not certainly always heads", which is far more sensible after only three tosses.

Worked, rainy days at a new weather station: a new station in Sunamganj records rain on 9 of its first 10 days in July. The MLE is 0.9. But meteorologists know nearby stations see rain on about 60 percent of July days, and they encode this as a prior Beta(6, 4), worth about 10 imaginary days with 6 rainy. Posterior: Beta(6 + 9, 4 + 1) = Beta(15, 5). Posterior mean = 15 / 20 = 0.75; MAP = 14 / 18 = 0.78. The estimate moves strongly towards the data (from 0.6 to 0.75) but not all the way to 0.9. After 100 days of data, the prior's 10 imaginary days would barely matter.

MAP estimation: often we want one number, not a whole distribution. The maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate is the theta with the highest posterior: theta_MAP = argmax p(D | theta) p(theta). In log form: maximise ln p(D | theta) + ln p(theta). It is MLE plus a penalty term from the prior. With a flat prior, MAP equals MLE.

Laplace smoothing is MAP: the classic fix for zero counts, estimate (k + 1) / (n + 2) instead of k / n, is exactly the MAP estimate with a Beta(2, 2) prior, and also the posterior mean with a flat Beta(1, 1) prior. For 3 heads in 3 tosses it gives 4 / 5 = 0.8, matching our worked example. In naive Bayes text classifiers (deep-cse-6-1-16 and the next lesson) this stops one unseen word from making a whole class impossible.

Regularisation is MAP: in machine learning, ridge (L2) regularisation adds lambda times the sum of squared weights to the loss. That is exactly MAP with a Gaussian prior centred at zero on each weight: the prior says "weights are probably small". Lasso (L1) corresponds to a Laplace prior. So when you met regularisation in deep-cse-6-1-10, you were already doing Bayesian estimation without the name.

The Gaussian mean with known variance: suppose data come from a Gaussian with known variance sigma^2 and unknown mean mu, and our prior for mu is Gaussian with mean mu0 and variance s0^2. The posterior for mu is also Gaussian (Gaussian is conjugate to itself for the mean), with mean (n s0^2 xbar + sigma^2 mu0) / (n s0^2 + sigma^2) and variance s0^2 sigma^2 / (n s0^2 + sigma^2), where xbar is the sample mean. The posterior mean is a weighted average of the prior mean and the sample mean.

Worked, the tea stall again: from other stalls in the area, the owner believes a typical stall gets about mu0 = 50 customers a morning, with uncertainty s0 = 5 (variance 25). Daily counts vary with sigma = 4 (variance 16). After 5 mornings with average 40: posterior mean = (5 x 25 x 40 + 16 x 50) / (5 x 25 + 16) = 5,800 / 141 = 41.1, posterior variance 400 / 141 = 2.84. After only 1 morning at 40: posterior mean = (25 x 40 + 16 x 50) / 41 = 43.9. After 50 mornings: 40.1. The estimate shrinks towards the prior when data are few and follows the data when data are many.

Full Bayesian prediction: MAP picks one theta, but the fully Bayesian approach keeps the whole posterior and averages over it when predicting: p(x | D) = integral of p(x | theta) p(theta | D) d theta. For the Gaussian mean case, the predictive density for the next sample is Gaussian with mean equal to the posterior mean and variance sigma^2 + posterior variance. For the tea stall after 5 days: variance 16 + 2.84 = 18.84, sd 4.34, slightly wider than the 4 we would use if we pretended mu were known exactly. The extra width honestly reflects our remaining uncertainty about the mean.

Learning one step at a time: Bayesian updating is naturally incremental. Today's posterior becomes tomorrow's prior. If the Sunamganj station sees rain on day 11, Beta(15, 5) simply becomes Beta(16, 5), mean 16 / 21 = 0.76; a dry day 12 makes it Beta(16, 6), mean 0.73. You never need to store the old days, only the two counts. Feeding all the data at once or one sample at a time gives exactly the same final posterior, which makes this ideal for systems that receive data as a stream.

Using it inside a classifier: for classification, each class gets its own parameter posterior from its own training samples. The Bayes classifier then uses the predictive densities p(x | wi, D) in place of the true p(x | wi). Classes with lots of data behave like plug-in MLE; classes with little data get wider, more cautious densities, which is exactly what we want for rare classes.

MLE vs MAP vs full Bayesian: MLE is simplest and fine with lots of data. MAP adds a prior, still gives one number, and is cheap; it is how regularisation and smoothing work. Full Bayesian keeps all uncertainty and gives the most honest predictions, but the integral is often hard, needing approximations or sampling. As the number of samples grows, all three usually converge to the same answer.

Choosing the prior: a prior can come from previous studies, from similar classes, from physical knowledge (lengths are positive), or from a deliberate preference for simple models (small weights). A weak prior (few imaginary samples) lets data speak quickly; a strong prior needs lots of data to overrule it. A prior that is confidently wrong can mislead, so with important decisions you should check how sensitive the result is to the prior.

Real-life example 1, a new shop's fraud rate: a mobile-wallet company opens agent points in a new upazila. The first agent has 0 frauds in 40 transactions. MLE says the fraud rate is 0, which is certainly too optimistic. Using the company-wide experience as a prior, Beta(2, 198) (about 1 fraud per 100), the posterior is Beta(2, 238), mean 2 / 240 = 0.0083. The agent looks slightly better than average, but not magically perfect, and monitoring continues at a sensible level.

Real-life example 2, rating a new restaurant: a food app in Dhaka shows a new restaurant with two ratings, both 5 stars. Sorting by plain average (an MLE) would put it above a restaurant with 2,000 ratings averaging 4.6. Many apps instead shrink new restaurants towards the city-wide average, say 4.0, using a few imaginary ratings. With five imaginary 4-star ratings, the new place shows (2 x 5 + 5 x 4) / 7 = 4.29, below the established 4.6 until more real ratings arrive.

Common mistakes: thinking Bayesian estimation ignores data (it combines data and prior); choosing a very strong prior without justification; mixing up MAP (the peak) and the posterior mean (the average), which differ for skewed posteriors like Beta(5, 2); forgetting that with a flat prior MAP equals MLE; and believing the prior matters forever (it fades as data grow). Exams ask you to update a Beta prior with counts and give the MAP and the mean, to compute the posterior mean of a Gaussian mean, to show that Laplace smoothing is MAP, and to compare MLE and Bayesian estimation.

Recap: Bayesian estimation treats parameters as random, with a prior that Bayes' rule turns into a posterior using the data. Conjugate priors (Beta for probabilities, Gaussian for means) make the update simple: add counts, or take a weighted average. MAP is the posterior peak and equals MLE plus a prior penalty; Laplace smoothing and regularisation are MAP. Full Bayesian prediction averages over the posterior and is the most honest. With little data the prior protects you; with lots of data the data take over.
key_points: Bayesian estimation treats theta as random: posterior p(theta | D) is proportional to p(D | theta) p(theta).
Beta prior with Bernoulli data is conjugate: Beta(a, b) plus k heads in n gives Beta(a + k, b + n - k).
Worked: 3 heads in 3 tosses, prior Beta(2, 2) gives MAP 0.8 and mean 0.71, while MLE says 1.
MAP = argmax of log-likelihood + log prior; a flat prior makes MAP equal MLE.
Laplace smoothing (k + 1)/(n + 2) and L2 regularisation are MAP estimates.
Gaussian mean posterior is a weighted average of prior mean and sample mean: tea stall 50 and 40 give 41.1 after 5 days.
Full Bayesian prediction averages over the posterior and widens the predictive spread to reflect uncertainty.
lessons.tip: Think of a Beta(a, b) prior as "a - 1 imaginary heads and b - 1 imaginary tails". Then every Bayesian coin question becomes simple addition of real and imaginary counts.
lessons.task: Find a new shop or app on your phone with very few ratings. Compute its plain average, then a shrunk average that adds five imaginary ratings equal to the overall average of its category. Compare its rank before and after shrinking.

quiz.q: A Beta(2, 2) prior is updated with 3 heads and 0 tails. What is the posterior?
quiz.explain: Add heads to a and tails to b: Beta(2 + 3, 2 + 0) = Beta(5, 2).

quiz.q: Which statement about MAP and MLE is true?
options: MAP and MLE are always different
With a flat prior, MAP equals MLE
MLE uses a prior, MAP does not
quiz.explain: MAP maximises likelihood times prior; with a constant prior that is the same as maximising the likelihood.

quiz.q: Laplace smoothing (k + 1)/(n + 2) corresponds to...
options: The MAP estimate with a Beta(2, 2) prior
A Gaussian prior on the variance
quiz.explain: The Beta(2, 2) prior adds one imaginary head and one imaginary tail, giving the MAP (k + 1)/(n + 2).

quiz.q: In the tea stall example, what happens to the posterior mean as the number of mornings grows large?
options: It stays at the prior mean 50
It becomes the average of 50 and 40 forever
It approaches the sample mean, about 40
quiz.explain: The weight on the data grows with n, so with many samples the posterior mean follows the sample mean.

quiz.q: How does ridge (L2) regularisation relate to Bayesian estimation?
options: It is MAP with a zero-centred Gaussian prior on the weights
It is the MLE with no prior
quiz.explain: Adding lambda times squared weights to the loss equals adding minus a Gaussian log prior that prefers small weights.

lessons.title: Naive Bayes and Bayesian Belief Networks
lessons.content:
A mango seller in Rajshahi judges ripeness by pressing the skin, smelling it and looking at the colour. She does not keep a mental table of every possible combination of softness, smell and colour; she just asks, one feature at a time, "does this look like a ripe one?" and adds up the impressions. That habit, treating each clue separately and combining them, is the idea behind the naive Bayes classifier. It is wrong in theory and surprisingly good in practice. In this lesson we look at why, and then at Bayesian belief networks, which let us describe exactly which features depend on which.

The problem, too many combinations: Bayes needs p(x | w), the joint density of all d features for each class. Suppose every feature is just yes or no. With 20 yes/no features, there are 2^20 = 1,048,576 combinations, so a full table needs 1,048,575 probabilities per class. With 30 features, over a billion. No training set is large enough to fill such tables; most combinations would never be seen even once. We need a simplifying assumption.

The naive assumption: assume the features are conditionally independent given the class: p(x1, ..., xd | w) = p(x1 | w) x p(x2 | w) x ... x p(xd | w). Inside one class, knowing one feature tells you nothing more about another. With 20 yes/no features this needs only 20 probabilities per class instead of over a million. Each one is easy to estimate from data, just a count.

Conditional vs plain independence: the assumption is not that features are independent overall. Softness and sweetness of mangoes are clearly related overall, because ripe mangoes are both soft and sweet. The assumption is that within ripe mangoes alone, softness tells you nothing extra about sweetness, and likewise within unripe ones. That is often roughly true when the class is the main cause of both features, and often false when features share another cause.

The naive Bayes classifier: decide the class maximising P(w) x product of p(xi | w), or in logs, ln P(w) + sum of ln p(xi | w). Each feature casts a log "vote" for each class, and the votes are added. Training means estimating P(w) and each p(xi | w) separately, usually by counting (for yes/no or category features) or by fitting a 1D Gaussian per feature per class (for numeric features). Recall the spam filter version and Laplace smoothing from deep-cse-6-1-16 and the last lesson.

Gaussian naive Bayes worked, the setup: mangoes, two features: softness on a scale of 0 to 10 and sugar content (Brix). Ripe: softness mean 7, sd 1; Brix mean 15, sd 2. Unripe: softness mean 3, sd 1; Brix mean 9, sd 2. Equal priors. A mango arrives with softness 5 and Brix 13.

Gaussian naive Bayes worked, the numbers: because the standard deviations are the same for both classes, the normalising constants cancel and we only need minus half the squared z-scores. Ripe: softness z = (5 - 7) / 1 = -2, contributing -2; Brix z = (13 - 15) / 2 = -1, contributing -0.5; total -2.5. Unripe: softness z = (5 - 3) / 1 = 2, contributing -2; Brix z = (13 - 9) / 2 = 2, contributing -2; total -4. Ripe wins by 1.5 in log score. The posterior of ripe = 1 / (1 + e^-1.5) = 0.82. Softness alone was a tie (the mango is exactly halfway); the sugar reading broke the tie.

Training by counting, worked: a Bernoulli naive Bayes for SMS sees 10 spam and 20 normal training messages. The word "free" appears in 6 spam and 1 normal message. With Laplace smoothing, P(free | spam) = (6 + 1) / (10 + 2) = 0.58 and P(free | normal) = (1 + 1) / (20 + 2) = 0.09. The priors are 10 / 30 = 0.33 and 0.67. So a message containing "free" gets a log vote of ln 0.58 for spam and ln 0.09 for normal, a likelihood ratio of about 6.4 in favour of spam, before any other word is considered. Each further word adds its own vote in the same way. Training a model with 5,000 words is just 5,000 such counts per class, which is why naive Bayes trains in one pass over the data.

Why it works despite being wrong: to classify, we only need the right class to get the highest score, not accurate probabilities. Even when features are correlated, the errors from the naive assumption often push all classes' scores in similar ways, so the ranking survives. Studies have shown naive Bayes can be optimal under zero-one loss in many situations where independence clearly fails. It is also very fast, needs little data, handles thousands of features (like words), and copes with missing features by simply leaving them out of the product.

Where it hurts, double counting: if two features carry the same information, naive Bayes counts it twice. Suppose the mango's Brix was measured twice by two identical meters, and both are fed in as separate features. The ripe score becomes -3 and the unripe -6, a gap of 3 instead of 1.5, so the posterior jumps from 0.82 to 0.95. Nothing new was learned, but the classifier became more confident. Naive Bayes probabilities are often overconfident, pushed towards 0 or 1, so do not use them directly as trustworthy risk numbers without calibration. And if correlated features push in opposite directions from other evidence, the ranking itself can go wrong.

Variants: Bernoulli naive Bayes uses yes/no features, such as "the word lottery appears". Multinomial naive Bayes uses counts, such as how many times each word appears, and is the classic choice for text. Gaussian naive Bayes uses a 1D Gaussian per numeric feature. Note that Gaussian naive Bayes is the same as the Gaussian classifier of lesson 06 with diagonal covariance matrices: axis-aligned ellipses, possibly different per class.

When to choose naive Bayes: use it as a quick first baseline, for text with thousands of word features, when training data are small, or when you need a model that trains and updates in seconds. Avoid relying on it when features are strongly correlated and you need trustworthy probabilities, or when a more flexible model clearly wins on a validation set.

Bayesian belief networks, the idea: naive Bayes says "every feature depends only on the class". Full joint tables say "everything depends on everything". Real situations are in between. A Bayesian belief network (Bayes net) is a drawing that says exactly which variables directly influence which, as a directed acyclic graph (DAG): circles for variables, arrows from cause to effect, and no loops. Each variable stores a small table of probabilities given its parents, called a conditional probability table (CPT).

The chain rule for Bayes nets: the joint probability of all variables is the product of each variable's probability given its parents: P(x1, ..., xn) = product of P(xi | parents(xi)). Variables are conditionally independent of their non-descendants given their parents. This is what makes the tables small.

A tiny network worked, Dhaka in monsoon: three yes/no variables. R = heavy rain, with P(R) = 0.3. W = waterlogging on the road, depending on rain: P(W | R) = 0.8, P(W | not R) = 0.1. J = traffic jam, depending on waterlogging: P(J | W) = 0.9, P(J | not W) = 0.4. The graph is R to W to J. Parameters: 1 + 2 + 2 = 5, instead of 7 for a full joint table over 3 yes/no variables. With 30 variables each having at most 3 parents, the saving is enormous.

Inference in the network, worked: what is the chance of a jam? First P(W) = 0.3 x 0.8 + 0.7 x 0.1 = 0.31. Then P(J) = 0.31 x 0.9 + 0.69 x 0.4 = 0.555. Now reason backwards: you are stuck in a jam; how likely is it raining? P(R and J) = 0.3 x (0.8 x 0.9 + 0.2 x 0.4) = 0.3 x 0.8 = 0.24. So P(R | J) = 0.24 / 0.555 = 0.43, up from the prior 0.3. If you can see the road is waterlogged, P(R | W) = 0.24 / 0.31 = 0.77, and then the jam adds nothing more about rain, because J depends on R only through W.

Naive Bayes is a Bayes net: draw the class at the top with an arrow to every feature, and no arrows between features. That is exactly the naive assumption. Adding a few arrows between features that are strongly related (for example, tree-augmented naive Bayes, where each feature may have one extra parent) keeps the model small but removes the worst double counting.

Inference and learning in general: computing posteriors in a general network is done by exact methods like variable elimination, which sum out variables in a clever order, or by approximate methods like sampling, because exact inference can become very expensive in large, densely connected networks. Learning the CPTs from complete data is just counting (with smoothing); learning the graph itself is a harder search problem. Bayes nets are used in medical diagnosis, fault finding in machines, and spam filtering.

Real-life example 1, an SMS spam filter in Bangla and English: an operator trains multinomial naive Bayes on labelled SMS. Words like "offer", "free", "bonus", "taka" and "click" get high P(word | spam). With Laplace smoothing, a new word never seen in spam does not make spam impossible. It trains in seconds on millions of messages and updates daily as spammers change their words. Overconfident probabilities do not matter much, because the operator only needs a ranking and a threshold.

Real-life example 2, diagnosing a motorbike that will not start: a workshop builds a small Bayes net: battery dead and fuel empty both influence "engine does not start"; battery dead also influences "horn does not work". If the engine does not start and the horn also fails, the network quickly raises the probability of a dead battery and lowers that of empty fuel, because the horn evidence "explains away" the problem. A mechanic does this reasoning by instinct; the network does it with numbers.

Common mistakes: thinking naive Bayes requires features to be independent overall (it is conditional independence given the class); trusting its probabilities as calibrated; forgetting smoothing, so one unseen value zeroes a class; drawing Bayes nets with cycles (not allowed); and adding up probabilities when you should multiply along the chain rule. Exams ask you to compute a naive Bayes decision for 2 or 3 features, count parameters with and without the naive assumption, write the joint of a small Bayes net and compute a marginal or a posterior.

Recap: naive Bayes assumes features are conditionally independent given the class, which cuts the number of parameters from exponential to linear in d. It classifies well, trains fast and handles many features, but double counts correlated evidence and gives overconfident probabilities. Bayesian belief networks generalise it: a DAG of direct influences with small conditional tables, joint probability by the chain rule, and inference by summing out variables.
key_points: Naive assumption: p(x | w) = product of p(xi | w), conditional independence given the class.
Parameter saving: 20 yes/no features need 20 numbers per class instead of 1,048,575.
Mango worked: log scores -2.5 (ripe) vs -4 (unripe) give P(ripe | x) = 0.82.
It classifies well because only the ranking matters, but correlated features are double counted (duplicate Brix pushes 0.82 to 0.95).
Bernoulli, multinomial and Gaussian variants; Gaussian NB equals diagonal-covariance Gaussian classifiers.
A Bayes net is a DAG with conditional probability tables; joint = product of P(xi | parents).
Monsoon net worked: P(J) = 0.555, P(R | J) = 0.43, P(R | W) = 0.77.
lessons.tip: For any naive Bayes question, work in log scores and write one line per feature: "class A gets ..., class B gets ...". Adding columns is quicker and less error-prone than multiplying tiny probabilities.
lessons.task: Draw a small Bayes net from your own life with three or four yes/no variables (for example: load-shedding, phone battery low, missed class). Invent the probability tables, then compute the probability of the last variable and one backwards posterior.

quiz.q: What does the naive Bayes assumption state?
options: All features are independent of the class
Features are conditionally independent given the class
All features are Gaussian with the same variance
quiz.explain: Within each class, the joint density is the product of single-feature densities.

quiz.q: How many probabilities per class does naive Bayes need for 20 yes/no features?
quiz.explain: One probability P(xi = yes | w) per feature, so 20, instead of 2^20 - 1 for a full table.

quiz.q: Feeding the same feature twice into naive Bayes usually makes the posterior...
quiz.explain: The same evidence is counted twice, doubling its log contribution and pushing posteriors towards 0 or 1.

quiz.q: In the monsoon network, P(R) = 0.3, P(R and J) = 0.24 and P(J) = 0.555. What is P(R | J)?
Which structure is NOT allowed in a Bayesian belief network?
options: A chain A to B to C
quiz.explain: Bayes nets must be directed acyclic graphs, so cycles are not allowed.

lessons.title: Nonparametric Density Estimation: Histograms, Parzen Windows and k-NN
lessons.content:
Look at a map of Dhaka at night from a plane. You cannot see the people, but the brightness of each area tells you how crowded it is: Gulistan blazing, the river dark. You did not assume the city has a bell-curve shape; you just looked at how much light falls in each patch. Nonparametric density estimation works the same way: instead of assuming the data follow a Gaussian or some other formula, it estimates the density at a point by counting how many samples fall nearby. This lesson covers the three classic ways to do that: histograms, Parzen windows and k-nearest-neighbour estimates.

The problem with parametric models: in lessons 07 and 08 we assumed a shape (usually Gaussian) and estimated its few parameters. When the assumption is right this is efficient. But real densities often have two humps (jatka and adult ilish), long tails (transaction amounts), sharp edges (ages cannot be negative) or odd shapes nobody can write as a formula. A Gaussian fitted to a two-humped density puts its peak in the valley between the humps, exactly where few samples are. We need methods that let the data decide the shape.

The basic idea: the probability P that a sample falls in a small region R around x is about p(x) times the volume V of R. If we have n samples and k of them fall in R, then P is about k / n. Putting these together: p(x) is approximately k / (n V). Every nonparametric density estimate is a version of this one formula. There are two ways to use it: fix the volume V and count k (histograms and Parzen windows), or fix k and measure the volume needed to catch k samples (k-nearest-neighbour estimates).

The histogram: divide the feature axis into bins of width h and count samples in each bin. The density estimate in a bin is (count) / (n h). Worked: 20 ilish lengths are measured, and 6 fall in the bin from 30 to 34 cm (width 4). The estimate there is 6 / (20 x 4) = 0.075 per cm. Check: the area of that bar is 0.075 x 4 = 0.3, which is 6 out of 20 samples. The total area of all bars is 1, as a density should be.

Problems with histograms: the result depends on where bins start, not just their width; shifting all bins by 1 cm can change the picture. The estimate jumps abruptly at bin edges, so two almost identical fish on either side of an edge get very different densities. And in many dimensions the number of bins explodes: 10 bins per feature in 10 features is 10^10 bins, almost all empty. Histograms are excellent for looking at one or two features, but poor as a classifier's density model.

Parzen windows, the idea: instead of fixed bins, centre a window on the point x where you want the estimate, and count samples inside that window. The window moves with x, so there are no fixed edges to worry about. With a box-shaped window of width h in 1D, p(x) = (number of samples within h / 2 of x) / (n h).

Parzen box window worked: samples 2, 3, 4, 7, 8 (n = 5), window width h = 2. At x = 3: the window covers 2 to 4, which contains 2, 3 and 4, so p(3) = 3 / (5 x 2) = 0.3. At x = 5.5: the window covers 4.5 to 6.5, containing no samples, so p(5.5) = 0. At x = 7.5: the window covers 6.5 to 8.5, containing 7 and 8, so p(7.5) = 2 / 10 = 0.2. The estimate shows two clusters, around 3 and around 7.5, with a gap between, exactly the shape a single Gaussian would have hidden.

Kernels, a smoother window: the box window still gives a jumpy estimate, because a sample counts fully inside the window and not at all just outside. The fix is to let each sample contribute a smooth bump instead of a block. In kernel density estimation, p(x) = (1/n) sum over samples of K((x - xi) / h) / h, where the kernel K is a smooth bump with area 1, most often a Gaussian. You can picture it as placing a small Gaussian hill on every sample and adding up all the hills.

Gaussian kernel worked: same samples 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, Gaussian kernel with h = 1 (the standard deviation of each bump). At x = 3 the estimate is 0.177; at x = 5 it is 0.072; at x = 7.5 it is 0.141. The valley at 5 is lower than the two peaks, and the curve is smooth everywhere. No shape was assumed; the two clusters emerged from the data.

The bandwidth trade-off: the width h is the one knob, and it matters more than the kernel shape. With h = 0.3, the estimate at 3 is 0.268 and at 5 almost zero (0.001): five sharp spikes, one per sample, which is overfitting; the model believes values between samples are nearly impossible. With h = 3, the estimate at 3 is 0.094 and at 5 is 0.100: the valley disappears and the two clusters blur into one broad hill, which is underfitting. A good h is in between. In practice h is chosen by cross-validation (pick the h that gives the highest likelihood to held-out samples) or by rules of thumb based on the sample spread and size; it should shrink slowly as n grows.

More than one feature: in d dimensions the window becomes a box or a ball, its volume is h^d, and the Gaussian kernel becomes a round multivariate Gaussian bump. A single bandwidth only makes sense if all features are on similar scales, so standardise them first (lesson 02), or give each feature its own bandwidth. For example, a 2D box window with h = 2 has area 4, so 3 samples out of 50 inside it give p = 3 / (50 x 4) = 0.015.

k-nearest-neighbour density estimation: instead of fixing the window and counting, fix k and grow a window around x until it contains k samples. Then p(x) = k / (n V), where V is the size of that window. In crowded areas the window stays small and the density is high; in empty areas it grows large and the density is low. The window adapts to the data automatically.

k-NN density worked: samples 2, 3, 4, 7, 8 and k = 3. At x = 5 the distances are 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, so the 3rd nearest sample is at distance 2. In 1D the window extends 2 on each side, so V = 4, and p(5) = 3 / (5 x 4) = 0.15. At x = 3 the distances are 1, 0, 1, 4, 5, so the 3rd nearest is at distance 1, V = 2 and p(3) = 3 / 10 = 0.3. A weakness: k-NN density estimates have heavy tails and do not integrate exactly to 1, so they are better for classification than as true densities.

From density to classification: any density estimate can be plugged into Bayes' rule. Estimate p(x | wi) for each class from that class's samples, multiply by priors, and pick the largest. With Parzen windows this is called a Parzen classifier. With the k-NN estimate something neat happens: grow one window around x until it holds k samples of any class. If ki of them belong to class wi, the estimates give P(wi | x) = ki / k. Choosing the largest posterior is then simply majority vote among the k nearest neighbours: the k-NN classifier (deep-cse-6-1-15) falls straight out of density estimation. The next lesson studies it in depth.

Costs of being nonparametric: there is no small set of parameters; the "model" is the whole training set. Every estimate at a new point needs distances to all n samples, so prediction is slow for large n unless clever data structures are used. Storage grows with the data. And the methods need many more samples than a correct parametric model to reach the same accuracy.

The curse of dimensionality: nonparametric methods suffer badly in high dimensions. Imagine data spread evenly in a unit cube. To catch 10 percent of the samples with a small cube around x, in 1D you need a side of 0.1, but in 10 dimensions you need a side of 0.1^(1/10) = 0.79, almost the whole range of every feature. So a "local" window is not local any more; it covers most of the space, and the estimate becomes blurry. To keep the window small, the number of samples must grow exponentially with d. That is why kernel and k-NN methods are usually paired with dimensionality reduction (lessons 16 and 17).

Real-life example 1, where are the accidents: a road safety team in Dhaka plots the GPS locations of 2,000 reported accidents. A Gaussian kernel density map with a bandwidth of about 200 metres shows bright spots at a few junctions on the airport road and at bus stops; a bandwidth of 2 km merges everything into a vague blob over the whole city, and 10 metres shows only scattered dots. With the right bandwidth, the map tells the police exactly where to place traffic wardens.

Real-life example 2, unusual electricity use: a power distribution company models each household's hourly consumption with a kernel density built from the past year. A new reading that falls where the estimated density is very low, for example a huge draw at 3 a.m. in a house that never used much at night, is flagged for checking as a possible illegal connection or meter fault. No Gaussian is assumed, so the model copes with households that have two normal patterns, weekday and weekend.

Common mistakes: confusing the bin or window width with the number of bins; forgetting the division by n V, so the estimate does not integrate to 1; choosing the bandwidth by eye on the training data (always too small); thinking the kernel shape matters more than the bandwidth; and using nonparametric methods directly on hundreds of features. Exams ask you to compute a histogram or Parzen box estimate at a point, a k-NN density estimate, to explain the bandwidth trade-off, to derive k-NN classification from k / (n V), and to explain the curse of dimensionality with a number.

Recap: nonparametric methods estimate densities from local counts, p(x) is about k / (n V). Histograms fix bins, Parzen windows fix a moving window, kernels smooth it, and k-NN fixes k and lets the window adapt. Bandwidth or k controls the smoothness trade-off. Plugged into Bayes, k-NN estimates give majority-vote classification. These methods need lots of data and suffer from the curse of dimensionality.
key_points: All nonparametric estimates use p(x) about k / (n V): fix V and count k, or fix k and measure V.
Histogram worked: 6 of 20 samples in a 4 cm bin gives 6 / (20 x 4) = 0.075 per cm.
Kernel density estimation places a smooth bump on every sample; bandwidth h matters more than the kernel shape.
Small h gives spiky overfitting, large h blurs clusters together; choose h by cross-validation.
k-NN density: p = k / (n V); with k = 3 at x = 5, V = 4 and p = 0.15. It leads to P(wi | x) = ki / k, the k-NN vote.
Curse of dimensionality: catching 10 percent of data in 10D needs a cube side of 0.79.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see a nonparametric method, ask "what is fixed, the window or the count?" That one question tells you whether you are looking at a Parzen-type or a k-NN-type method and which formula to use.
lessons.task: Write down the ages of 15 people you know. Draw a histogram with bin width 5 years and another with bin width 20 years. Then, at age 25, compute a Parzen box estimate with width 10. Which picture shows real groups, and which hides them?

quiz.q: What is the basic formula behind nonparametric density estimation?
options: p(x) = k x n x V
quiz.explain: The share of samples k/n in a small region, divided by the region's volume V, approximates the density.

quiz.q: With samples 2, 3, 4, 7, 8 and a box window of width 2, what is the Parzen estimate at x = 3?
quiz.explain: The window 2 to 4 holds 3 samples: 3 / (5 x 2) = 0.3.

quiz.q: What happens if the kernel bandwidth h is made very small?
options: The estimate becomes a single smooth hill
The estimate becomes spiky, one sharp peak per sample (overfitting)
quiz.explain: Tiny bumps on each sample leave near-zero density between them, which overfits the training data.

quiz.q: Using k-NN density estimation, if ki of the k nearest neighbours belong to class wi, the posterior estimate is...
quiz.explain: The class density estimates and priors combine so that P(wi | x) = ki / k, which gives the majority-vote rule.

quiz.q: Why do kernel and k-NN methods struggle in high dimensions?
options: A window holding a fixed share of the data must cover most of each feature's range, so it is no longer local
Distances cannot be computed in high dimensions
They need fewer samples as d grows
quiz.explain: In 10D, catching 10 percent of uniform data needs a cube side of 0.79, so estimates become blurry unless samples grow exponentially.

lessons.title: Nearest Neighbour Rules: Theory and Practice
lessons.content:
When you move to a new neighbourhood and want to know if a shop is good, you ask the people living nearest to it. When a doctor sees an unusual rash, she remembers the most similar case she has seen before. "Find the most similar known example and copy its answer" is perhaps the oldest recognition strategy there is. In pattern recognition it is the nearest neighbour rule. You met k-NN in the Machine Learning course (deep-cse-6-1-15) as a practical tool. Here we look at it as a pattern recognition rule: its geometry, a famous result about how good it can be, and the techniques that make it fast and clean enough for real systems.

The 1-NN rule: store all labelled training samples. For a new sample x, find the single training sample closest to x and give x its label. There is no training phase at all, just storage. It needs a distance (lesson 02), usually Euclidean on standardised features.

The geometry, Voronoi cells: around each training sample draw the region of all points that are closer to it than to any other sample. These regions are convex polygons in 2D (polytopes in higher dimensions), and together they tile the whole feature space. This tiling is the Voronoi tessellation. The 1-NN classifier gives every point in a cell the label of that cell's sample. Its decision boundary is made of the cell edges that separate samples of different classes, so it is piecewise linear and can follow very complicated shapes.

1-NN worked: class A samples are (1, 1), (2, 2), (1, 3); class B samples are (5, 4), (6, 5), (4, 6). A query arrives at (3, 3). Its distances are: (2, 2) 1.41, (1, 3) 2.00, (5, 4) 2.24, (1, 1) 2.83, (4, 6) 3.16, (6, 5) 3.61. The nearest is (2, 2), class A, so 1-NN says A.

The k-NN rule: take the k nearest samples and use a majority vote. With k = 3 the nearest three are (2, 2) A, (1, 3) A and (5, 4) B, so A wins 2 to 1. As lesson 10 showed, this is not an ad hoc trick: it is the Bayes rule applied to k-NN density estimates, with P(wi | x) estimated as ki / k. Larger k averages over more neighbours, giving smoother boundaries and less sensitivity to a single noisy sample, but blurring fine detail.

Distance-weighted voting: closer neighbours should probably count more. A common choice is a weight of 1 / distance. For our query with k = 3: A gets 1 / 1.41 + 1 / 2.00 = 0.71 + 0.50 = 1.21, while B gets 1 / 2.24 = 0.45. A wins more clearly. Weighting also breaks ties naturally and makes the result less sensitive to the exact choice of k. If a query sits exactly on a training sample (distance 0), we simply use that sample's label.

How good is 1-NN, the Cover-Hart result: in 1967 Cover and Hart proved a famous bound. As the number of training samples grows to infinity, the error rate P of the 1-NN rule satisfies P* <= P <= P* (2 - c P* / (c - 1)), where P* is the Bayes error and c the number of classes. In particular P is never more than 2 P*. In words: with unlimited data, half of all the classification information is contained in the single nearest neighbour.

Cover-Hart worked: for two classes with Bayes error P* = 0.05, the bound gives P <= 0.05 x (2 - 2 x 0.05) = 0.05 x 1.9 = 0.095. So with enough data, the simple 1-NN rule has between 5 and 9.5 percent error, while the best possible is 5. Why up to double? Intuitively, the nearest neighbour's label is itself a noisy guess: at a point where the posterior of the true class is 0.95, the neighbour has the wrong label about 5 percent of the time, and the query itself is in the wrong class about 5 percent of the time, so the chance they disagree is about 2 x 0.95 x 0.05 = 0.095. With k-NN and k growing (but slower than n), the error approaches the Bayes error itself.

The catch in that result: the bound is asymptotic, for infinitely many samples. With finite data, especially in high dimensions, the nearest neighbour may be far away and not similar at all, and the bound says nothing. That is the curse of dimensionality from lesson 10 again. In practice k-NN works best with a modest number of good, well-scaled features.

Choosing k: for two classes use odd k to avoid ties. A classic rule of thumb is k around the square root of n, but the reliable method is cross-validation: try k = 1, 3, 5, ..., 21 and keep the one with the lowest validation error. Small k means low bias and high variance (jumpy boundaries); large k means higher bias and lower variance (smooth boundaries). With very imbalanced classes, large k lets the majority class win almost everywhere, so weighting by distance or by inverse class frequency helps.

Cleaning the training set, editing: training sets contain noise and mislabelled samples, and 1-NN copies every mistake into a little island in feature space. Wilson's editing removes each training sample that is misclassified by its own k nearest neighbours (excluding itself), usually with k = 3. The result is a cleaner set with smoother boundaries. Editing removes samples mostly near the boundary and in noisy regions.

Editing worked: add a mislabelled sample to our data, a point at (5, 5) wrongly marked A, sitting right inside the B group. Its three nearest neighbours (excluding itself) are (5, 4) at 1.00, (6, 5) at 1.00 and (4, 6) at 1.41, all B, so it is misclassified and removed. Check a genuine B sample such as (5, 4): its neighbours are (5, 5) A, (6, 5) B and (4, 6) B, a 2 to 1 vote for B, so it stays. Every A sample in the left group also has two A neighbours out of three and stays. Only the noisy point goes. Without editing, 1-NN would have carved a small "A island" around (5, 5) and called nearby B queries A.

The (k, l) rule, a reject option for k-NN: in lesson 05 we rejected when the top posterior was too low. The nearest neighbour version is the (k, l) rule: look at k neighbours and decide only if at least l of them agree; otherwise reject. With k = 5 and l = 4, a vote of 4 to 1 or 5 to 0 gives a decision, while 3 to 2 sends the sample to a human. Raising l lowers the error on accepted samples at the cost of more rejections, the same trade-off as before.

Shrinking the training set, condensing: 1-NN must compare a query with every stored sample, so fewer samples means faster predictions. Hart's condensed nearest neighbour keeps only the samples needed to classify the rest correctly. Start the store with one sample. Go through the others; if the current store misclassifies a sample by 1-NN, add it to the store. Repeat passes until nothing is added.

Condensing worked: start with store {(1, 1) A}. (2, 2) and (1, 3) are classified A by the store: correct, skip. (5, 4) is closest to (1, 1), so classified A: wrong, add it. Now the store is {(1, 1) A, (5, 4) B}. (6, 5) is closest to (5, 4): B, correct. (4, 6) is 5.83 from (1, 1) and 2.24 from (5, 4): B, correct. A second pass changes nothing. Six samples became two, and all six training samples are still classified correctly. Real condensing on large data often keeps 10 to 30 percent of samples; editing first and then condensing works better than condensing noisy data.

The cost in numbers: with one million stored samples of 100 features each, one brute-force query needs about 100 million subtractions, squarings and additions, and the store needs 100 million numbers in memory. At thousands of queries per second that is impossible on a normal server, which is why the next two ideas matter.

Making search fast: the brute-force search costs n distance computations per query, too slow for millions of samples. A k-d tree splits the space recursively along one feature at a time (like dividing a map first by east-west, then north-south), so most samples can be skipped; it works well up to roughly 10 to 20 dimensions. Ball trees use nested spheres instead. For very high dimensions, approximate nearest neighbour methods (hashing, graph-based indexes) trade a tiny chance of missing the true nearest neighbour for huge speed-ups; they power modern image and text search.

Choosing the metric: k-NN is only as good as its distance. Standardising features is the minimum. Mahalanobis distance accounts for correlation. For handwritten digits, plain pixel distance treats a slightly shifted or rotated "7" as far from the original; specialised distances such as tangent distance were designed to ignore small shifts and rotations, and dramatically improved nearest neighbour digit recognition. Metric learning methods learn a distance from labelled data so that same-class samples come close and different-class samples move apart.

Real-life example 1, recognising a returning customer's signature: a bank stores 5 genuine signature samples per customer, each turned into a feature vector (stroke lengths, slants, pen-lift counts). A cheque's signature is compared with the stored samples, and also with a large pool of forgeries and other people's signatures. If its nearest neighbours are this customer's genuine samples, accept; otherwise send to an officer. Adding a new customer means simply storing their samples; nothing needs retraining.

Real-life example 2, recommending similar products on an online shop: a Bangladeshi e-commerce site represents each product by features such as category, price band, colour and text description. When you view a kurta, the site finds its nearest neighbours in feature space and shows "similar items". It uses an approximate nearest neighbour index, because exact search over a million products for every page view would be far too slow.

Common mistakes: forgetting to scale features; using even k for two classes; claiming 1-NN is twice the Bayes error (it is at most twice, asymptotically); evaluating 1-NN on its own training data (always 100 percent, since each sample is its own nearest neighbour); and condensing before removing noise. Exams ask you to classify a query with 1-NN and 3-NN by hand, sketch Voronoi cells for 3 or 4 points, state and apply the Cover-Hart bound, and run a few steps of editing or condensing.

Recap: the nearest neighbour rule labels a query by its closest stored samples. 1-NN boundaries follow Voronoi cells; k-NN votes and smooths them. With infinite data, 1-NN error is at most twice the Bayes error, and k-NN approaches Bayes. In practice, choose k by cross-validation, scale features, weight by distance, edit noisy samples, condense to save memory and time, and use tree or approximate indexes for fast search.
key_points: 1-NN copies the label of the closest training sample; its boundary follows the Voronoi tessellation.
Worked: query (3, 3) has nearest (2, 2) A at 1.41; 3-NN votes A, A, B, so A.
Distance-weighted voting with 1/d gives A 1.21 vs B 0.45 for the same query.
Cover-Hart: asymptotically P* <= P(1-NN) <= P*(2 - cP*/(c - 1)) <= 2P*; P* = 0.05 gives at most 0.095.
Choose k by cross-validation; small k is jumpy (high variance), large k is smooth (high bias).
Wilson editing removes noisy samples; Hart condensing keeps only needed ones (6 samples became 2 in the worked case).
k-d trees and approximate nearest neighbour indexes make search fast; the metric must suit the data.
lessons.tip: Always sketch the training points and the query before computing anything. With six points on graph paper you can usually see the nearest neighbours instantly and then use the arithmetic only to confirm.
lessons.task: Take 8 to 10 photos of leaves or coins, measure two features for each and label them. Then measure a new item and classify it by 1-NN and 3-NN by hand. Finally, try condensing your set and see how many items you really need to keep.

quiz.q: What does the decision boundary of a 1-NN classifier follow?
options: A circle around the class mean
The edges of the Voronoi cells between samples of different classes
The axes of the feature space
quiz.explain: Each sample owns a Voronoi cell, and the boundary is made of cell edges where the labels change.

quiz.q: According to Cover and Hart, with unlimited data the 1-NN error is at most...
quiz.explain: Asymptotically P* <= P(1-NN) <= 2P*, so 1-NN is never worse than twice the Bayes error.

quiz.q: For the query (3, 3), the three nearest neighbours have labels A, A, B. With weights 1/d (distances 1.41, 2.00, 2.24), which class wins?
options: A, with total weight about 1.21 vs 0.45

quiz.q: What does Hart's condensing do?
options: Keeps only the samples needed to classify the rest correctly by 1-NN
quiz.explain: Condensing adds a sample to the store only if the current store misclassifies it, giving a much smaller consistent set.

quiz.q: Why is testing 1-NN on its own training data misleading?
options: Every sample is its own nearest neighbour, so accuracy is always 100 percent
quiz.explain: Each training sample is at distance zero from itself, so the apparent error is zero, which says nothing about new data.

lessons.title: Linear Discriminant Functions and the Perceptron
lessons.content:
On a school playground the teacher draws one chalk line: girls' team on this side, boys' team on that side. One straight line, and every child knows which side they belong to. Many classification problems can be solved the same way, by a single straight cut through feature space. In lesson 06 straight boundaries appeared as a consequence of Gaussian assumptions. Now we turn the idea around: forget about densities, assume from the start that the boundary is a straight line (a hyperplane), and learn its position directly from the samples. This is the linear discriminant approach, and its oldest learning rule is the perceptron.

Why go linear directly: estimating densities needs many samples and assumptions about their shape. But for classification we only need the boundary. If we believe a linear boundary is good enough, we can learn its few numbers straight from data, without ever estimating a density. Linear classifiers are fast, need little memory, are easy to interpret, and are the building block of neural networks and SVMs.

The linear discriminant function: g(x) = w . x + w0 = w1 x1 + w2 x2 + ... + wd xd + w0. The vector w is the weight vector and w0 the bias (or threshold). For two classes, decide w1 if g(x) > 0 and w2 if g(x) < 0. The decision boundary g(x) = 0 is a hyperplane: a line in 2D, a plane in 3D.

The geometry, w is the normal: the weight vector w points perpendicular to the boundary, towards the side where g is positive (the w1 side). Changing the size of w without changing its direction does not move the boundary. The bias w0 slides the boundary along w; with w0 = 0 the boundary passes through the origin.

Distance to the boundary, worked: the signed distance of a point x from the hyperplane is r = g(x) / ||w||. Take g(x) = 3 x1 + 4 x2 - 12, so ||w|| = 5. For the point (4, 3), g = 12 + 12 - 12 = 12, so the point is 12 / 5 = 2.4 units away, on the positive side. For the origin, g = -12, so it is 2.4 units away on the negative side; in general the origin's distance is w0 / ||w||. So g(x) is not just a sign; its size tells how confidently a point lies on one side, which SVMs will exploit in lesson 15.

Augmented vectors, a neat trick: to treat w0 like the other weights, add a constant 1 to each feature vector: y = (1, x1, ..., xd), and a = (w0, w1, ..., wd). Then g(x) = a . y, a simple dot product with no separate bias. The boundary in the new (d + 1)-dimensional space passes through the origin. All the learning rules below use this form.

Normalised samples, a second trick: we want a . y > 0 for class 1 samples and a . y < 0 for class 2. Multiply every class 2 augmented vector by -1. Now the goal is a single condition: a . y > 0 for every sample. A weight vector satisfying this for all samples is called a separating vector or solution vector. If one exists, the data are linearly separable.

The perceptron criterion: how wrong is a given a? Look only at the misclassified samples, those with a . y <= 0. The perceptron criterion is J(a) = sum over misclassified y of (-a . y). It is never negative, and it is zero exactly when no sample is misclassified. Each term is proportional to how far that sample sits on the wrong side. Gradient descent on J gives the update: add the misclassified samples to a, scaled by a learning rate.

The perceptron rule, single-sample version: go through the samples one at a time. If a . y <= 0 (misclassified, or exactly on the boundary), update a = a + eta y. If correct, leave a alone. Repeat passes over the data until a whole pass makes no update. With eta = 1 and integer data, the arithmetic is just adding vectors.

Perceptron worked, the data: class 1: (2, 3) and (3, 3). Class 2: (0, 0) and (1, 1). Augmented and normalised: y1 = (1, 2, 3), y2 = (1, 3, 3), y3 = (-1, 0, 0), y4 = (-1, -1, -1). Start with a = (0, 0, 0), eta = 1.

Perceptron worked, pass 1: y1: a . y1 = 0, not positive, update a = (1, 2, 3). y2: 1 + 6 + 9 = 16 > 0, fine. y3: -1, update a = (0, 2, 3). y4: 0 - 2 - 3 = -5, update a = (-1, 1, 2).

Perceptron worked, passes 2 and 3: y1: -1 + 2 + 6 = 7, fine. y2: -1 + 3 + 6 = 8, fine. y3: 1, fine. y4: 1 - 1 - 2 = -2, update a = (-2, 0, 1). Pass 3: y1 gives -2 + 0 + 3 = 1, y2 gives 1, y3 gives 2, y4 gives 2 - 0 - 1 = 1. All positive: done after 4 updates. The final discriminant is g(x) = x2 - 2: class 1 if x2 > 2. Check: (2, 3) and (3, 3) give 1, while (0, 0) gives -2 and (1, 1) gives -1. A horizontal line at height 2 separates the classes.

Batch vs single-sample: the batch perceptron computes a . y for all samples first and then adds all the misclassified ones at once, a = a + eta x (sum of misclassified y). It follows the true gradient of J and moves more smoothly, but each step costs a full pass. The single-sample version used above reacts after every sample, which is cheaper per step and usually faster in practice; it is the ancestor of stochastic gradient descent used to train every modern neural network.

Asking for a margin: a solution that only just satisfies a . y > 0 leaves samples sitting right on the boundary, so tiny noise flips them. A simple improvement is to demand a . y > b for some positive margin b, updating whenever a . y <= b. The perceptron then keeps pushing the line until every sample is at least a little inside its own side. This idea, "do not just separate, separate with room to spare", is the seed of the support vector machine in lesson 15.

The convergence theorem: if the data are linearly separable, the perceptron rule finds a separating vector in a finite number of updates, whatever the starting point (for fixed eta). The proof shows the weight vector moves closer to a solution with each correction while its length grows only slowly, so the number of corrections is bounded. The bound grows when the classes are close together (small margin) and when samples are far from the origin.

Limits of the perceptron: the solution it finds depends on the sample order and starting point; it stops at the first separating line, often one that just grazes the samples, not a "best" one. Worse, if the data are not linearly separable, it never stops: some sample is always misclassified, and the weights keep jumping. Fixes include a decreasing learning rate, the pocket algorithm (keep the best weights seen so far), or switching to rules that always converge, like the MSE methods of the next lesson.

The XOR lesson: the classic non-separable case is XOR: (0, 0) and (1, 1) in one class, (0, 1) and (1, 0) in the other. No single straight line separates them. Minsky and Papert's 1969 book pointed out such limits of single-layer perceptrons, and interest in neural networks cooled for years until multi-layer networks trained by backpropagation (deep-cse-7-8) solved it. Another fix is to add features: with a third feature x1 x2, XOR becomes linearly separable, an early glimpse of the kernel trick.

More than two classes, one-vs-rest: train c binary classifiers, each separating one class from all others, and pick the class whose classifier gives the highest score. For 10 Bangla digits that is 10 classifiers. Simple, but each classifier faces an imbalanced task (one digit against nine), and regions exist where several or none claim the point if we only use signs.

One-vs-one: train a classifier for every pair of classes, c (c - 1) / 2 of them, and let them vote. For 10 digits that is 45 small classifiers, each trained only on two digits' samples. Votes can tie, leaving small ambiguous regions.

The linear machine: the cleanest approach defines one linear discriminant per class, gi(x) = wi . x + wi0, and assigns x to the class with the largest gi. This divides the space into convex regions with no ambiguous areas, because there is always a largest score. The multiclass perceptron updates it simply: if a sample of class i is wrongly given to class j, add the sample to wi and subtract it from wj. The softmax output layer of a neural network is a linear machine with probabilities.

Real-life example 1, approving small loans: a microfinance organisation in a village uses two features for quick screening: monthly income in thousand taka and existing debt in thousand taka. Past applicants are labelled repaid or defaulted. A perceptron learns a line such as 2 x income - 3 x debt - 10 > 0 for "likely to repay". The officer can read the weights directly: every thousand of debt counts one and a half times as much as every thousand of income. Borderline cases near the line get an interview.

Real-life example 2, an early optical character reader: the original Mark I Perceptron in the late 1950s used a grid of 400 light sensors and adjustable weights to learn to recognise simple shapes and letters. The same idea, a weighted sum of pixel features followed by a threshold, still sits at the end of every modern digit recogniser, only now the features feeding it are learned by many layers.

Common mistakes: forgetting to augment with the constant 1, so the boundary is forced through the origin; forgetting to negate class 2 samples (or doing it and then checking the wrong sign); thinking g(x) is the distance (it must be divided by ||w||); expecting the perceptron to converge on non-separable data; and confusing one-vs-rest with one-vs-one counts. Exams love a hand-run of the perceptron on four points, computing a distance to a line, and explaining why XOR fails.

Recap: a linear discriminant g(x) = w . x + w0 splits space with a hyperplane whose normal is w; distance is g(x) / ||w||. Augmenting and normalising reduce learning to finding a with a . y > 0 for all samples. The perceptron adds misclassified samples to a and converges if the data are separable, but not otherwise. For many classes use one-vs-rest, one-vs-one, or best of all a linear machine.
key_points: Linear discriminant g(x) = w . x + w0; boundary g = 0 is a hyperplane with normal w.
Signed distance r = g(x)/||w||: for 3x1 + 4x2 - 12 the point (4, 3) is 12/5 = 2.4 away.
Augment y = (1, x) and negate class 2 samples, so the goal is a . y > 0 for all samples.
Perceptron rule: if a . y <= 0, set a = a + eta y; repeat until a full pass has no updates.
Worked: four points converge after 4 updates to a = (-2, 0, 1), the line x2 = 2.
Convergence is guaranteed only for linearly separable data; XOR is the classic failure.
Multiclass: one-vs-rest (c classifiers), one-vs-one (c(c-1)/2), or a linear machine with no ambiguous regions.
lessons.tip: When running the perceptron by hand, keep a three-column table: sample, a . y, new a. Write every dot product even when it is positive; it makes errors easy to spot and shows exactly when the pass is clean.
lessons.task: On graph paper, mark the four XOR points. Try to draw one line that separates them, and convince yourself it is impossible. Then add a third coordinate x1 x2 to each point and find a plane (a rule using x1, x2 and x1 x2) that does separate them.

quiz.q: In g(x) = w . x + w0, what is the direction of w relative to the decision boundary?
options: Perpendicular to it, pointing to the positive side
quiz.explain: The weight vector is the normal of the hyperplane and points towards the region where g is positive.

quiz.q: For g(x) = 3x1 + 4x2 - 12, what is the distance of (4, 3) from the boundary?
What does the perceptron rule do when a normalised sample y has a . y <= 0?
options: Adds eta times y to a
quiz.explain: A misclassified sample is added to the weight vector, pulling the boundary towards classifying it correctly.

quiz.q: What happens if the perceptron is run on data that are not linearly separable?
options: It converges to the best possible line
It never stops updating, because some sample is always misclassified
quiz.explain: The convergence theorem needs separability; otherwise the weights keep changing forever.

quiz.q: How many pairwise classifiers does one-vs-one need for 10 classes?

lessons.title: Minimum Squared Error and the LMS Rule
lessons.content:
Imagine a cricket coach who does not just say "out" or "not out" after each practice shot, but gives every shot a score: aim for exactly 1 for a good shot and exactly -1 for a bad one, and tell the player how far off he was. Even when the player is already doing fine, the coach keeps nudging him towards the target. That is the spirit of the minimum squared error (MSE) approach to linear classifiers. The perceptron of the last lesson only reacts to mistakes and is helpless when data cannot be separated. MSE gives every sample a target value and fits the line by least squares, which always has an answer. This lesson covers the closed-form pseudoinverse solution, the step-by-step LMS (Widrow-Hoff) rule, and the strengths and weaknesses of this approach.

The problem MSE solves: the perceptron's criterion only counts misclassified samples, so when the classes overlap it never settles. We would like a criterion that uses all the samples, has a single best solution, and can be computed even for overlapping classes. Squared error is the natural candidate: it is smooth, it has a formula for its minimum, and least squares is something you already know from line fitting (deep-cse-2-6 and deep-cse-6-1-05).

From inequalities to equations: with augmented, normalised samples y (lesson 12), we wanted a . y > 0 for all samples. MSE replaces each inequality by an equation a . y = b, where b is a chosen positive target, often 1 for every sample. Stack all n samples as rows of a matrix Y (n rows, d + 1 columns) and the targets as a vector b. We want Y a = b. With more samples than unknowns there is usually no exact solution, so we minimise the sum of squared errors J(a) = ||Y a - b||^2.

The pseudoinverse solution: setting the gradient of J to zero gives the normal equations Y^T Y a = Y^T b. If Y^T Y can be inverted, a = (Y^T Y)^-1 Y^T b. The matrix (Y^T Y)^-1 Y^T is called the pseudoinverse of Y, written Y+. This is the same formula as in linear regression, now used for classification.

Pseudoinverse worked, the data: one feature, to keep matrices 2 by 2. Class 1 at x = 2 and x = 3; class 2 at x = 0 and x = 1. Augmented and normalised rows of Y: (1, 2), (1, 3), (-1, 0), (-1, -1). Targets b = (1, 1, 1, 1).

Pseudoinverse worked, the arithmetic: Y^T Y = [[4, 6], [6, 14]] (for instance the top-left entry is 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4 and the bottom-right is 4 + 9 + 0 + 1 = 14). Y^T b = (1 + 1 - 1 - 1, 2 + 3 + 0 - 1) = (0, 4). The determinant is 4 x 14 - 6 x 6 = 20, so the inverse is (1/20) [[14, -6], [-6, 4]]. Then a = (1/20)(14 x 0 - 6 x 4, -6 x 0 + 4 x 4) = (-1.2, 0.8). The discriminant is g(x) = 0.8 x - 1.2, and the boundary g = 0 is at x = 1.5, exactly halfway between the classes.

Checking the fit: Y a gives (0.4, 1.2, 1.2, 0.4). All four are positive, so all samples are correctly classified. But none equals the target 1 exactly; the errors are -0.6, 0.2, 0.2 and -0.6, with squared sum 0.8. MSE does not care about "correct side"; it only cares about being close to 1. That will matter in a moment.

The LMS rule, a step-by-step version: inverting Y^T Y is expensive for many features and impossible when data arrive one at a time. The Widrow-Hoff or least mean squares (LMS) rule does gradient descent on the squared error, one sample at a time: a = a + eta (b_k - a . y_k) y_k. The term in brackets is the error for that sample. Unlike the perceptron, LMS updates after every sample, even correctly classified ones, unless the output equals the target exactly.

LMS worked: start with a = (0, 0) and eta = 0.1. Sample (1, 2): output 0, error 1, so a = (0.1, 0.2). Sample (1, 3): output 0.1 + 0.6 = 0.7, error 0.3, so a = (0.13, 0.29). Sample (-1, 0): output -0.13, error 1.13, so a = (0.017, 0.29). Sample (-1, -1): output -0.307, error 1.307, so a = (-0.114, 0.159). After this first pass the boundary is at x = 0.114 / 0.159, about 0.72. With further passes and a decreasing eta, a approaches the pseudoinverse answer (-1.2, 0.8) and the boundary approaches 1.5.

Choosing the learning rate: too small and LMS crawls; too large and it overshoots and diverges. A safe rule is to keep eta below about 2 divided by the largest eigenvalue of the sample correlation matrix (which is related to the squared length of the samples), and to scale features first so that no single feature has huge values. Letting eta shrink over time, such as eta(k) = eta(1) / k, makes LMS settle down even when the data are noisy.

When Y^T Y cannot be inverted: with more features than samples, or with features that copy each other, Y^T Y is singular and the formula breaks. The usual fix is to add a small multiple of the identity: a = (Y^T Y + lambda I)^-1 Y^T b. This is ridge regression, and as lesson 08 showed, it is MAP estimation with a Gaussian prior that prefers small weights. It also makes the answer less sensitive to noise.

Many classes with MSE: for c classes, give each sample a target vector with 1 in its own class position and 0 elsewhere (one-hot), and solve for one weight vector per class with the same pseudoinverse, all at once. Classify by the largest output, a linear machine. It is quick and often a decent baseline, though the faraway-point weakness remains.

Why Widrow and Hoff mattered: in 1960 Bernard Widrow and Ted Hoff built ADALINE, an adaptive linear element trained by LMS, in hardware. LMS is still used in adaptive filters, such as echo cancellation in phone calls and noise cancellation in headphones (deep-cse-5-7), because it is cheap and works sample by sample in real time.

MSE vs the perceptron: MSE always gives a solution, even for overlapping classes, and it is unique when Y^T Y is invertible. The perceptron gives a separating vector when one exists but none otherwise. The flip side: MSE does not guarantee a separating vector even when one exists, because it minimises squared error, not mistakes.

MSE can fail on separable data, worked: add one more class 1 sample far away at x = 10, clearly on the correct side. Recompute the pseudoinverse with five samples: a becomes about (-0.350, 0.172), and the boundary jumps from 1.5 to about 2.04. Now the class 1 sample at x = 2 gives a . y = -0.006: it is misclassified! The faraway point produces a huge output, which MSE treats as a big error to be reduced, so it drags the line towards itself and spoils a sample that was fine. The data are perfectly separable, yet MSE fails. The perceptron would not be bothered by a correctly classified faraway point.

The deeper reason: squared error punishes outputs that are "too correct" just as much as outputs that are wrong. A sample far inside its own region produces a large a . y, far above the target 1, and MSE pulls the boundary to reduce that. This is why for classification we often prefer losses that stop punishing once a sample is safely correct: the perceptron criterion, the hinge loss of SVMs, or the log loss of logistic regression.

Ho-Kashyap, getting the best of both: the Ho-Kashyap procedure treats the targets b themselves as unknowns that must stay positive. It alternates: solve for a by pseudoinverse given b, then increase the components of b where the error is positive. For separable data it finds a separating vector; for non-separable data it gives evidence of that, by the errors failing to become non-negative.
