It is less used today, but it shows clearly how MSE and separability fit together.

The link to Fisher and to Bayes: with a special choice of targets, b equal to n / n1 for class 1 samples and n / n2 for class 2 samples, the MSE solution gives the same direction as Fisher's linear discriminant (next lesson). And as the number of samples grows, the MSE discriminant approaches the best mean-squared approximation to the Bayes discriminant g0(x) = P(w1 | x) - P(w2 | x). So MSE is not arbitrary: it tries to approximate the posterior difference with a straight line.

Link to neural networks and logistic regression: a single neuron with a linear output trained by LMS is exactly ADALINE. Put a sigmoid on the output and train with log loss instead of squared error and you get logistic regression (deep-cse-6-1-11). Stack many such units in layers and train with backpropagation, a generalisation of LMS, and you have a neural network (deep-cse-7-8). LMS is the grandparent of all of them.

Real-life example 1, a cheap fruit sorter: a cooperative in Rajshahi wants a microcontroller to sort mangoes as export or local from three sensor readings. It needs a classifier that can be computed with a few multiplications and adapted as the season changes. An LMS-trained linear discriminant updates its weights with each newly labelled mango that a worker checks, slowly following the season's change in mango size, without any need to store old data.

Real-life example 2, echo cancellation on a phone call: during a video call from Dhaka to a relative abroad, your microphone picks up your own speaker's sound and would send it back as an annoying echo. An adaptive filter trained by LMS constantly learns how the speaker sound appears in the microphone and subtracts its prediction. It is the same update, weight plus learning rate times error times input, running thousands of times per second.

Common mistakes: forgetting to normalise class 2 samples before building Y; thinking MSE always separates separable data (the faraway point example shows otherwise); using a learning rate so large that LMS diverges; computing (Y Y^T)^-1 instead of (Y^T Y)^-1; and confusing LMS (updates on every sample) with the perceptron (updates only on mistakes). Exams ask for a pseudoinverse solution on 3 or 4 points, one or two LMS steps, and a comparison of MSE with the perceptron.

Recap: MSE replaces a . y > 0 by a . y = b and solves by least squares, a = (Y^T Y)^-1 Y^T b, which always has an answer. LMS reaches the same solution step by step with a = a + eta (b - a . y) y. MSE handles overlapping data and approximates the Bayes discriminant, but may misclassify separable data because it punishes outputs that are too correct. It is the ancestor of ADALINE, adaptive filters, logistic regression and neural networks.
key_points: MSE replaces a . y > 0 with a . y = b and minimises ||Ya - b||^2.
Pseudoinverse: a = (Y^T Y)^-1 Y^T b; worked on 4 points gives a = (-1.2, 0.8), boundary x = 1.5.
LMS (Widrow-Hoff): a = a + eta (b_k - a . y_k) y_k, updating on every sample.
First LMS step from a = 0 with eta = 0.1 on (1, 2) gives a = (0.1, 0.2).
MSE always gives an answer, even for overlapping classes, unlike the perceptron.
MSE can misclassify separable data: a far class 1 point at x = 10 moves the boundary to 2.04 and spoils x = 2.
MSE approximates the Bayes discriminant P(w1|x) - P(w2|x) and leads to ADALINE, logistic regression and neural networks.
lessons.tip: For pseudoinverse questions, compute Y^T Y and Y^T b column by column with a small table of the rows of Y. With one feature, Y^T Y is just [[n, sum of first column times second], [same, sum of squares]], which you can fill in under a minute.
lessons.task: With a calculator, repeat the pseudoinverse example after adding one class 1 point at x = 6 instead of 10. Does the sample at x = 2 stay correctly classified? Try x = 8 too and find roughly where the faraway point starts to cause a mistake.

quiz.q: What does the MSE approach minimise?
options: The sum of squared differences between a . y and the targets b
quiz.explain: MSE sets targets b and minimises ||Ya - b||^2, the squared error over all samples.

quiz.q: For Y rows (1,2), (1,3), (-1,0), (-1,-1) and b = (1,1,1,1), the pseudoinverse gives a = (-1.2, 0.8). Where is the boundary?
How does the LMS rule differ from the perceptron rule?
options: LMS updates on every sample using the error b - a . y, not only on mistakes
LMS only works for three classes
LMS needs the inverse of Y^T Y at each step
quiz.explain: LMS uses the continuous error for each sample; the perceptron only reacts to misclassified ones.

quiz.q: Why can MSE misclassify linearly separable data?
options: It always forces the boundary through the origin
It ignores half of the samples
It cannot handle more than one feature
It treats very large correct outputs as errors and moves the boundary to reduce them
quiz.explain: Squared error punishes outputs far above the target, so a faraway correct sample can drag the line and spoil others.

quiz.q: Which device famously used LMS training in 1960?
quiz.explain: Widrow and Hoff's ADALINE was an adaptive linear element trained with the LMS rule.

lessons.title: Fisher's Linear Discriminant
lessons.content:
Hold a torch above two piles of marbles on a table and look at their shadows on the wall. Turn the torch one way and the two shadows overlap into one blob. Turn it another way and the shadows sit clearly apart. Fisher's linear discriminant answers a simple but powerful question: in which direction should we shine the torch so that the shadows of the two classes are as separate as possible? It squeezes many features down to one number per sample, chosen specifically to separate the classes. Ronald Fisher proposed it in 1936 to tell apart three species of iris flowers from their petal and sepal measurements, and the idea is still used everywhere.

The problem it solves: with many features, classifiers need more data and more computation, and we cannot see the data. Projecting onto one line makes everything simple: a 1D problem with a single threshold. But a careless projection can destroy the information that separates the classes. We need the best line for separation, not just any line.

Projection, the basic operation: projecting a sample x onto a direction w gives the number y = w . x. All samples become points on a line. Different w give different lines and different shadows. Fisher's goal is to choose w so that, on that line, the two classes are far apart and each class is tightly bunched.

Why the line through the means is not enough: the obvious choice is w along the difference of the class means, m2 - m1. That makes the projected means as far apart as possible for a given length of w. But if each class is a long tilted oval, projecting along the means' direction can make both shadows wide and overlapping. What matters is the gap between the means compared with the spread of each class along that direction, not the gap alone.

Projected means and scatter: after projection, the class means become m1~ = w . m1 and m2~ = w . m2. The scatter of class i on the line is si~^2 = sum over its samples of (w . x - mi~)^2, an unnormalised variance. We want (m1~ - m2~)^2 large and s1~^2 + s2~^2 small.

The Fisher criterion: J(w) = (m1~ - m2~)^2 / (s1~^2 + s2~^2). The numerator is the squared distance between projected class means; the denominator is the total within-class scatter on the line. Fisher chooses the w that maximises J. Multiplying w by any number does not change J, so only the direction matters.

Scatter matrices: to maximise J we write it with matrices. The within-class scatter matrix for class i is Si = sum over its samples of (x - mi)(x - mi)^T, and the total within-class scatter is Sw = S1 + S2. The between-class scatter matrix is Sb = (m1 - m2)(m1 - m2)^T. Then J(w) = (w^T Sb w) / (w^T Sw w), a ratio of two quadratic forms.

The solution: setting the derivative of J to zero gives Sb w = lambda Sw w. Because Sb w always points along m1 - m2, the answer simplifies beautifully: w is proportional to Sw^-1 (m1 - m2). This is Fisher's linear discriminant direction. Notice the resemblance to lesson 06: for Gaussian classes sharing a covariance, the Bayes boundary normal is Sigma^-1 (m1 - m2). Fisher arrived at the same direction without assuming Gaussians.

Worked example, the data: class 1 has (1, 1), (2, 3), (3, 2), class 2 has (4, 3), (5, 5), (6, 4). Means: m1 = (2, 2) and m2 = (5, 4).

Worked example, scatter matrices: deviations for class 1 from (2, 2) are (-1, -1), (0, 1), (1, 0). S1 = sum of outer products = [[1, 1], [1, 1]] + [[0, 0], [0, 1]] + [[1, 0], [0, 0]] = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]. Class 2 has deviations (-1, -1), (0, 1), (1, 0) from (5, 4), the same pattern, so S2 = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]. Then Sw = [[4, 2], [2, 4]].

Worked example, the direction: the determinant of Sw is 4 x 4 - 2 x 2 = 12, so Sw^-1 = (1/12) [[4, -2], [-2, 4]]. With m1 - m2 = (-3, -2): w = (1/12)(4 x -3 - 2 x -2, -2 x -3 + 4 x -2) = (1/12)(-8, -2). Any multiple will do, so flip the sign and scale: w = (4, 1).

Worked example, the projections: with w = (4, 1), class 1 projects to 4 + 1 = 5, 8 + 3 = 11 and 12 + 2 = 14 (mean 10). Class 2 projects to 19, 25 and 28 (mean 24). The scatters are 42 for each class, so J = (24 - 10)^2 / (42 + 42) = 196 / 84 = 2.33. A threshold halfway at 17 separates the classes perfectly: below 17 is class 1, above is class 2.

Classifying new samples, worked: a new sample at (4, 2) projects to 4 x 4 + 2 = 18, just above 17, so class 2. A sample at (3, 4) projects to 12 + 4 = 16, so class 1, even though its x2 value of 4 equals class 2's mean x2. A sample at (3.5, 3) projects to exactly 17: a tie, the place to reject or ask for more evidence. Notice how heavily the direction (4, 1) leans on x1. Within each class, x1 and x2 are positively correlated (Sw has off-diagonal 2), so much of the variation in x2 is "explained" by x1 and carries little extra class information; Fisher discovers this and turns the direction mostly towards x1.

Why Sw^-1 appears, in plain words: multiplying by Sw^-1 first "unstretches" the data so that each class looks like a round cloud, the same whitening idea as the Mahalanobis distance in lesson 06. In that unstretched space, the best direction really is just the line joining the means. Fisher's formula does both steps at once: undo the within-class shape, then point from one mean to the other.

Compare with other directions: projecting on the mean difference (3, 2) gives J = 2.22; projecting on the x1 axis alone gives 2.25; on the x2 axis alone only 1.0, and there the classes touch (class 1's 3 and class 2's 3 project to the same value). Fisher's direction gives the highest J, as the theory promises. Here the differences are modest because the data are small and simple; with long, tilted class clouds Fisher can beat the naive direction by a huge margin.

Choosing the threshold: Fisher gives only the direction. To classify we still need a threshold on y. Simple choices: halfway between the projected means (17 above), or a point that accounts for priors, or the Bayes boundary of 1D Gaussians fitted to the projected classes (lessons 04 to 07). With very different class sizes or costs, the threshold should move, just as in lesson 05.

The recipe in five steps: compute each class mean; compute each class's scatter matrix from deviations about its own mean and add them to get Sw; invert Sw (for 2 by 2, swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, divide by the determinant); multiply by m1 - m2 to get w; project every sample and pick a threshold. Every exam problem on Fisher follows these five steps.

Many classes, multiple discriminant analysis: for c classes, define Sw as the sum of the c within-class scatters and Sb as the sum over classes of ni (mi - m)(mi - m)^T, where m is the overall mean. The best projection uses the top eigenvectors of Sw^-1 Sb. Since Sb is built from c mean vectors around their overall mean, its rank is at most c - 1, so LDA gives at most c - 1 useful directions. For 10 digit classes that is at most 9 dimensions, whatever the number of pixels. For 3 iris species, at most 2, which is why Fisher's iris plot is a neat 2D picture.

LDA vs PCA: both project to fewer dimensions, but they answer different questions. PCA (lesson 16) keeps the directions of largest total variance and never looks at labels; it is unsupervised. LDA keeps the directions that best separate the labelled classes; it is supervised. A direction with huge variance can be useless for classification (for example, fish weight varying a lot within each species), and LDA will ignore it, while PCA will keep it. On the other hand, LDA needs labels and is limited to c - 1 directions.

When LDA struggles: if Sw is singular, which happens when there are more features than samples (common with images: 10,000 pixels and 500 face photos), Sw^-1 does not exist. The standard fix in face recognition is to run PCA first to reduce dimensions, then LDA, the Fisherfaces method; another fix is to add a small multiple of the identity to Sw (regularisation). LDA also assumes classes differ mainly in their means; if two classes have the same mean but different spreads (one class surrounding the other), no linear projection separates them.

Real-life example 1, Fisherfaces for office attendance: an office in Gulshan uses face recognition for attendance. Each 100 by 100 face image has 10,000 pixels. PCA first reduces each face to about 150 numbers, then LDA projects to at most (number of employees - 1) dimensions that best separate different people while ignoring changes in lighting and expression within each person. A new photo is projected and matched to the nearest employee. Fisherfaces became popular because it handles lighting changes better than PCA-only eigenfaces.

Real-life example 2, grading tea leaves in Sylhet: a tea estate measures five features of processed tea leaves (colour, size, moisture, aroma score, density) and has graders' labels "premium", "standard" and "dust". LDA gives two discriminant directions (c - 1 = 2). Plotting all samples on these two axes shows three clearly separated clouds, which convinces the managers to trust an automated grader using these two numbers and a nearest-mean rule.

Common mistakes: using Sb instead of Sw inside the inverse; forgetting that only the direction of w matters (any multiple is fine); claiming LDA gives c directions instead of at most c - 1; computing scatter with deviations from the overall mean instead of each class's own mean for Sw; and confusing LDA with PCA. Exams usually give two small classes in 2D and ask for the means, Sw, the Fisher direction, the projections and a threshold, plus a comparison with PCA.

Recap: Fisher's discriminant finds the projection w that maximises J(w) = (difference of projected means)^2 / (sum of projected scatters). The answer is w proportional to Sw^-1 (m1 - m2). On the worked data, w = (4, 1) gave J = 2.33 and perfect separation with threshold 17. For c classes, LDA gives at most c - 1 directions from Sw^-1 Sb. LDA is supervised and separation-oriented, unlike PCA, and needs care when features outnumber samples.
key_points: Fisher projects samples to y = w . x and maximises J(w) = (m1~ - m2~)^2 / (s1~^2 + s2~^2).
Within-class scatter Sw = S1 + S2; between-class Sb = (m1 - m2)(m1 - m2)^T; J = w^T Sb w / w^T Sw w.
Solution: w proportional to Sw^-1 (m1 - m2); only the direction matters.
Fisher still needs a threshold (17 in the worked case), possibly shifted for priors and costs.
For c classes, LDA gives at most c - 1 directions from the eigenvectors of Sw^-1 Sb.
LDA is supervised and seeks separation; PCA is unsupervised and seeks variance. Use PCA then LDA (Fisherfaces) when features outnumber samples.
lessons.tip: Remember Fisher as "between over within": the projected means should be far apart (between) and each class tight (within). If you can say that sentence, you can rebuild the formula J = w^T Sb w / w^T Sw w from memory.
lessons.task: Take the worked data and project it on three directions of your choice, for example (1, 1), (1, -1) and (2, 1). For each, compute the projected values, the two means, the two scatters and J. Check that none beats w = (4, 1).

quiz.q: What does Fisher's criterion J(w) measure?
options: The total variance of all samples
The squared gap between projected class means divided by the total within-class scatter on the line
quiz.explain: J is between-class separation over within-class spread along the projection direction.

quiz.q: Fisher's optimal direction is proportional to...
options: The largest-variance eigenvector of the data
quiz.explain: Maximising J gives w proportional to the inverse within-class scatter times the mean difference.

quiz.q: For 10 classes, how many discriminant directions can multiple discriminant analysis give at most?
quiz.explain: Sb has rank at most c - 1, so LDA gives at most 9 useful directions for 10 classes.

quiz.q: How does LDA differ from PCA?
options: PCA uses the between-class scatter matrix
LDA uses labels to find separating directions, PCA finds maximum-variance directions without labels
They always give the same directions
quiz.explain: LDA is supervised and separation-oriented; PCA is unsupervised and variance-oriented.

quiz.q: Why is Fisherfaces (PCA followed by LDA) used for face recognition?
options: With more pixels than training images, Sw is singular, so PCA first reduces dimensions to make LDA possible
LDA cannot handle more than two people
PCA removes the need for a threshold
quiz.explain: Thousands of pixels and a few hundred images make Sw non-invertible; PCA shrinks the space first.

lessons.title: Support Vector Machines and the Kernel Trick
lessons.content:
On a narrow village road, two lines of parked rickshaws face each other, and the traffic police want to paint a centre line so that the road is split fairly. Any line between the two rows separates them, but the sensible one is right in the middle, leaving the widest possible gap on each side. If one rickshaw shifts a little, nothing goes wrong. The support vector machine (SVM) chooses its boundary in exactly this spirit: among all separating lines, pick the one with the widest gap, the maximum margin. You met the basic idea in deep-cse-6-1-19. Here we recap it briefly and then go deeper into the pattern recognition view: the dual form, why only dot products matter, the kernel trick worked with numbers, and how SVMs compare with the classic linear discriminants of lessons 12 to 14.

Why margin matters: the perceptron stops at the first separating line, MSE can even miss separating lines, and Fisher picks a direction based on means and scatter. None of them asks "how safe is this boundary?". A boundary that barely clears the samples will misclassify new samples that differ only slightly. Statistical learning theory, developed by Vapnik and colleagues, shows that a larger margin gives a tighter guarantee on error for new data, roughly independent of the number of features. That is the core reason SVMs generalise well even in very high dimensions.

Recap, the setup: labels yi are +1 or -1. The classifier is f(x) = sign(w . x + b). We scale w and b so that the samples closest to the boundary satisfy yi (w . xi + b) = 1, and all others satisfy yi (w . xi + b) >= 1. With this scaling, the distance from the boundary to the closest samples is 1 / ||w||, and the full margin, from one side to the other, is 2 / ||w||. Maximising the margin is the same as minimising ||w||^2 / 2 subject to these constraints. The closest samples, the ones that touch the margin, are the support vectors.

Worked hard margin: two samples only, (1, 1) with label -1 and (3, 3) with label +1. The widest gap is the perpendicular bisector through (2, 2), so w points along (1, 1); write w = (a, a). The constraints with equality are 3a + 3a + b = 1 and a + a + b = -1. Subtracting gives 4a = 2, so a = 0.5 and b = -2. So w = (0.5, 0.5), ||w|| = 0.707, and the margin 2 / ||w|| = 2.83, exactly the distance between the two points, the square root of 8. Both samples are support vectors.

The dual form: the margin problem can be rewritten in terms of one number alpha_i >= 0 per sample, using Lagrange multipliers. The dual says: maximise sum of alpha_i - 1/2 sum over i and j of alpha_i alpha_j yi yj (xi . xj), subject to sum of alpha_i yi = 0. The solution gives w = sum of alpha_i yi xi. Only support vectors get alpha_i > 0; for every other sample alpha_i = 0, so they could be deleted without changing the answer. In our example, w = alpha x (3, 3) - alpha x (1, 1) = alpha x (2, 2), and matching w = (0.5, 0.5) gives alpha = 0.25 for both points.

The key observation, only dot products: in the dual, the samples appear only inside dot products xi . xj. And at prediction time, w . x + b = sum of alpha_i yi (xi . x) + b, again only dot products with the support vectors. The SVM never needs the coordinates of samples on their own; it only needs how similar each pair is, measured by a dot product. That observation opens the door to the kernel trick.

Predicting with support vectors, worked: classify x = (2, 3) using only the two support vectors. f(x) = 0.25 x (+1) x [(3, 3) . (2, 3)] + 0.25 x (-1) x [(1, 1) . (2, 3)] + b = 0.25 x 15 - 0.25 x 5 - 2 = 0.5, positive, so label +1. The same answer comes from w . x + b = 1 + 1.5 - 2 = 0.5. With a kernel we would simply replace each dot product by K(support vector, x).

The problem kernels solve: many problems are not linearly separable, for example a class that forms a ring around another (XOR in lesson 12 was another). Lesson 12 showed that adding new features like x1 x2 can make data separable. But adding all degree-2 products of 100 features gives over 5,000 new features, and degree 3 gives over 170,000; computing and storing them becomes expensive, and for some useful feature maps the new space is even infinite-dimensional.

The kernel trick: a kernel K(x, z) is a function that equals the dot product of x and z after some feature map phi, K(x, z) = phi(x) . phi(z), but computed directly from x and z without ever building phi. Replace every xi . xj in the SVM by K(xi, xj) and you get a linear SVM in the big feature space, computed at the cost of the small one. The boundary is linear in phi space, which looks curved back in the original space.

Kernel trick worked: take the polynomial kernel K(x, z) = (x . z)^2 in 2D. Its feature map is phi(x) = (x1^2, square root of 2 x1 x2, x2^2). Let x = (1, 2) and z = (3, 1). Directly: x . z = 3 + 2 = 5, so K = 25. Through the feature map: phi(x) = (1, 2.83, 4) and phi(z) = (9, 4.24, 1); their dot product is 9 + 12 + 4 = 25. Same answer, but the kernel needed one dot product and one squaring, while the map needed building two 3D vectors. For high degree and many features the saving becomes enormous.

Common kernels: linear K = x . z (plain SVM). Polynomial K = (x . z + c)^p, with degree p. Gaussian or RBF K = exp(-gamma ||x - z||^2), which measures similarity by distance and corresponds to an infinite-dimensional feature map. Sigmoid kernels are sometimes used but are not valid kernels for all settings. A function is a valid kernel when every matrix of pairwise kernel values is symmetric and positive semi-definite (Mercer's condition).

RBF kernel and gamma, worked: for x = (1, 2) and z = (3, 1), the squared distance is 4 + 1 = 5. With gamma = 0.5, K = exp(-2.5) = 0.082: these points count as quite dissimilar. With gamma = 0.1, K = exp(-0.5) = 0.61: fairly similar. Large gamma makes each support vector's influence very local, giving wiggly boundaries that can overfit; small gamma makes influence wide and boundaries smooth, possibly underfitting. The RBF SVM then behaves like a smart, weighted nearest neighbour rule using only the support vectors.

Soft margin and C: real data overlap, so we allow some samples inside the margin or on the wrong side, with slack variables. The objective becomes ||w||^2 / 2 + C x sum of slacks. The equivalent loss per sample is the hinge loss, max(0, 1 - yi f(xi)). Worked: a sample with yi f(xi) = 1.5 has loss 0 (safely correct); 0.4 has loss 0.6 (correct but inside the margin); -0.5 has loss 1.5 (wrong side). Notice the contrast with MSE in lesson 13: samples that are "too correct" cost nothing, which fixes the faraway-point problem. Large C punishes violations heavily (narrow margin, risk of overfitting); small C tolerates them (wide margin, smoother boundary). C and gamma are tuned together by cross-validation, usually on a grid.

Multiclass SVMs: SVMs are naturally two-class. For c classes, use one-vs-rest (c SVMs) or one-vs-one (c(c - 1)/2 SVMs with voting), as in lesson 12. Popular SVM libraries such as LIBSVM use one-vs-one by default; each small SVM trains only on two classes, which is fast even though there are many of them.

Comparing the linear methods: the perceptron finds any separating line, if one exists. MSE always finds an answer by least squares but can misplace the line. Fisher finds the best projection for separating means relative to scatter, with a closed formula. The SVM finds the maximum-margin line and depends only on the support vectors, so samples far from the boundary have no influence at all. With kernels, the SVM extends to curved boundaries at little extra cost. A useful bonus: the expected leave-one-out error is at most the expected number of support vectors divided by n, so a model with few support vectors tends to generalise well.

Limits of SVMs: training time grows roughly between n^2 and n^3 with the number of samples, so plain kernel SVMs become slow beyond a few hundred thousand samples. Choosing the kernel, C and gamma takes careful cross-validation. Outputs are distances from the boundary, not probabilities; extra calibration (such as fitting a sigmoid to the scores, Platt scaling) is needed for posteriors. And features must be scaled, because the RBF kernel uses distances.

Real-life example 1, Bangla handwritten digit recognition: before deep learning, a strong recipe for digits was: normalise each digit image, extract features such as gradient direction histograms, then train an RBF SVM with one-vs-one voting, tuning C and gamma by cross-validation. On standard Bangla numeral datasets such systems reached high accuracy, and SVMs remain a solid baseline when the training set is only a few thousand images.

Real-life example 2, detecting faulty jute bags on a production line: a factory camera extracts 40 texture features from each bag. Only 3 percent of bags are faulty. A linear SVM with class weights (a bigger C for the rare faulty class) finds a boundary determined by a few hundred support vectors out of 20,000 training bags. Because only support vectors matter, the factory can retrain quickly as new borderline examples are labelled, without storing all past bags.

Common mistakes: thinking the margin is 1 / ||w|| (that is half of it); forgetting that only support vectors determine the solution; believing the kernel computes phi explicitly; not scaling features before an RBF kernel; tuning C or gamma on the test set; and reading SVM scores as probabilities. Exams ask for the margin from a given w, finding w and b for two or three points, verifying a kernel equals a feature-map dot product, explaining the effect of C and gamma, and the hinge loss for given scores.

Recap: SVMs choose the separating hyperplane with the maximum margin 2 / ||w||, determined by support vectors. The dual form depends on data only through dot products, so replacing them by a kernel K(x, z) = phi(x) . phi(z) gives curved boundaries without building phi; (x . z)^2 for (1, 2) and (3, 1) gave 25 both ways. Soft margins use the hinge loss and C; RBF kernels add gamma. SVMs generalise well, but need scaling, tuning and care with large data.
key_points: SVM maximises the margin 2/||w|| subject to yi (w . xi + b) >= 1; the closest samples are support vectors.
Worked: points (1, 1) and (3, 3) give w = (0.5, 0.5), b = -2, margin 2.83.
Dual form: w = sum of alpha_i yi xi; only support vectors have alpha_i > 0; data enter only via dot products.
Kernel trick: K(x, z) = phi(x) . phi(z); (x . z)^2 for (1, 2) and (3, 1) gives 25 directly and via phi.
RBF kernel exp(-gamma ||x - z||^2): gamma 0.5 gives 0.082, gamma 0.1 gives 0.61 for squared distance 5.
Soft margin uses hinge loss max(0, 1 - y f(x)) and C; correct samples beyond the margin cost nothing.
Multiclass via one-vs-rest or one-vs-one; scale features and tune C and gamma by cross-validation.
lessons.tip: When stuck on an SVM question, draw the two dashed margin lines w . x + b = +1 and -1 as well as the boundary. Support vectors sit on the dashed lines, and the margin is the gap between them, 2/||w||.
lessons.task: Pick any two 2D points, for example (2, 1) and (1, 3). Compute (x . z)^2 directly, then build phi(x) = (x1^2, 1.414 x1 x2, x2^2) for each and take their dot product. Confirm they match. Then compute the RBF kernel with gamma 1 and 0.1.

quiz.q: For an SVM with weight vector w, what is the width of the full margin?
quiz.explain: Each side is 1/||w|| from the boundary, so the full margin is 2/||w||.

quiz.q: In the dual SVM solution, which samples have non-zero alpha?
options: Only misclassified samples far from the boundary
Only samples of the positive class
quiz.explain: Samples strictly outside the margin get alpha = 0; only support vectors determine w.

quiz.q: For x = (1, 2) and z = (3, 1), what is the polynomial kernel (x . z)^2?
quiz.explain: x . z = 3 + 2 = 5, and 5^2 = 25, the same as phi(x) . phi(z).

quiz.q: What usually happens if gamma in an RBF kernel is made very large?
options: The boundary becomes a straight line
Each support vector influences only a tiny region, giving wiggly, overfitted boundaries
quiz.explain: Large gamma makes similarity drop quickly with distance, so the model memorises local detail.

quiz.q: A sample has y f(x) = 0.4. What is its hinge loss?
quiz.explain: max(0, 1 - 0.4) = 0.6; it is correctly classified but inside the margin.

lessons.title: Feature Extraction with PCA and Eigenfaces
lessons.content:
Imagine describing every student in your class with 50 measurements: height, arm length, leg length, shoe size, hand span, and so on. You would soon notice that most of these numbers rise and fall together: a tall student usually has long arms, long legs and big shoes. Much of the 50 numbers is really one story, "how big is this person", told 50 times. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) finds such hidden stories automatically. It creates a few new features, combinations of the old ones, that keep most of the variation in the data, so that 50 numbers might become 3 with little loss. You met PCA in deep-cse-6-1-23. Here we treat it as a pattern recognition feature extractor: why it works, a full worked example with reconstruction error, the eigenfaces pipeline for face recognition, and its limits.

Feature extraction vs feature selection: there are two ways to reduce features. Feature selection keeps some of the original features and drops the rest (next lesson). Feature extraction builds new features as functions of all the originals, for example weighted sums. PCA is the classic linear feature extraction method: each new feature is a weighted sum of the old ones.

Why reduce at all: fewer features mean less storage and faster classifiers; they reduce the curse of dimensionality for density and nearest neighbour methods (lesson 10); they remove noise living in directions with tiny variance; they make singular covariance matrices invertible; and with 2 or 3 features we can finally plot and look at the data. In pattern recognition PCA is often the first step before LDA, Bayes or k-NN.

The idea, directions of largest spread: imagine a cloud of points shaped like a cigar. The first principal component is the direction along the cigar, where the data spread the most. The second is perpendicular to the first and captures the most of what is left, and so on. If the cigar is thin, projecting every point onto the first direction loses very little: the points barely move.

Two views that give the same answer: PCA can be defined as the projection that keeps the maximum variance, or as the projection that gives the minimum average squared reconstruction error (the distance between each point and its projection). Remarkably, both definitions give the same directions: the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, sorted by eigenvalue. The eigenvalue of each direction equals the variance of the data along it.

The PCA recipe: first, subtract the mean from every sample (centring). Second, compute the covariance matrix. Third, find its eigenvalues and eigenvectors and sort them from largest eigenvalue down. Fourth, keep the top k eigenvectors as the new axes. Fifth, project each centred sample onto these axes: the k projection values are the new features. To reconstruct, go back: mean plus the sum of each projection value times its eigenvector.

Worked example, the data: the four points from lesson 03: (1, 2), (3, 3), (5, 7), (7, 8). Mean (4, 5). Centred: (-3, -3), (-1, -2), (1, 2), (3, 3). Covariance (dividing by n = 4): [[5, 5.5], [5.5, 6.5]].

Worked example, eigenvalues: for a 2 by 2 matrix, eigenvalues satisfy lambda^2 - (trace) lambda + (determinant) = 0. Trace = 5 + 6.5 = 11.5, determinant = 5 x 6.5 - 5.5 x 5.5 = 32.5 - 30.25 = 2.25. So lambda = (11.5 plus or minus the square root of (132.25 - 9)) / 2 = (11.5 plus or minus 11.10) / 2, giving lambda1 = 11.30 and lambda2 = 0.20. The total variance is 11.5, and the first component keeps 11.30 / 11.5 = 98.3 percent of it.

Worked example, the first direction: the eigenvector for lambda1 satisfies (5 - 11.30) v1 + 5.5 v2 = 0, so v2 = 1.146 v1. Normalised to length 1: u1 = (0.658, 0.753), a direction pointing up and to the right, along the cloud. The second eigenvector is perpendicular: u2 = (-0.753, 0.658).

Worked example, projections: project each centred point on u1. (-3, -3) gives -3 x 0.658 - 3 x 0.753 = -4.23. (-1, -2) gives -2.16. (1, 2) gives 2.16. (3, 3) gives 4.23. Each sample is now one number. Check: the average of the squares, (17.92 + 4.68 + 4.68 + 17.92) / 4 = 11.30, exactly lambda1, as promised.

Worked example, reconstruction: rebuild each point from its one number as mean + value x u1. The point (1, 2) has value -4.23, so it becomes (4 - 4.23 x 0.658, 5 - 4.23 x 0.753) = (1.22, 1.81), close to (1, 2). The point (3, 3) becomes (2.58, 3.37). The average squared reconstruction error over the four points is 0.20, exactly lambda2, the variance we threw away. That is the general rule: the reconstruction error equals the sum of the discarded eigenvalues.

PCA is just a rotation: keeping all d components loses nothing; it only rotates the axes so that they line up with the cloud, and in the new axes the features are uncorrelated (the new covariance matrix is diagonal, with the eigenvalues on the diagonal). Information is lost only when we drop the smallest components.

Choosing k: plot the eigenvalues from largest to smallest (a scree plot) and look for an elbow where they flatten. Or keep enough components to explain a target share of variance, such as 90 or 95 percent: add eigenvalues until the running total divided by the trace passes the target. Or, best for classification, choose k by cross-validated accuracy of the final classifier.

Choosing k, worked: suppose 7 features give eigenvalues 50, 25, 12, 6, 4, 2 and 1, total 100. The running shares are 50, 75, 87, 93, 97, 99 and 100 percent. For a 90 percent target keep 4 components; for 95 percent keep 5. The scree plot drops steeply over the first three values and flattens after the fourth, so an elbow reading would suggest 3 or 4. Different rules give slightly different answers, which is why a final check with the classifier itself is wise.

Scaling matters: PCA follows variance, and variance depends on units. If one feature is income in taka (variance in millions) and another is age in years (variance around 100), the first component will simply be "income". Standardise features first (lesson 02) unless they are already in the same units, as pixels are.

Eigenfaces, the pipeline: Turk and Pentland (1991) applied PCA to faces. Step 1: collect aligned face images of the same size, for example 100 by 100 grey pixels, giving 10,000 numbers per face. Step 2: compute the mean face and subtract it from every face. Step 3: compute the principal components; each one is a 10,000-number vector that can be displayed as a ghostly face image, an eigenface. Step 4: describe every face by its projections on the top k eigenfaces, perhaps 50 to 150 numbers. Step 5: to recognise a new face, centre it, project it, and find the nearest stored face in this small space, with a distance threshold to reject strangers.

Eigenfaces, the computational trick: the covariance of 10,000-pixel images is a 10,000 by 10,000 matrix, 100 million entries, too big to handle easily. But with only n = 400 training faces, there are at most 399 non-zero eigenvalues. The trick: compute the small 400 by 400 matrix of dot products between centred faces, find its eigenvectors, and multiply each by the data matrix to get the eigenfaces. The answer is the same, at a tiny fraction of the cost. The same idea underlies computing PCA through the singular value decomposition (deep-cse-2-5).

Eigenfaces, reconstruction as a detector: a face reconstructed from 100 eigenfaces looks like the original. A non-face image, such as a picture of a car, reconstructs badly, because eigenfaces only know face-like patterns. So the reconstruction error, the "distance from face space", can tell whether an image patch contains a face at all.

Whitening: after projecting, divide each component by the square root of its eigenvalue. Now every new feature has variance 1 and they are uncorrelated: the cloud becomes a round ball. Whitening makes Euclidean distance in the new space equal to Mahalanobis distance in the old one (lesson 06), and many algorithms work better on whitened inputs. Be careful: whitening also blows up tiny, noisy components, so drop those first.

Limits of PCA: it is unsupervised, so the directions of large variance need not separate classes; lighting changes in face images have huge variance and dominate the first eigenfaces, which is exactly why Fisherfaces (lesson 14) adds LDA after PCA. PCA is linear, so curved structures such as data lying on a circle are not compressed well. It is sensitive to outliers, because squared deviations let one extreme point pull a component. And the new features are mixtures of all originals, harder to interpret than selected features.

Beyond linear PCA: kernel PCA applies the kernel trick of lesson 15 to PCA, finding curved directions of variance. Independent Component Analysis (ICA) looks for statistically independent rather than merely uncorrelated components, famous for separating mixed sound sources, such as two people talking at once into two microphones. Autoencoder neural networks learn nonlinear compressions; a linear autoencoder with squared loss learns the same subspace as PCA. These are only named here; Computer Vision (deep-cse-8-3) and Deep Learning (deep-cse-8-1) go further.

Real-life example 1, compressing sensor data from a garment factory: a factory in Gazipur logs 60 sensor readings per sewing line every minute: temperatures, vibrations, motor currents. Many sensors move together. PCA shows that 6 components explain 95 percent of the variance. The factory stores the 6 numbers instead of 60 and flags a line when its reconstruction error jumps, which usually means a machine is behaving in a new, possibly faulty way.

Real-life example 2, finding a face in a crowd photo: a simple security tool slides a 64 by 64 window over a photo of a busy station and, for each window, computes the distance from face space using eigenfaces trained on cropped faces. Windows with small error are candidate faces, then passed to a recogniser. Modern systems use deep networks, but this was one of the first practical face finders and shows PCA's two uses at once: compression and detection.

Common mistakes: forgetting to subtract the mean; mixing up eigenvalues and eigenvectors (eigenvalues are variances, eigenvectors are directions); using unscaled features with different units; claiming the first component always separates the classes best; and choosing k on the test set. Exams ask for a full 2D PCA by hand (covariance, eigenvalues, eigenvector, projection, explained variance, reconstruction error), the eigenfaces steps, the small-matrix trick, and PCA vs LDA.

Recap: PCA finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance, the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, and projects data onto the top k. Variance kept equals the kept eigenvalues and reconstruction error equals the discarded ones: in the worked case 98.3 percent kept and error 0.20. Eigenfaces apply PCA to face images, with a small-matrix trick for speed and reconstruction error for detection. PCA is simple and powerful but unsupervised, linear and sensitive to scale and outliers.
key_points: PCA is linear feature extraction: new features are projections on the top eigenvectors of the covariance matrix.
Maximum variance and minimum reconstruction error give the same directions; each eigenvalue is the variance along its eigenvector.
Worked: covariance [[5, 5.5], [5.5, 6.5]] has eigenvalues 11.30 and 0.20; first direction (0.658, 0.753) keeps 98.3 percent.
Projections -4.23, -2.16, 2.16, 4.23 have variance 11.30; average reconstruction error 0.20 equals the dropped eigenvalue.
Choose k by scree plot, target explained variance (90 to 95 percent) or classifier cross-validation; standardise first.
Eigenfaces: mean face, eigenfaces from a small n by n matrix, project, nearest match; reconstruction error detects faces.
PCA is unsupervised, linear and outlier-sensitive; kernel PCA, ICA and autoencoders go beyond it.
lessons.tip: For a 2 by 2 covariance matrix, remember the shortcut: eigenvalues come from lambda^2 - trace x lambda + determinant = 0. With trace and determinant you can do any 2D PCA exam question in a few lines.
lessons.task: Take 6 friends' heights and arm spans (or estimate them). Centre the data, compute the 2 by 2 covariance matrix, its eigenvalues and the first eigenvector. What percentage of variance does the first component explain? What does the direction mean in words?

quiz.q: What do the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix represent in PCA?
options: The directions of the new axes
The variance of the data along each principal direction
quiz.explain: Each eigenvalue is the variance of the projections onto its eigenvector.

quiz.q: For covariance [[5, 5.5], [5.5, 6.5]], eigenvalues are 11.30 and 0.20. What share of variance does the first component explain?
If you keep only the first component in that example, what is the average squared reconstruction error?
quiz.explain: The reconstruction error equals the sum of the discarded eigenvalues.

quiz.q: Why is PCA computed from a small n by n matrix in eigenfaces?
options: The small matrix gives different, better eigenfaces
Faces have fewer pixels than images
With far fewer images than pixels, the n by n matrix has the same non-zero eigenvalues and is much cheaper
PCA only works on square images
quiz.explain: With n = 400 faces of 10,000 pixels, solving a 400 by 400 problem gives the same components as the 10,000 by 10,000 one.

quiz.q: Why should features usually be standardised before PCA?
options: PCA follows variance, so a feature with large units would dominate the components
quiz.explain: Variance depends on units, so without scaling the largest-unit feature captures the first component.

lessons.title: Feature Selection and the Curse of Dimensionality
lessons.content:
A cricket selector has statistics for 40 things about each player: batting average, strike rate, catches, shoe size, favourite food, birth month and many more. Picking the team using all 40 would be silly; shoe size and birth month add only noise, and with only a few seasons of data, those noisy numbers could even fool the selector into odd choices. A good selector picks the handful of statistics that actually predict match performance. Feature selection does this for a classifier: choose a small subset of the original features that gives the best recognition. Unlike PCA (lesson 16), it keeps original, interpretable features and simply drops the rest.

Why not use every feature: it seems that more information can never hurt. With infinite data, that is true: the Bayes error can only stay the same or drop when a feature is added. But we never have infinite data. Each new feature adds parameters to estimate, and with a fixed training set the estimates become worse. Beyond some point, adding features makes a real classifier less accurate. Feature selection also saves measurement cost (a medical test not needed is a test not paid for), speeds up the system and makes it easier to explain.

The curse of dimensionality, again: lesson 10 showed that in high dimensions, local neighbourhoods are no longer local: to catch 10 percent of uniform data in 10 dimensions, a cube needs a side of 0.79. Another view: to keep the same density of samples, the number needed grows exponentially with d. With 10 bins per feature, 1 feature needs about 10 samples to put one in each bin, 2 features need 100, 3 need 1,000, and 10 features need 10 billion. Most real data sets are tiny compared with that.

The peaking phenomenon: G. F. Hughes showed in 1968 that, for a fixed number of training samples, the accuracy of a designed classifier first rises as features are added and then falls. The best number of features peaks at some value that grows with the number of samples. This is called the peaking or Hughes phenomenon. It is the practical reason feature selection matters: there is an optimal number of features for your amount of data, and it is usually much smaller than the number you could measure.

Two goals of selection: remove irrelevant features, which carry no information about the class (birth month for cricket performance), and remove redundant features, which repeat information already present (length in cm and length in inches). Naive Bayes in lesson 09 showed how redundant features cause double counting; distance methods suffer when irrelevant features add random noise to every distance.

Three families of methods: filter methods score each feature, or subset, with a quick statistic computed from the data, independent of any classifier, and keep the best. Wrapper methods use the actual classifier: try subsets, measure cross-validated accuracy, keep the best subset. Embedded methods do selection as part of training itself, such as L1 (lasso) regularisation that pushes useless weights to exactly zero, or decision trees that only split on useful features.

Filter scores, the Fisher score: for one feature and two classes, F = (m1 - m2)^2 / (s1^2 + s2^2), the same between-over-within idea as Fisher's discriminant (lesson 14) applied to a single feature. Worked: feature A has class means 10 and 14 and class variances 4 and 4, so F = 16 / 8 = 2. Feature B has means 5 and 6 and variances 1 and 1, so F = 1 / 2 = 0.5. Feature A separates the classes better and ranks higher. Other filters use correlation with the label, the chi-squared statistic for categorical features, or mutual information.

Mutual information: mutual information I(X; Y) measures how much knowing feature X reduces uncertainty about class Y, in bits. It is zero when X and Y are independent and captures non-linear relationships that correlation misses. Many filter methods rank features by mutual information with the class while penalising mutual information with already chosen features, which handles redundancy too.

Spotting redundancy, worked: suppose a fish data set has length in cm, length in inches and body depth. Length in cm and inches have correlation 1.0: one is just 2.54 times the other. A correlation filter that ranks features by their link to the class would put both lengths at the top, because both are equally good. A redundancy check then looks at the correlation between already chosen features and drops any new one whose correlation with a chosen feature is above, say, 0.95. Here the inches feature is dropped and body depth, which carries new information, is kept. Methods such as minimum-redundancy maximum-relevance (mRMR) formalise this balance with mutual information.

Selection vs extraction, which to use: selection keeps original measurements, so a doctor can still read "glucose and BMI matter", and unused sensors need not be bought or measured at all. Extraction like PCA or LDA can capture information spread thinly over many features and often reaches higher accuracy with fewer numbers, but every original feature must still be measured and the new features are harder to explain. In practice, people often select first to remove junk, then extract.

The weakness of single-feature filters: they judge each feature alone. Two features can each be useless on their own but powerful together; XOR from lesson 12 is the extreme case, where neither x1 nor x2 alone says anything about the class, but both together decide it perfectly. Single-feature scores would throw both away. Also, two highly correlated features may both score high, and a filter would keep both even though the second adds nothing.

The search problem: with d features there are 2^d - 1 non-empty subsets. For d = 20 that is 1,048,575 subsets; even choosing exactly 5 of 20 has 15,504 options. Testing every subset with a wrapper (training a classifier and cross-validating each time) is far too slow for any realistic d. So we need search strategies.

Sequential forward selection (SFS): start with no features. At each step, try adding each remaining feature, keep the one that improves the score most, and repeat until adding stops helping or a target size is reached. It needs at most d + (d - 1) + ... evaluations, roughly d^2 / 2, instead of 2^d.

SFS worked: four features A, B, C, D, scored by cross-validated accuracy. Singles: A 0.70, B 0.65, C 0.60, D 0.55, so pick A. Pairs with A: A+B 0.78, A+C 0.82, A+D 0.74, so add C (interesting: C was weak alone but complements A well). Triples with A and C: A+C+B 0.83, A+C+D 0.81, so adding B gives a tiny gain of 0.01. If we stop when the gain is below 0.02, the answer is {A, C}. Using all four features gives 0.80, lower than {A, C}: a little peaking effect in our table.

Sequential backward selection (SBS): start with all features and remove one at a time, each time dropping the feature whose removal hurts least (or helps most). Worked with the same table: all four 0.80. Remove one: B+C+D 0.70, A+C+D 0.81, A+B+D 0.79, A+B+C 0.83. Dropping D helps most, giving A+B+C at 0.83. Remove one more: B+C 0.72, A+C 0.82, A+B 0.78. Dropping B costs only 0.01, so if we prefer smaller sets, keep {A, C}. SBS considers features in context from the start, which helps with interacting features, but its early steps train classifiers on many features, which is slower.

The nesting problem and fixes: in SFS, once a feature is added it can never be removed; in SBS, once removed it never returns. A feature chosen early may become redundant later. Plus-l take-away-r adds l features by SFS steps and then removes r by SBS steps, repeatedly. Sequential floating forward selection (SFFS) goes further: after each addition, it keeps removing features as long as that improves the score, so the subset size "floats". Floating methods are a popular practical choice.

Optimal search, branch and bound: if the criterion is monotonic, meaning that removing a feature can never increase the score (true for some separability measures like Mahalanobis distance between classes, not for cross-validated accuracy), then branch and bound can find the truly best subset of size k without checking all of them. It explores a tree of removals and prunes any branch whose score already falls below the best complete subset found so far.

Embedded selection with L1: train a linear model with an L1 penalty, lambda times the sum of absolute weights. Unlike L2, the L1 penalty drives many weights exactly to zero, and the features with zero weight are dropped. Increasing lambda gives sparser models. This is fast, considers features jointly, and is a common choice for text and gene data with thousands of features.

Avoiding selection bias: a classic mistake is to select features using all the data, then cross-validate the classifier on those features. The selection has already seen the test folds, so the accuracy estimate is optimistic, sometimes wildly so when there are thousands of features and few samples. Correct practice: do feature selection inside each training fold, as part of the pipeline being validated.

Real-life example 1, early detection of diabetic patients: a district hospital has 30 possible measurements for each patient: age, weight, blood pressure, family history, several blood tests, and so on. Some tests are expensive. Using SFFS with a logistic regression classifier and cross-validation, the analysts find that 6 features (fasting glucose, HbA1c, BMI, age, waist size, family history) give accuracy within 1 percent of using all 30. The hospital adopts the cheaper 6-feature screen, saving money for thousands of patients.

Real-life example 2, spam filtering with a huge vocabulary: an SMS filter could use 50,000 distinct words as features. A mutual information filter keeps the top 2,000 words most informative about spam, which removes rare and neutral words like "the" or "and". The naive Bayes classifier trained on these 2,000 words is faster and slightly more accurate than one using all 50,000, a direct example of peaking.

Common mistakes: assuming more features always help; judging features only one at a time and missing interactions; selecting features on the full data set before cross-validation (selection bias); confusing feature selection (keep originals) with extraction (build new ones, like PCA); and believing SFS finds the optimal subset (it is greedy). Exams ask you to compute a Fisher score, run SFS or SBS on a small accuracy table, explain peaking, compare filter, wrapper and embedded methods, and count subsets.

Recap: with finite data, extra features eventually hurt (peaking), and the number of samples needed grows exponentially with dimension. Feature selection keeps a small subset of original features. Filters (Fisher score, mutual information) are fast but judge features alone; wrappers (SFS, SBS, floating search) use the real classifier but cost more; embedded methods (L1, trees) select while training. Always do selection inside cross-validation.
key_points: Peaking (Hughes): with fixed training size, accuracy rises then falls as features are added.
Samples needed grow exponentially with d: 10 bins per feature means 10^d cells.
Filter, wrapper and embedded are the three families of feature selection.
Fisher score F = (m1 - m2)^2 / (s1^2 + s2^2): means 10 vs 14 with variances 4 and 4 give F = 2.
20 features have 1,048,575 subsets, so greedy searches like SFS and SBS are used.
SFS worked: A (0.70), then A+C (0.82), then A+C+B (0.83); all four give only 0.80.
Floating search fixes nesting; L1 gives embedded selection; always select inside each cross-validation fold.
lessons.tip: Keep a small table of subsets and scores as you run SFS or SBS by hand, one row per step. Exams often hide a feature that is weak alone but strong in a pair, and the table makes that visible.
lessons.task: Choose a decision you make, such as which mango to buy. List 8 possible features (colour, smell, softness, price, size, seller, time of day, weather). Rank them by how much you think each helps, then try picking with only your top 2 and top 4 for a week. Did the extra features really help?

quiz.q: What is the peaking (Hughes) phenomenon?
options: With a fixed number of samples, classifier accuracy first rises and then falls as more features are added
Accuracy always rises with more features
PCA always finds the peak of the data
The Bayes error rises with every feature
quiz.explain: Adding features adds parameters to estimate; beyond some point the estimates get worse and accuracy drops.

quiz.q: Feature A has class means 10 and 14 with variances 4 and 4. What is its Fisher score?
Which method type uses the actual classifier's cross-validated accuracy to judge subsets?
quiz.explain: Wrappers wrap the selection around the real classifier and evaluate each subset with it.

quiz.q: In the SFS example, why is C added after A even though C alone scored lowest after D?
options: C has the highest Fisher score
A+C scores 0.82, the best pair with A, because C complements A
quiz.explain: SFS adds the feature that most improves the current subset, which can be a feature weak on its own.

quiz.q: Why is selecting features on the full data set before cross-validation a mistake?
options: The selection has seen the test folds, so the accuracy estimate is too optimistic
Cross-validation cannot run on selected features
quiz.explain: Selection must be done inside each training fold; otherwise information leaks from test data.

lessons.title: Template Matching and Dynamic Time Warping
lessons.content:
Your grandmother says "kemon acho" slowly, stretching every vowel. Your little cousin says it in half a second. A friend says it with a cold. You recognise all three instantly, because your brain compares what you hear with a remembered pattern and quietly stretches and squeezes it in time until the two line up. This lesson is about the simplest way computers recognise patterns: keep a stored example, the template, and measure how well a new sample matches it. For images we slide the template around; for sounds, signatures and gestures, which can be fast or slow, we also need to bend time. That bending is dynamic time warping (DTW).

What template matching is: store one or a few typical examples of each class, the templates. To classify a new sample, compare it with every template and pick the class whose template matches best. It is the nearest neighbour idea of lesson 11 applied to raw patterns, such as images or signals, rather than to short feature vectors. It needs no training beyond choosing good templates, which makes it attractive when you have only one or two examples per class.

Why we need it: before statistical classifiers were practical, early character readers, simple speech systems and industrial inspection used templates. Today template matching still finds a logo on a product, locates a known part on a circuit board, finds a printed form's corner marks to align it, and powers signature and keyword spotting with very few examples.

Sliding a template over an image: to find where a small template appears in a larger image, place the template at each position, compute a match score between the template and the image patch under it, and record the score. The best position is the location of the object. This is closely related to correlation and convolution from Signals and DSP (deep-cse-3-7, deep-cse-5-7) and to image processing (deep-cse-6-4).

Score 1, sum of squared differences: SSD = sum of (t_i - s_i)^2 over the template positions. Zero means a perfect match; smaller is better. Worked in 1D: template t = (1, 3, 2), signal s = (0, 1, 3, 2, 1, 2, 6, 4). Slide over the six windows of length 3. Window (0, 1, 3) gives 1 + 4 + 1 = 6. Window (1, 3, 2) gives 0, a perfect match at position 1. Window (3, 2, 1) gives 6. Window (2, 1, 2) gives 5. Window (1, 2, 6) gives 17. Window (2, 6, 4) gives 14. SSD finds the exact copy at position 1.

The brightness problem: look at the last window, (2, 6, 4). It is exactly twice the template: the same shape, just with stronger contrast, as if the lights were brighter. SSD gives it 14, a poor match. In real images, lighting changes all the time, so SSD often fails to find the object.

Score 2, normalised cross-correlation (NCC): subtract the mean from the template and from the window, then compute their correlation coefficient: NCC = sum of (t_i - t_mean)(s_i - s_mean) divided by the square root of (sum of (t_i - t_mean)^2 x sum of (s_i - s_mean)^2). It ranges from -1 to +1, where +1 means the same shape. Because means are subtracted and the result is divided by the spreads, NCC ignores changes in brightness (adding a constant) and contrast (multiplying by a positive constant).

NCC worked: for the same signal, the window (1, 3, 2) gives NCC = 1.0 and the window (2, 6, 4) also gives 1.0, because it is just 2 times the template. The window (2, 1, 2) gives -0.87, a nearly opposite shape; (3, 2, 1) gives -0.5; (0, 1, 3) gives 0.33. NCC finds both copies of the shape, whatever their brightness. This is why NCC is the standard score in template matching.

Limits of plain template matching: templates are rigid. A digit written slightly rotated, larger, slanted or with a thicker pen matches poorly. Handling every rotation and scale means storing or testing many versions of each template, which is slow. Partial occlusion (part of the object hidden) also ruins scores. And the cost grows with image size times template size, unless the correlation is computed with FFTs. For these reasons, modern systems match features or learned representations rather than raw pixels, but the idea is the same.

Sequences of different speed: speech, handwriting trajectories, signatures, gestures and sensor recordings are sequences in time. The same word can be spoken in 0.4 seconds or 0.8 seconds, and not uniformly faster: one person stretches the first vowel, another the last. Comparing two sequences point by point fails as soon as they are out of step, and if lengths differ, it is not even defined. We need to align them first.

Why point-by-point fails, worked: take A = (0, 1, 3, 1, 0, 0) and B = (0, 0, 1, 3, 1, 0), the same bump with B starting one step later. Comparing position by position, the absolute differences are 0, 1, 2, 2, 1, 0, a total of 6, so the two look quite different. DTW lets the first 0 of A cover both leading 0s of B and the last 0 of B cover both trailing 0s of A, and every other value matches exactly: DTW distance 0. A tiny shift in time fooled the simple comparison completely.

Choosing templates: with one template per class, the template should be a typical, clean example. With several, they should cover the main variations, such as a slanted and an upright "4", or a word spoken by a man and by a woman. A common trick is to cluster the training examples of each class (lesson 21) and keep the cluster centres, or the most central example of each cluster, as templates. More templates improve accuracy but cost more matching time.

The DTW idea: find the best alignment, a warping path that pairs each element of sequence A with one or more elements of sequence B, such that the path starts at the beginning of both sequences, ends at the end of both, and always moves forward in time (never backwards). The DTW distance is the total cost of the cheapest such path, where the cost of pairing a_i with b_j is usually |a_i - b_j| or its square.

The DTW recurrence: fill a table D where D(i, j) is the cheapest cost of aligning the first i elements of A with the first j elements of B. D(i, j) = cost(a_i, b_j) + minimum of D(i - 1, j), D(i, j - 1) and D(i - 1, j - 1). The three options mean: b_j is matched with a_(i-1) too (A is stretched), a_i is matched with b_(j-1) too (B is stretched), or both step forward together. Start with D(0, 0) = 0 and infinity on the other borders. The answer is D(n, m). This is dynamic programming, the same idea as edit distance (lesson 23) and as in Algorithms (deep-cse-3-1).

DTW worked, an exact stretch: A = (1, 3, 4, 2) and B = (1, 1, 3, 4, 2), the same word with the first sound held longer. Point-by-point comparison is impossible (lengths 4 and 5). DTW pairs both 1s of B with the single 1 of A and matches the rest exactly, so the DTW distance is 0. Time warping has removed the speed difference completely.

DTW worked, the table: now A = (1, 3, 4, 2) and B = (1, 2, 3, 5, 2), with cost |a - b|. Row for a = 1: 0, 1, 3, 7, 8. Row for a = 3: 2, 1, 1, 3, 4. Row for a = 4: 5, 3, 2, 2, 4. Row for a = 2: 6, 3, 3, 5, 2. The bottom-right cell gives DTW = 2. Tracing back the minimum choices gives the path: 1 with 1 (cost 0), 3 with 2 (cost 1), 3 with 3 (cost 0), 4 with 5 (cost 1), 2 with 2 (cost 0). The single 3 in A was stretched over B's 2 and 3, and the total cost is 2.

Constraints and cost: the full table needs n x m cells, so comparing two 1,000-step sequences means a million cells, and comparing against many templates multiplies that. A warping window (the Sakoe-Chiba band) only allows paths within w steps of the diagonal, which speeds things up and also prevents absurd alignments, such as matching one sound to half of the other word. Slope constraints limit how many steps in a row one sequence may stretch. Lower bounds such as LB_Keogh quickly rule out templates that cannot possibly be the best match.

DTW in practice: isolated-word speech recognition in the 1970s and 1980s used DTW against stored templates for each word, often after converting sound into a sequence of short-time spectral feature vectors; the cost of a pair is then the Euclidean distance between two vectors. DTW also compares online signatures (pen position and pressure over time), gestures from phone accelerometers, and time series like daily electricity load. Hidden Markov models (next two lessons) replaced DTW for large-vocabulary speech because they learn variation statistically from many examples instead of relying on a few templates.

Real-life example 1, voice command on a feature phone: a cheap phone for farmers lets users record "call Ammu" once as a template, then speak it later to dial. The phone converts both recordings into sequences of spectral features and compares them with DTW, so saying it faster or slower still works. Template matching suits this job: there is only one example per command, and only the user's own voice needs to match.

Real-life example 2, inspecting printed labels at a medicine factory: a factory in Tongi checks that each medicine box carries the correct logo and batch label. A camera image is searched with NCC template matching for the logo; a score above 0.9 at the expected place passes, anything lower sends the box aside. NCC tolerates small lighting changes on the conveyor. Boxes that are rotated or partly covered fail, which is acceptable here because they need human attention anyway.

Common mistakes: using SSD where brightness varies; forgetting to subtract means in NCC; thinking DTW is a true metric (it can violate the triangle inequality); allowing unrestricted warping so that very different sequences get small distances; and confusing DTW's three moves. Exams ask for SSD and NCC at a few positions, a small DTW table with the optimal path, the effect of a warping window, and a comparison of template matching with statistical classifiers.

Recap: template matching compares a sample with stored examples. SSD measures raw differences but is fooled by brightness; NCC subtracts means and normalises, scoring 1.0 for both (1, 3, 2) and (2, 6, 4). For sequences of different speed, DTW finds the cheapest forward-moving alignment with D(i, j) = cost + min of three neighbours; (1, 3, 4, 2) vs (1, 2, 3, 5, 2) gave 2. Windows and lower bounds make DTW fast; HMMs take over when there are many examples to learn from.
key_points: Template matching compares a sample with stored class examples and picks the best match.
SSD = sum of squared differences; zero is perfect but brightness changes ruin it.
NCC subtracts means and normalises, ranging -1 to 1; (1, 3, 2) and (2, 6, 4) both score 1.0.
Rigid templates fail with rotation, scale and occlusion; modern systems match features instead.
DTW aligns sequences of different speed with D(i, j) = cost(a_i, b_j) + min(D(i-1, j), D(i, j-1), D(i-1, j-1)).
A Sakoe-Chiba window and lower bounds speed DTW up and prevent absurd warps.
lessons.tip: For DTW by hand, fill the table row by row and write the cost |a - b| small in the corner of each cell before adding the minimum neighbour. Then trace back from the bottom-right corner by always stepping to the smallest of the three neighbours.
lessons.task: Clap a rhythm of 5 claps and write the gaps between claps in tenths of a second. Ask a friend to copy it slower. Write their gaps too, then compute a small DTW table between your two sequences. Is the DTW distance smaller than the point-by-point difference?

quiz.q: Why does normalised cross-correlation handle lighting changes better than SSD?
options: It only uses the brightest pixel
It subtracts means and divides by spreads, so adding or scaling brightness does not change it
quiz.explain: NCC is unchanged by adding a constant or multiplying by a positive constant, which models brightness and contrast changes.

quiz.q: For template (1, 3, 2), what is the NCC of the window (2, 6, 4)?
quiz.explain: The window is exactly 2 times the template, the same shape, so NCC = 1.0 even though SSD = 14.

quiz.q: What does dynamic time warping do?
options: Finds the cheapest forward-moving alignment between two sequences, allowing stretching
quiz.explain: DTW warps time so that similar sequences spoken or written at different speeds line up.

quiz.q: In the DTW recurrence, D(i, j) equals cost(a_i, b_j) plus...
options: The sum of all previous cells
The minimum of D(i-1, j), D(i, j-1) and D(i-1, j-1)
quiz.explain: Each cell adds the local cost to the cheapest of the three ways to arrive there.

quiz.q: What is the DTW distance between (1, 3, 4, 2) and (1, 1, 3, 4, 2) with cost |a - b|?
quiz.explain: Both 1s in the second sequence align with the single 1 in the first, and all other elements match exactly.

lessons.title: Hidden Markov Models I: The Model and the Forward Algorithm
lessons.content:
Your cousin lives in Sylhet, and you talk on the phone every evening. You never ask about the weather, but every day he mentions whether he carried an umbrella. From "umbrella, umbrella, no umbrella" you start guessing: probably rainy, rainy, then sunny. You cannot see the weather; you only see its effects. And you know that rainy days tend to follow rainy days. A hidden Markov model (HMM) is the mathematical version of exactly this situation: a hidden sequence of states that we cannot observe, each producing an observation that we can. HMMs were the workhorse of speech recognition for decades and are still used for handwriting, gesture recognition, gene finding and part-of-speech tagging. This lesson builds the model and solves its first problem, computing how likely an observed sequence is.

Why sequences need a new model: the classifiers so far treat each sample independently. But in speech, the sound now depends on the sound just before; in handwriting, one stroke leads into the next; in weather, today depends on yesterday. DTW (lesson 18) handles timing by matching templates, but it learns nothing about typical variation. We want a probabilistic model of sequences that can be trained from many examples and plugged into Bayes' rule, so that we can say "this sound sequence is most likely the word 'ek'".

Markov chains first: a Markov chain is a sequence of states where the next state depends only on the current one, not on the full history. This is the Markov property. A chain is described by its states, the initial probabilities pi (where it starts) and the transition matrix A, where a_ij is the probability of going from state i to state j. Each row of A adds to 1.

Markov chain worked: two weather states, Rainy (R) and Sunny (S). Transitions: R to R 0.7, R to S 0.3, S to R 0.4, S to S 0.6. If today is rainy, the chance of rain in two days is the sum over tomorrow's possibilities: 0.7 x 0.7 (rain, rain) + 0.3 x 0.4 (sun, then rain) = 0.49 + 0.12 = 0.61. In matrix language, this is the R-to-R entry of A squared. Run the chain long enough and the state probabilities settle to a stationary distribution, here 4/7 rainy and 3/7 sunny, whatever the starting state.

Making it hidden: in an HMM, we do not see the states. Each state emits an observation according to an emission (or observation) probability. In our example, the observations are U (umbrella) or N (no umbrella): P(U | R) = 0.9, P(N | R) = 0.1, P(U | S) = 0.2, P(N | S) = 0.8. These form the emission matrix B. So an HMM is fully described by lambda = (A, B, pi). We take pi = (0.6 for R, 0.4 for S).

The two assumptions: first, the Markov assumption on hidden states: the state at time t depends only on the state at time t - 1. Second, output independence: the observation at time t depends only on the state at time t. These are simplifications; real speech has longer memory. But they make the computations fast, and with enough states the model is surprisingly accurate. Engineers accept a slightly wrong model in exchange for exact, fast calculations, a trade that has paid off again and again in practice.

The three classic problems: Rabiner's famous tutorial lists three problems. Evaluation: given a model lambda and an observation sequence O, what is P(O | lambda)? This lets us compare models: the word model with the highest likelihood wins. Decoding: given lambda and O, what is the most likely hidden state sequence? This tells us, for instance, which phoneme was spoken at each moment. Learning: given observation sequences, how do we adjust A, B and pi to maximise P(O | lambda)? This is how models are trained. This lesson solves evaluation; the next solves decoding and sketches learning.

Evaluation the slow way: P(O | lambda) is the sum, over every possible hidden state sequence Q, of P(O, Q | lambda) = pi(q1) b(q1, o1) x a(q1, q2) b(q2, o2) x ... For our observation U, U, N there are 2^3 = 8 possible weather sequences. For the sequence R, R, S, the joint probability is 0.6 x 0.9 x 0.7 x 0.9 x 0.3 x 0.8 = 0.0816. Adding all eight gives 0.1362. That works for 3 steps, but with N states and T steps there are N^T sequences. A speech model with 5 states over 100 frames has 5^100 sequences, about 10^70. Impossible.

The forward variable: define alpha_t(i) = P(o1, ..., ot, state at time t is i | lambda): the probability of seeing the first t observations and ending in state i. The trick is that alpha for time t + 1 can be computed from alpha at time t, because of the Markov property: all paths into state j at time t + 1 only care which state they came from at time t.

The forward algorithm: initialisation: alpha_1(i) = pi(i) b_i(o1). Induction: alpha_(t+1)(j) = [sum over i of alpha_t(i) a_ij] x b_j(o_(t+1)). Termination: P(O | lambda) = sum over i of alpha_T(i). Each step costs N^2 multiplications, so the total is about N^2 T: for 5 states and 100 frames, 2,500 operations instead of 10^70. This is dynamic programming again, like DTW.

Forward worked, step 1: observation U. alpha_1(R) = 0.6 x 0.9 = 0.54. alpha_1(S) = 0.4 x 0.2 = 0.08.

Forward worked, step 2: observation U. Into R: (0.54 x 0.7 + 0.08 x 0.4) x 0.9 = (0.378 + 0.032) x 0.9 = 0.41 x 0.9 = 0.369. Into S: (0.54 x 0.3 + 0.08 x 0.6) x 0.2 = (0.162 + 0.048) x 0.2 = 0.042.

Forward worked, step 3: observation N. Into R: (0.369 x 0.7 + 0.042 x 0.4) x 0.1 = (0.2583 + 0.0168) x 0.1 = 0.0275. Into S: (0.369 x 0.3 + 0.042 x 0.6) x 0.8 = (0.1107 + 0.0252) x 0.8 = 0.1087. Total P(O | lambda) = 0.0275 + 0.1087 = 0.1362, exactly the brute-force answer, with far fewer multiplications.

What else alpha tells us: dividing the final alphas by their sum gives the probability of each state at the last step given everything seen: P(sunny on day 3 | U, U, N) = 0.1087 / 0.1362 = 0.80. This "filtering" is useful on its own, for example to track the current state of a machine from sensor readings.

Evidence piles up, worked: after day 1 alone (umbrella), the probability of rain is 0.54 / (0.54 + 0.08) = 0.87. After day 2 (umbrella again), it is 0.369 / (0.369 + 0.042) = 0.90: a second umbrella plus the fact that rain tends to continue makes us more sure. After day 3 (no umbrella), it falls to 0.0275 / 0.1362 = 0.20. Each new observation updates our belief, and the transition matrix carries yesterday's belief into today. This is Bayes' rule (lesson 03) applied again and again along the sequence.

The underflow problem and scaling: every alpha is a product of many probabilities below 1, so it shrinks fast. With 1,000 frames of speech, values like 10^-1000 appear, far below the smallest number a computer's double can hold (about 10^-308), and everything becomes 0. The fix is scaling: after each step, divide the alphas by their sum c_t, so they add to 1, and remember the c_t values. Then P(O) is the product of all c_t, and log P(O) is the sum of their logs, which never underflows. Worked: the sums are 0.62, then 0.663, then 0.331, and 0.62 x 0.663 x 0.331 = 0.1362, the same answer as before.

Model shapes: in our weather model every state can follow every other (an ergodic model). For speech and handwriting, a left-to-right model is used instead: states are visited in order, each state may repeat itself or move on, never go back. A word like "ek" might get 3 to 5 states for its beginning, middle and end sounds. The self-loops let a slow speaker stay longer in each state, which is how HMMs handle speed differences that DTW handled with warping.

The backward variable: similarly, beta_t(i) = P(o_(t+1), ..., o_T | state at t is i) is computed from the end backwards. Combining alpha and beta gives, for every time t, the probability of each state given the whole sequence, called smoothing. These quantities are the ingredients of the Baum-Welch learning algorithm in the next lesson.

Classification with HMMs: to recognise isolated words, train one HMM per word (for Bangla digits, ten models for "shunno" to "noy"). For a new utterance, convert the audio into a sequence of feature vectors, compute P(O | lambda_word) with the forward algorithm for each model, multiply by the word's prior, and pick the largest: this is Bayes decision theory (lesson 04) with HMM likelihoods. For continuous feature vectors, the emissions B are Gaussians or mixtures of Gaussians (lesson 22) instead of a table.

Real-life example 1, guessing a machine's health: a rice mill's motor can be in hidden states Good, Worn or Failing. Each hour a vibration sensor gives a reading of Low, Medium or High. Worn motors produce more Medium and High readings and tend to stay worn or get worse. With an HMM, the mill runs the forward algorithm on the latest readings and gets the probability that the motor is now Failing, scheduling maintenance before it breaks during the harvest rush.

Real-life example 2, spoken digit dialling for a helpline: a government helpline lets callers say their area code in Bangla. Each spoken digit is matched against ten trained HMMs. The forward algorithm scores "paanch" highest for a caller's utterance, and the system confirms "five?" before routing. Because the models were trained on many speakers from different districts, they cope with accents much better than single templates and DTW could.

Common mistakes: confusing transition probabilities (state to state) with emission probabilities (state to observation); forgetting pi at the first step; multiplying alphas instead of summing over incoming paths; thinking the forward algorithm finds the best path (it sums over all paths; Viterbi in the next lesson takes the max); and underestimating how quickly N^T explodes. Exams ask you to define lambda = (A, B, pi), state the three problems, run the forward algorithm for 2 or 3 steps, and compare its cost with brute force.
