Recap: an HMM has hidden states following a Markov chain (A, pi) and observations emitted by each state (B). The three problems are evaluation, decoding and learning. The forward algorithm solves evaluation with alpha_(t+1)(j) = [sum of alpha_t(i) a_ij] b_j(o_(t+1)), costing N^2 T instead of N^T. For U, U, N with our weather model, P(O) = 0.1362, and the last day is sunny with probability 0.80. Word recognition trains one HMM per word and picks the highest likelihood.
key_points: A Markov chain's next state depends only on the current state; transitions a_ij form matrix A.
An HMM lambda = (A, B, pi) has hidden states and observations emitted with probabilities B.
Three problems: evaluation P(O | lambda), decoding (best state path), learning (estimate A, B, pi).
Brute force sums over N^T paths; the forward algorithm needs about N^2 T operations.
Forward: alpha_1(i) = pi(i) b_i(o1); alpha_(t+1)(j) = [sum alpha_t(i) a_ij] b_j(o_(t+1)); P(O) = sum alpha_T(i).
Word recognition: one HMM per word, pick the highest prior times P(O | model).
lessons.tip: Draw the trellis: one column per time step, one dot per state, arrows between columns. Write each alpha next to its dot. The forward algorithm is just "sum the arrows coming in, then multiply by the emission", and the picture keeps you from mixing up A and B.
lessons.task: For one week, record each evening whether you carried an umbrella (or wore a jacket). Guess the weather sequence yourself. Then use the lesson's model and run the forward algorithm for the first three days of your record. Does the most likely last-day weather match what really happened?

quiz.q: In an HMM, what does the emission matrix B describe?
options: The probability of moving from one hidden state to another
The probability of each observation given the hidden state
quiz.explain: B gives P(observation | state); A gives state-to-state transitions and pi the starting probabilities.

quiz.q: With rain-to-rain 0.7, rain-to-sun 0.3 and sun-to-rain 0.4, what is the chance of rain in two days if today is rainy?
Why is the forward algorithm needed for evaluation?
options: Summing over all N^T state sequences is far too slow; forward needs only about N^2 T steps
It finds the single best state path
quiz.explain: Dynamic programming reuses partial sums, turning an exponential sum into a linear-in-T computation.

quiz.q: In the worked example, alpha_1(R) = 0.54 and alpha_1(S) = 0.08. With the second observation U, what is alpha_2(R)?
How are isolated words recognised with HMMs?
options: Train one HMM per word and choose the word whose model gives the highest likelihood times prior
Use one HMM for all words and read the states
Compare raw audio samples point by point
quiz.explain: Each word model scores the utterance with the forward algorithm, and Bayes' rule picks the best word.

lessons.title: Hidden Markov Models II: Viterbi Decoding and Training
lessons.content:
Last lesson your cousin in Sylhet said "umbrella, umbrella, no umbrella", and the forward algorithm told us how likely that report was. But you probably want a more direct answer: what was the weather each day? Not a probability spread over eight possibilities, but one best guess: "rainy, rainy, sunny". Finding the single most likely hidden state sequence is the decoding problem, and the Viterbi algorithm solves it efficiently. Then there is the question we skipped: where do the numbers in A, B and pi come from? Learning them from data is the third problem, solved by the Baum-Welch algorithm. This lesson covers both, plus the practical tricks that made HMMs the engine of speech recognition for thirty years.

What decoding means: given a model lambda = (A, B, pi) and observations O = o1, ..., oT, find the state sequence Q = q1, ..., qT that maximises P(Q | O, lambda). Because P(O) does not depend on Q, this is the same as maximising the joint probability P(O, Q | lambda). In speech, decoding tells us which phoneme or word was being spoken at each frame; in handwriting, which letter each pen stroke belongs to; in part-of-speech tagging, which word is a noun and which a verb.

Why not pick the best state at each step separately: we could take, at each time t, the state that is most likely given all observations (from forward-backward smoothing). But the resulting sequence may be impossible. If a transition has probability 0, say a left-to-right speech model that cannot jump back, the separately chosen states might include exactly that forbidden jump. We need the best whole path, not a collection of locally best states.

The brute-force answer: in lesson 19 we listed all 8 weather sequences for U, U, N. The largest joint probability was R, R, S with 0.6 x 0.9 x 0.7 x 0.9 x 0.3 x 0.8 = 0.0816. The next best was R, R, R with 0.0238. So the answer is rainy, rainy, sunny. But again, N^T paths are too many in real problems.

The Viterbi variable: define delta_t(j) = the highest probability of any single path that ends in state j at time t and explains the first t observations. It is exactly like the forward variable alpha, with one change: instead of summing over incoming paths, we keep the maximum. We also store a backpointer psi_t(j), the previous state that gave this maximum, so we can recover the path at the end.

The Viterbi algorithm: initialisation: delta_1(i) = pi(i) b_i(o1). Recursion: delta_(t+1)(j) = [max over i of delta_t(i) a_ij] x b_j(o_(t+1)), and psi_(t+1)(j) = the i that achieved the max. Termination: the best path probability is the max over i of delta_T(i), and the last state is the i that achieved it. Backtracking: follow the backpointers from the last state to the first. The cost is about N^2 T, the same as the forward algorithm. Andrew Viterbi invented it in 1967 for decoding error-correcting codes; the same algorithm now runs in every mobile phone's modem.

Viterbi worked, step 1: observation U. delta_1(R) = 0.6 x 0.9 = 0.54. delta_1(S) = 0.4 x 0.2 = 0.08. Same as alpha so far.

Viterbi worked, step 2: observation U. Into R: candidates 0.54 x 0.7 = 0.378 (from R) and 0.08 x 0.4 = 0.032 (from S). Best is from R, so delta_2(R) = 0.378 x 0.9 = 0.3402, backpointer R. Into S: candidates 0.54 x 0.3 = 0.162 (from R) and 0.08 x 0.6 = 0.048 (from S). Best from R, so delta_2(S) = 0.162 x 0.2 = 0.0324, backpointer R. Compare with the forward step: alpha_2(R) was 0.369 because it added 0.032; Viterbi keeps only the bigger 0.378.

Viterbi worked, step 3: observation N. Into R: candidates 0.3402 x 0.7 = 0.2381 and 0.0324 x 0.4 = 0.0130; best from R, delta_3(R) = 0.2381 x 0.1 = 0.0238, backpointer R. Into S: candidates 0.3402 x 0.3 = 0.1021 and 0.0324 x 0.6 = 0.0194; best from R, delta_3(S) = 0.1021 x 0.8 = 0.0816, backpointer R.

Viterbi worked, backtracking: the largest final delta is delta_3(S) = 0.0816, so the last day was sunny. Its backpointer says day 2 was R, and the backpointer of delta_2(R) says day 1 was R. The best path is rainy, rainy, sunny with probability 0.0816, exactly the brute-force winner, found with 12 multiplications and comparisons instead of listing 8 paths. For long sequences the saving is astronomical.

How sure is the best path: compare the Viterbi probability with the forward total. The best path has 0.0816 and all paths together have 0.1362, so given the observations the best path has probability 0.0816 / 0.1362 = 0.60. The other seven paths share the remaining 40 percent. A 60 percent winner is a reasonable guess, not a certainty; real recognisers report such confidence scores so that an uncertain result can be confirmed with the user, as the helpline in lesson 19 did.

Logs instead of products: like the forward algorithm, Viterbi multiplies many small numbers and underflows on long inputs. But because Viterbi uses max instead of sum, there is an easy fix: work with logarithms. Products become sums, and the max of logs picks the same path. Worked with base-10 logs: log 0.6 + log 0.9 + log 0.7 + log 0.9 + log 0.3 + log 0.8 = -0.222 - 0.046 - 0.155 - 0.046 - 0.523 - 0.097 = -1.088, and 10^-1.088 = 0.0816. Real recognisers run Viterbi entirely in log space, adding costs like a shortest-path search.

Viterbi as shortest path: if we use cost = -log probability, then every arrow in the trellis has a positive cost and Viterbi finds the cheapest path from the first column to the last. That is a shortest path problem on a layered graph, solved by dynamic programming exactly as in Algorithms (deep-cse-3-1). It is also the same structure as DTW: fill a table, keep the best predecessor, trace back.

Learning when states are known: if training data comes with the hidden states labelled, learning is just counting. Worked: suppose a weather diary records R, R, S, S, S, R. Transitions out of R: R to R once, R to S once, so a_RR = 1/2 and a_RS = 1/2. Transitions out of S: S to S twice, S to R once, so a_SS = 2/3 and a_SR = 1/3. Emission probabilities are counted the same way, from how often each observation appears in each state. This is maximum likelihood estimation (lesson 07).

Learning when states are hidden, Baum-Welch: usually we only have observations, not states. The Baum-Welch algorithm is an EM algorithm (lesson 22 explains EM in detail). Start with a guess for lambda. E-step: run forward and backward to compute, for each time, the expected probability of being in each state and of making each transition. M-step: re-estimate A, B and pi from these expected counts, exactly like the counting above but with fractional counts. Repeat. Each round never decreases P(O | lambda), so the likelihood climbs until it settles at a local maximum.

Baum-Welch in practice: because it finds only a local maximum, the starting guess matters. Speech systems often initialise by splitting each training word evenly among its states, or by first running Viterbi training (assign each frame to its best state, count, repeat), which is faster and is the "hard" version of Baum-Welch, just as k-means is the hard version of Gaussian mixture EM. Many training sequences are used together, and probabilities that come out as zero are smoothed slightly so that unseen events are not ruled out forever.

Left-to-right models and connected words: a speech HMM for one phoneme typically has 3 emitting states in a left-to-right chain with self-loops. Word models are made by joining phoneme models, and sentences by joining word models with a language model giving word-to-word probabilities. Viterbi then runs over this huge combined network, keeping only the most promising paths at each frame (beam search), and the best path spells out the recognised sentence. Beam search gives up the guarantee of the exact best path, but in practice it loses almost nothing and runs many times faster.

Handwriting and other uses: online handwriting recognition treats pen movement as a sequence of observations, with letter HMMs chained into words. Gesture recognition, protein sequence families, and gene finding in DNA use the same machinery. Part-of-speech tagging uses words as observations and tags as hidden states; Viterbi decodes "boro" as an adjective or a noun from its neighbours.

What replaced HMMs: from around 2010, deep neural networks first replaced the Gaussian emission models inside HMMs (hybrid DNN-HMM systems), then recurrent networks, connectionist temporal classification (CTC) and transformers learned to map sound to text end-to-end. Yet the ideas remain: CTC decoding uses a forward-backward recursion and beam search over a trellis, and Viterbi is still in every phone's modem. Deep Learning (deep-cse-8-1) and Natural Language Processing (deep-cse-8-2) continue the story.

Real-life example 1, Bangla part-of-speech tagging: a Bangla grammar checker needs to know each word's role. It uses an HMM where the hidden states are tags (noun, verb, adjective, and so on), the transition matrix learned from a tagged corpus says, for example, that a verb often ends a Bangla sentence, and the emission matrix says how often each word appears with each tag. For a new sentence, Viterbi finds the most likely tag sequence in a fraction of a second, even for words that can be both noun and adjective.

Real-life example 2, tracking a delivery rider: a courier company in Dhaka receives noisy GPS points from riders' phones every 10 seconds. The hidden states are the actual road segments; the observations are the GPS points, which can be 30 metres off and fall on the wrong road. Transition probabilities favour connected roads, and emission probabilities fall with distance from the road. Viterbi map matching produces the most likely route actually travelled, used for fair payment and delivery-time estimates.

Common mistakes: using sum instead of max in Viterbi, or max instead of sum in forward; forgetting to store backpointers; choosing the best state at each time separately and calling it the Viterbi path; expecting Baum-Welch to find the global optimum; and mixing up the three problems. Exams ask for a 3-step Viterbi with backpointers, the difference between forward and Viterbi, counting-based estimates of A, the idea of Baum-Welch as EM, and the role of logs.

Recap: decoding finds the single most likely hidden path. Viterbi replaces the forward algorithm's sum with a max and stores backpointers, costing N^2 T. For U, U, N it gives rainy, rainy, sunny with probability 0.0816. Logs turn products into sums and prevent underflow. With labelled states, learning is counting; with hidden states, Baum-Welch (EM) uses forward-backward expected counts and climbs to a local maximum. Left-to-right HMMs with Viterbi powered speech and handwriting recognition for decades.
key_points: Decoding finds the most likely hidden state sequence; choosing each state separately can give an impossible path.
Viterbi: delta_(t+1)(j) = [max over i of delta_t(i) a_ij] b_j(o_(t+1)), with backpointers; cost N^2 T.
Log probabilities turn products into sums; Viterbi becomes a shortest-path search.
Labelled states: count transitions, for example R R S S S R gives a_RR = 1/2 and a_SS = 2/3.
Baum-Welch is EM: forward-backward expected counts, re-estimate, repeat; reaches a local maximum.
Left-to-right models with self-loops handle speaking speed; deep networks later replaced HMM emissions.
lessons.tip: Forward and Viterbi share one trellis. Fill it once with sums (forward) and once with maxes (Viterbi), side by side. Exams love asking for both on the same small model, and doing them together shows exactly where they differ.
lessons.task: Run Viterbi on the same weather model for the observation sequence N, U, U. Draw the trellis, write each delta and backpointer, and trace back the best path. Then check your answer by listing all 8 paths and their probabilities.

quiz.q: How does the Viterbi algorithm differ from the forward algorithm?
options: It sums over all incoming paths
It takes the maximum over incoming paths and stores backpointers
quiz.explain: Viterbi keeps only the best incoming path at each state, so it finds the single best sequence instead of the total probability.

quiz.q: In the worked example, what is the best state path for U, U, N?
quiz.explain: delta_3(S) = 0.0816 is the largest, and backpointers lead to R, R before it.

quiz.q: Why do real systems run Viterbi with logarithms?
options: Products of many small probabilities underflow; logs turn them into sums without changing the best path
Logs make the algorithm find a different path
Logs remove the need for backpointers
quiz.explain: The logarithm is increasing, so maximising the sum of logs gives the same path and avoids underflow.

quiz.q: A labelled diary reads R, R, S, S, S, R. What is the estimated a_SS?
quiz.explain: Out of S there are three transitions: S to S twice and S to R once, so a_SS = 2/3.

quiz.q: What does the Baum-Welch algorithm do?
options: Estimates A, B and pi from observations alone using EM with forward-backward expected counts
Guarantees the global maximum of the likelihood
quiz.explain: Baum-Welch alternates expected counts (E-step) and re-estimation (M-step) and climbs to a local maximum.

lessons.title: Clustering I: Criteria, Fuzzy C-Means, K-Medoids and Validity
lessons.content:
A new shop owner in Chawkbazar receives a sack of mixed spices with no labels. Nobody tells her the categories. Still, by looking at colour, smell and grain size, she sorts them into heaps: the red powders together, the small black seeds together, the long brown sticks together. Nobody gave her labelled examples; she found the groups herself. That is clustering, also called unsupervised learning: finding natural groups in data without class labels. You met k-means and hierarchical clustering in Machine Learning (deep-cse-6-1). In pattern recognition we look more carefully at what makes a clustering good, how to allow soft membership, how to resist outliers, and how to decide the number of clusters.

Why cluster at all: labels are expensive; clustering finds structure first. It is used to discover customer groups, to compress data (replace each point with its cluster centre, as in colour quantisation of images), to build templates for template matching (lesson 18), to initialise Gaussian mixtures (lesson 22) and HMMs, and to spot outliers that belong to no group. It is also a way to explore: before designing a classifier, look at what groups the data naturally forms.

What makes a good clustering: points in the same cluster should be similar (compact clusters), and points in different clusters should be different (well separated). This needs a similarity or distance measure, usually Euclidean distance after standardising features (lesson 02), and a criterion function that scores a whole clustering. Different criteria give different answers, which is why clustering has no single correct result.

The sum-of-squared-error criterion: the most common criterion is SSE, the sum over all points of the squared distance to their own cluster's mean. Smaller is better. Worked: points 1, 2, 3, 8, 9, 10 on a line. One cluster with mean 5.5 gives SSE = 4.5^2 + 3.5^2 + 2.5^2 + 2.5^2 + 3.5^2 + 4.5^2 = 77.5. Two clusters {1, 2, 3} and {8, 9, 10} with means 2 and 9 give SSE = 1 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 1 = 4. Splitting into the two natural groups cuts SSE from 77.5 to 4.

k-means recap: k-means minimises SSE for a chosen k. Start with k centres, assign each point to the nearest centre, move each centre to the mean of its points, and repeat until nothing changes. Each step can only lower SSE, so it always stops, but possibly in a local minimum, so we run it several times from different starts (k-means++ picks well-spread starting centres). It tends to find round clusters of similar size and is pulled by outliers. On our six points, starting centres at 1 and 2 move to 1 and 6.4 after one round, then to 2 and 9 after the second, the natural answer.

The trouble with hard assignment: k-means puts each point fully in one cluster. But some points are honestly in between: a mango that is half ripe, a customer who shops both cheap and premium, a pixel on the border between sky and tree. Forcing a yes-or-no decision loses this information and makes the centres jump when a border point switches sides.

Fuzzy c-means (FCM): Bezdek's fuzzy c-means gives each point a membership u_ij between 0 and 1 in every cluster j, with the memberships of each point adding to 1. It minimises the sum of u_ij^m times squared distance, where m > 1 is the fuzzifier, usually 2. Larger m makes memberships softer; as m approaches 1, FCM becomes k-means.

FCM update rules: given centres, the membership of point i in cluster j is u_ij = 1 / sum over k of (d_ij / d_ik)^(2 / (m - 1)). With m = 2 this is 1 / sum of (d_ij / d_ik)^2. Given memberships, each centre is the weighted mean of all points with weights u_ij^m. Alternate the two updates until the memberships stop changing, just like k-means alternates assignment and mean.

FCM worked: two centres at 2 and 9, m = 2. Point 5 is 3 from the first centre and 4 from the second. Membership in cluster 1 = 1 / (1 + (3/4)^2) = 1 / 1.5625 = 0.64, and in cluster 2 it is 0.36. Point 3 is 1 and 6 away: membership 1 / (1 + (1/6)^2) = 0.973 in cluster 1. Point 8 gets 0.973 in cluster 2. So clear points get memberships near 1, while the in-between point 5 is shared 64 to 36, which honestly describes its position.

Where FCM is used: medical image segmentation is the classic case: in a brain MRI, a pixel at the edge of grey matter and white matter partly belongs to both, and FCM's soft memberships give smoother, more realistic boundaries. FCM is also used for soft customer segmentation and in fuzzy control systems. A weakness: memberships must sum to 1, so a far-away outlier still gets 0.5 in each of two clusters; possibilistic c-means relaxes this.

k-medoids: k-means centres are means, which outliers pull hard. k-medoids uses medoids instead: actual data points that minimise the sum of distances to the other members of their cluster. Worked: cluster values 1, 2, 3 and 100. The mean is 26.5, a value nowhere near most of the data. The sum of distances from each candidate to all four is 102 for 1, 100 for 2, 100 for 3, and 294 for 100, so the medoid is 2 (3 ties). One wild value moved the mean by 24.5 but did not move the medoid at all.

Why medoids help further: a medoid is always a real example, which is easier to explain ("this customer is typical of group 3"). k-medoids works with any dissimilarity, even ones that are not Euclidean, such as DTW distance between signatures or edit distance between strings, since it only needs pairwise distances, not averages. The classic algorithm is PAM (partitioning around medoids), which tries swapping medoids with non-medoids and keeps swaps that lower the total cost. It is slower than k-means, roughly quadratic in the number of points per iteration.

Choosing k, the elbow method: SSE always falls as k rises, reaching 0 when every point is its own cluster, so we cannot simply minimise it. Instead plot SSE against k and look for the elbow. Worked with our six points: k = 1 gives 77.5, k = 2 gives 4, k = 3 gives 2.5, k = 4 gives 1. The huge drop from 1 to 2 and tiny drops after mean the elbow is at k = 2.

The silhouette coefficient: for each point, let a be its average distance to the other points in its own cluster and b its average distance to the points of the nearest other cluster. The silhouette is s = (b - a) / max(a, b), between -1 and 1. Near 1 means well placed; near 0 means on the border; negative means probably in the wrong cluster. The average silhouette over all points scores the whole clustering, and the k with the highest average is a good choice.

Silhouette worked: for point 2 in {1, 2, 3}, a = (1 + 1) / 2 = 1 and b = (6 + 7 + 8) / 3 = 7, so s = (7 - 1) / 7 = 0.857. For point 1, a = (1 + 2) / 2 = 1.5 and b = (7 + 8 + 9) / 3 = 8, so s = 1 - 1.5 / 8 = 0.81. For point 3, a = 1.5 and b = 6, so s = 0.75. By symmetry the other cluster has the same values, so the average silhouette is 0.81, a strong clustering.

Other validity checks: the gap statistic compares SSE with what random, structureless data would give. The Davies-Bouldin index compares within-cluster spread with between-centre distances (smaller is better). Information criteria like BIC choose k for Gaussian mixtures (lesson 22). And when some labels exist, external measures such as purity or the adjusted Rand index compare clusters with the true classes. No single index is always right; use two or three plus a look at the data.

Hierarchical clustering recap: agglomerative clustering starts with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters, recording the merges in a tree called a dendrogram. Cutting the tree at a height gives a clustering. Cluster distance can be single linkage (closest pair), complete linkage (farthest pair) or average linkage. Worked: for our six points, the final merge joins {1, 2, 3} with {8, 9, 10} at height 5 with single linkage (3 to 8) and at height 9 with complete linkage (1 to 10). A big jump in merge height suggests cutting just below it, here giving 2 clusters.

Linkage behaviour: single linkage can follow long, thin, snake-shaped clusters but suffers from chaining, where a line of points joins two real groups. Complete linkage gives compact, round clusters but is sensitive to outliers. Ward's method merges the pair that increases SSE least, behaving like a hierarchical k-means. Density-based methods like DBSCAN, which grow clusters through dense regions and label sparse points as noise, handle odd shapes and outliers well.

Real-life example 1, segmenting mobile banking customers: a mobile financial service in Bangladesh has millions of users with features such as number of cash-outs per month, average transaction size, bill payments and remittance received. k-means with k chosen by silhouette finds five groups: small daily users, monthly remittance receivers, merchants, bill payers and dormant accounts. Each group gets different offers. Because a few merchants have huge volumes that would drag means, the analysts also check with k-medoids, and the medoids give real example customers for the marketing team.

Real-life example 2, segmenting a crop field image: an agricultural drone photographs a rice field in Rangpur. Each pixel's colour values are clustered with fuzzy c-means into healthy crop, stressed crop and soil. Border pixels between healthy and stressed areas get split memberships, producing a smooth stress map rather than a blocky one. Farmers use it to target fertiliser to the stressed patches only.

Common mistakes: clustering unscaled features; trusting a single k-means run; choosing k by minimising SSE (which always picks the largest k); reading clusters as true classes without checking; using k-means for non-round clusters; and forgetting that fuzzy memberships of an outlier still sum to 1. Exams ask for SSE of a given clustering, one round of k-means, FCM memberships, a medoid, a silhouette value, an elbow reading, and single vs complete linkage merge heights.

Recap: clustering finds groups without labels, judged by compactness and separation. SSE is the standard criterion: 77.5 for one cluster versus 4 for two on our points. Fuzzy c-means gives soft memberships, 0.64 and 0.36 for an in-between point. k-medoids uses real points and resists outliers: medoid 2 versus mean 26.5. Choose k with the elbow, the silhouette (0.81 here) and other indices. Hierarchical clustering builds a dendrogram whose linkage choice shapes the clusters.
key_points: Clustering finds natural groups without labels; good clusters are compact and well separated.
SSE criterion: points 1, 2, 3, 8, 9, 10 give 77.5 with one cluster and 4 with two.
Fuzzy c-means memberships: u = 1 / sum (d_ij / d_ik)^2 for m = 2; point 5 gets 0.64 and 0.36.
k-medoids uses real points; for 1, 2, 3, 100 the medoid is 2 while the mean is 26.5.
Elbow: SSE drops 77.5, 4, 2.5, 1 for k = 1 to 4, so k = 2.
Silhouette s = (b - a) / max(a, b); point 2 gives 0.857 and the average is 0.81.
Single linkage chains, complete linkage is compact; final merge heights 5 and 9 in the example.
lessons.tip: When an exam gives points on a line, draw them on a number line first. The natural clusters, the SSE, the medoid and the silhouette distances all become obvious from the picture, and you avoid arithmetic slips.
lessons.task: Write down the prices of 10 snacks you buy often. Cluster them by hand into 2 and then 3 groups, compute the SSE for each, and compute the silhouette of one snack. Which k looks more natural, and does the silhouette agree?

quiz.q: For points 1, 2, 3, 8, 9, 10 split into {1, 2, 3} and {8, 9, 10}, what is the SSE?
quiz.explain: Means 2 and 9; squared distances 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1 add to 4.

quiz.q: In fuzzy c-means with m = 2 and centres 2 and 9, what is point 5's membership in the first cluster?
Why is k-medoids more robust to outliers than k-means?
options: Its centres are real data points minimising total distance, so a single extreme value barely moves them
It ignores outliers completely by deleting them
quiz.explain: For 1, 2, 3, 100 the medoid stays at 2 while the mean jumps to 26.5.

quiz.q: A point has average distance a = 1.5 to its own cluster and b = 6 to the nearest other cluster. What is its silhouette?
Why can we not choose k simply by minimising SSE?
options: SSE keeps falling as k grows and reaches 0 when every point is its own cluster
SSE is undefined for k above 2
SSE does not depend on k
quiz.explain: Minimising SSE alone always picks the largest k, so we use the elbow, silhouette or other indices.

lessons.title: Gaussian Mixture Models and the EM Algorithm
lessons.content:
At a school sports day, someone records the height of every child in the field, but forgets to write down who is in class 3 and who is in class 8. Plot the heights and you see two humps: one around 125 cm and one around 155 cm. Each hump looks like a bell curve. The data is a mixture of two Gaussians, and we would like to recover both bell curves (their centres, widths and sizes) and, for each child, the probability of being in each class. A Gaussian mixture model (GMM) describes such data, and the expectation-maximisation (EM) algorithm fits it. EM is one of the most important algorithms in pattern recognition: it also trains HMMs (lesson 20), handles missing data, and explains why k-means works.

What a GMM is: a GMM says that each data point was produced in two steps. First, a hidden component k is chosen with probability w_k (the mixing weights, which add to 1). Second, the point is drawn from a Gaussian with mean mu_k and variance sigma_k^2 (or covariance matrix Sigma_k in many dimensions). The density of x is p(x) = sum over k of w_k N(x | mu_k, sigma_k^2). With enough components, a GMM can approximate almost any density shape, which makes it a flexible tool for density estimation (lessons 07 and 10) as well as for clustering.

Why not just use maximum likelihood directly: for one Gaussian, the maximum likelihood estimates are simply the sample mean and variance (lesson 07). For a mixture, the log-likelihood contains the log of a sum, log(w_1 N1 + w_2 N2), which has no closed-form maximum. But notice: if we knew which component produced each point, the problem would be easy, just fit each Gaussian to its own points. EM exploits this. It guesses the hidden assignments softly, fits as if they were known, and repeats.

The E-step: using the current parameters, compute for each point x_i and component k the responsibility r_ik = w_k N(x_i | mu_k, sigma_k^2) / sum over j of w_j N(x_i | mu_j, sigma_j^2). This is just Bayes' rule (lesson 03): the posterior probability that component k produced x_i. The responsibilities of each point add to 1, like fuzzy memberships in lesson 21, but derived from probabilities.

The M-step: using the responsibilities as soft counts, update the parameters. Let N_k = sum over i of r_ik, the effective number of points in component k. Then w_k = N_k / n, mu_k = (sum of r_ik x_i) / N_k, and sigma_k^2 = (sum of r_ik (x_i - mu_k)^2) / N_k. These are the ordinary mean and variance formulas, with each point counted by its responsibility.

EM worked, the setup: six points 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 9. Two components, both with variance fixed at 1 and weights fixed at 0.5 to keep the arithmetic simple; only the means are learned. Start with a poor guess: mu_1 = 2 and mu_2 = 5.

EM worked, E-step: for each point, the responsibility of component 1 is proportional to exp(-(x - 2)^2 / 2), and of component 2 to exp(-(x - 5)^2 / 2) (the equal weights and variances cancel). For x = 3: exp(-0.5) = 0.607 versus exp(-2) = 0.135, so r_1 = 0.607 / (0.607 + 0.135) = 0.818. For x = 2: exp(0) = 1 versus exp(-4.5) = 0.011, so r_1 = 0.989. For x = 1: r_1 = 0.999. For x = 7, 8 and 9, component 2 is far closer, so r_1 is about 0.

EM worked, M-step: mu_1 = (0.999 x 1 + 0.989 x 2 + 0.818 x 3) / (0.999 + 0.989 + 0.818) = 5.43 / 2.81 = 1.94. mu_2 gets the remaining shares: (0.001 x 1 + 0.011 x 2 + 0.182 x 3 + 7 + 8 + 9) / (0.001 + 0.011 + 0.182 + 3) = 24.57 / 3.19 = 7.69. The second mean jumped from 5 to 7.69 toward the right-hand group. One more round gives mu_1 = 2.00 and mu_2 = 8.00, and then nothing changes: EM has found the two groups.

Why one Gaussian is not enough, worked: fit a single Gaussian to 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 9 and you get mean 5 and variance 9.67. Its density is highest at 5, about 0.128, exactly where there is no data at all. The two-component mixture with means 2 and 8 and variances 0.67 gives density only 0.0006 at 5, but 0.244 at 2, where the data really is. A single bell curve smears two groups into one wide hump; the mixture describes the two humps faithfully. Any classifier or outlier detector built on the wrong density would make poor decisions, for example calling the value 5 "typical".

A useful picture: think of EM as a negotiation between the points and the components. In the E-step every point asks, "how much do I belong to each component?" and splits itself accordingly. In the M-step every component says, "given the shares of points I received, here is my best centre and width." They take turns until nobody wants to change. The negotiation can settle on a poor deal if it starts badly, which is why we try several starts.

The log-likelihood climbs: the log-likelihood of the data was -24.96 with the starting means 2 and 5, -11.82 after one round, and -11.67 after two, where it stays. This is guaranteed: each EM round can never decrease the likelihood. So EM always converges, usually quickly at first and then slowly. But, like k-means, it converges to a local maximum, which depends on the start.

Why EM works, intuitively: EM builds a lower bound on the log-likelihood that touches it at the current parameters (E-step), then maximises that easier bound (M-step). Since the bound touches the true curve at the old point and is below it everywhere, raising the bound raises the true likelihood too. You do not need the proof for most exams, but you should know the guarantee: monotonic increase to a local optimum.

k-means as hard EM: if all components share the same small variance and we replace soft responsibilities with hard 0 or 1 assignments (each point fully to its nearest mean), the E-step becomes "assign to nearest centre" and the M-step becomes "move centre to the mean of its points". That is exactly k-means. So k-means is a limiting, hard version of GMM-EM, just as Viterbi training is the hard version of Baum-Welch. GMMs add what k-means lacks: clusters of different sizes and shapes, and honest probabilities for border points.

Full covariance in more dimensions: in d dimensions each component has a mean vector and a covariance matrix. Full covariances allow tilted, elongated ellipses, but each needs d(d + 1)/2 numbers: 55 for d = 10. Diagonal covariances (axis-aligned ellipses) need only d numbers, and a shared (tied) covariance needs even fewer. This is the same bias-variance trade-off as quadratic vs linear discriminants in lesson 06. Speech systems commonly used diagonal-covariance GMMs with many components.

Initialisation: because EM finds local maxima, starts matter. Common choices: run k-means first and use its centres, cluster sizes and variances; or try several random starts and keep the one with the highest final likelihood. A bad start can leave two components sharing one group while another group is covered by a single wide component.

Singularities: a danger unique to GMMs: if a component collapses onto a single data point, its variance shrinks toward 0 and its density at that point goes to infinity, so the likelihood goes to infinity too. This is a useless solution. Fixes include adding a small minimum variance, a prior on variances, or restarting a component that collapses.

Choosing the number of components with BIC: more components always raise the likelihood, so we penalise complexity. The Bayesian information criterion is BIC = -2 ln L + p ln n, where p is the number of free parameters and n the number of points; smaller is better. Worked with our six points: one Gaussian (p = 2) has ln L = -15.32, so BIC = 30.64 + 2 x 1.79 = 34.2. Two Gaussians with their own variances and a weight (p = 5) have ln L about -11.46, so BIC = 22.92 + 5 x 1.79 = 31.9. The smaller BIC prefers two components, as our eyes do.

EM beyond mixtures: EM applies whenever a model has hidden variables. Baum-Welch for HMMs (lesson 20) is EM with hidden states. EM fills in missing feature values in a data set by treating them as hidden. It also underlies probabilistic PCA, topic models for documents, and image segmentation with mixtures of colours. The pattern is always the same: guess the hidden parts softly, fit, repeat.

GMMs as classifiers: for supervised classification, fit one GMM per class to the class's training data, giving a flexible class-conditional density p(x | class). Then use Bayes' rule (lesson 04) to classify. Classic speaker identification did exactly this: a GMM with 32 to 256 components per speaker, fitted to that speaker's voice features, and a new recording assigned to the speaker whose GMM gives the highest likelihood.

Real-life example 1, speaker verification for a phone bank: a bank lets customers in Chattogram check their balance by speaking. During enrolment, the system fits a GMM to the customer's voice features from a few sentences. At each call, it computes the likelihood of the new speech under the customer's GMM and under a general background GMM trained on thousands of voices. If the ratio is high enough, the voice is accepted. This GMM-UBM approach was the standard method for about fifteen years.

Real-life example 2, separating fish by size at a market: a fisheries researcher measures 500 fish of one species from Cox's Bazar landing stations, without knowing their ages. The length histogram shows overlapping humps, one per age group. Fitting a GMM with EM and choosing three components by BIC gives the mean length and share of each age group, which helps set rules on mesh size to protect young fish.

Common mistakes: forgetting to normalise responsibilities so they sum to 1; using hard assignments and calling it EM; expecting EM to find the global maximum; letting a variance collapse to zero; choosing the number of components by likelihood alone; and confusing mixing weights with responsibilities (weights are per component, responsibilities per point and component). Exams ask for one E-step and M-step in 1D, the formulas for w, mu and sigma^2, the link to k-means, the monotonic likelihood property, and BIC.

Recap: a GMM is a weighted sum of Gaussians with hidden component labels. EM alternates the E-step (responsibilities by Bayes' rule: 0.818 for point 3 in our example) and the M-step (weighted means and variances: new means 1.94 and 7.69, then 2 and 8). The log-likelihood rises every round (-24.96, -11.82, -11.67) to a local maximum. k-means is hard EM. Initialise with k-means, guard against collapse, and choose the number of components with BIC (34.2 vs 31.9 favoured two).
key_points: A GMM: p(x) = sum of w_k N(x | mu_k, sigma_k^2), with hidden component labels and weights summing to 1.
E-step: responsibilities r_ik by Bayes' rule; M-step: w_k = N_k / n, weighted means and variances.
Worked: points 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 9 with start means 2 and 5; r_1(3) = 0.818; new means 1.94 and 7.69, then 2 and 8.
The log-likelihood never decreases: -24.96, -11.82, -11.67; EM reaches a local maximum.
k-means is hard EM; GMMs add different cluster sizes, shapes and soft probabilities.
Initialise with k-means, keep a minimum variance to prevent collapse.
BIC = -2 ln L + p ln n; for the example, 34.2 for one Gaussian versus 31.9 for two.
lessons.tip: In an EM exam question, make a table with one row per point and columns for each component's unnormalised value, the sum and the responsibility. The M-step then just uses the responsibility column as weights. Tables prevent most EM errors.
lessons.task: Collect the shoe sizes of 15 to 20 people in your family and neighbourhood, adults and children together. Plot a histogram. Guess two starting means and run one E-step and one M-step by hand, with variances fixed at 1. Did the means move toward the adult and child groups?

quiz.q: What does the E-step of EM compute for a Gaussian mixture?
options: Responsibilities, the posterior probability that each component produced each point
quiz.explain: The E-step applies Bayes' rule with the current parameters to get soft assignments.

quiz.q: With means 2 and 5, equal weights and variance 1, what is the responsibility of component 1 for point 3?
What happens to the log-likelihood over EM iterations?
options: It can rise or fall randomly
It never decreases and converges to a local maximum
It always reaches the global maximum in one step
quiz.explain: Each EM round is guaranteed not to lower the likelihood, but the final point may be a local maximum.

quiz.q: How is k-means related to EM for Gaussian mixtures?
options: k-means is EM with soft responsibilities
k-means is a hard version of EM with equal small variances and 0 or 1 assignments
quiz.explain: Replacing soft responsibilities with nearest-centre assignments turns GMM-EM into k-means.

quiz.q: Why is BIC used to choose the number of mixture components?
options: It penalises the number of parameters, since likelihood alone always rises with more components
It removes the need for initialisation
quiz.explain: BIC = -2 ln L + p ln n balances fit against complexity; smaller is better.

lessons.title: Structural and Syntactic Pattern Recognition
lessons.content:
How would you describe the Bangla letter "ক" to a friend over the phone? You would probably not list pixel values or feature numbers. You would say something like: "a vertical line, with a loop on the left joined to it, and a short line across the top." You describe it by its parts and how they connect. Structural pattern recognition works this way: it represents a pattern as a set of simple primitives (strokes, line segments, corners) together with the relations between them, and recognises patterns by comparing these structures. When the structure is written as a string and its rules as a grammar, it is called syntactic pattern recognition. This lesson shows chain codes, grammars, string edit distance and graph matching, and explains when structure beats numbers.

Statistical vs structural: everything so far in this course has been statistical: a pattern is a feature vector, a point in d-dimensional space, and classes are regions separated by boundaries. That works well when a fixed set of measurements captures the pattern. But some patterns are about arrangement: a chromosome's banding sequence, a circuit diagram, a chemical molecule, a handwritten letter whose parts can vary in size but must connect correctly. A feature vector of fixed length struggles to say "a loop attached to the left of a vertical stroke". Structure says it directly.

Primitives and relations: the first step is to choose primitives, small pieces easy to detect: line segments in 8 directions, arcs, corners, endpoints, junctions. The second is to choose relations: "followed by", "above", "left of", "connected to", "inside". A pattern becomes a string (if primitives follow one another in order, like a traced boundary), a tree (if parts contain sub-parts), or a graph (if parts connect in arbitrary ways).

Chain codes: Freeman's chain code is a classic way to turn a boundary into a string. Trace the boundary pixel by pixel and record the direction of each step using 8 codes: 0 east, 1 north-east, 2 north, 3 north-west, 4 west, 5 south-west, 6 south, 7 south-east. Each step becomes one digit, and the whole outline becomes a string of digits. Using 4 directions (0 east, 1 north, 2 west, 3 south) gives a simpler code for shapes made only of horizontal and vertical steps.

Chain code worked: trace a 2 by 2 square anticlockwise from its bottom-left corner. Two steps east (0, 0), two north (2, 2), two west (4, 4), two south (6, 6). The chain code is 00224466. Its length tells us the perimeter: 8 steps of length 1, so 8 units. A diagonal step (odd code) would count as square root of 2, about 1.41.

Making chain codes invariant: the plain code depends on the starting point and rotation. The first difference fixes rotation: replace each code by (current - previous) mod 8, counting around the loop. For 00224466 the differences are 2, 0, 2, 0, 2, 0, 2, 0: a turn of 90 degrees every two steps. Rotate the square by 90 degrees and its chain code becomes 22446600, but the difference code is still 2, 0, 2, 0, 2, 0, 2, 0. To remove the starting point, rotate the difference string circularly to the version that is smallest as a number, called the shape number.

Grammars recap: in Theory of Computation (deep-cse-3-5) you met formal grammars: a set of production rules that generate the strings of a language. In syntactic pattern recognition, each class is a language: the set of strings describing all valid patterns of that class. Recognition means parsing: if the string of a new pattern can be generated by the grammar of class A, it belongs to class A.

Grammar worked, a staircase: let primitive a be a unit step right and b a unit step up. A staircase is ab, abab, ababab, and so on. The grammar S -> abS | ab generates exactly these strings. Parse ababab: S -> abS -> ababS -> ababab, accepted. The string abba (right, up, up, right) cannot be generated, so it is not a staircase. The grammar captures "repeat right-then-up any number of times", which no fixed-length feature vector expresses so neatly.

What grammars can and cannot do: regular grammars (finite automata) handle simple repeated structures. Context-free grammars describe nested structure, such as a shape with balanced parts, like a^n b^n, a rectangle whose opposite sides must have equal lengths. Context-sensitive grammars are more powerful but costly to parse. A practical problem: real patterns are noisy, so a single wrong primitive makes a perfect grammar reject a valid pattern. Stochastic grammars attach probabilities to rules and choose the most probable parse, and error-correcting parsers allow a few edits.

Attributed grammars: pure strings lose numeric detail: a long stroke and a short stroke both become "a". Attributed grammars attach attributes such as length, angle, curvature or position to each primitive, and rules can check them: "the crossbar of A must be roughly horizontal and between 30 and 70 percent of the height". This blends structural and statistical ideas, and it is how many practical character and diagram recognisers work.

String edit distance: to compare two structural strings with noise, count the minimum number of insertions, deletions and substitutions that turn one into the other. This is the Levenshtein edit distance. The classic example: "kitten" to "sitting" needs 3 edits: substitute k with s, substitute e with i, and insert g. Edit distance turns structural descriptions into something nearest neighbour classifiers can use: classify a string by the nearest stored prototype string.

Edit distance recurrence: fill a table where D(i, j) is the distance between the first i symbols of A and the first j of B. D(i, 0) = i and D(0, j) = j. Then D(i, j) = minimum of D(i - 1, j) + 1 (delete), D(i, j - 1) + 1 (insert), and D(i - 1, j - 1) + (0 if the symbols match, otherwise 1). It is the same dynamic programming shape as DTW (lesson 18), except DTW stretches instead of inserting and deleting.

Edit distance worked: A = GATE and B = GOAT. Row for G: 1, 0, 1, 2, 3. Row for A: 2, 1, 1, 1, 2. Row for T: 3, 2, 2, 2, 1. Row for E: 4, 3, 3, 3, 2. The distance is 2: keep G, insert O, keep A and T, delete E. For chain codes, 00224466 and 0022446 differ by 1 (one missing step), and 00224466 vs 00224566 differ by 1 (one direction changed), which matches our sense that these outlines are nearly the same square.

Nearest prototype with edit distance, worked: store three prototype outlines: a 2 by 2 square 00224466, a 3 by 1 rectangle 00024446 and a 1 by 1 square 0246. A scanned shape gives the noisy code 0022466, a square with one west step lost by the scanner. Its edit distances are 1 to the big square, 3 to the rectangle and 3 to the small square. The nearest prototype is the 2 by 2 square, which is the right answer even though the code is not a perfect match. This is the nearest neighbour rule of lesson 11, with edit distance in place of Euclidean distance.

Weighted edits: not all mistakes are equal. In chain codes, replacing direction 0 with 1 (a 45-degree difference) is a small error, while 0 with 4 (opposite direction) is large. So the substitution cost can be the angle difference. In spelling, swapping keys that sit next to each other on the keyboard can cost less. Weighted edit distance keeps the same recurrence with these costs.

Graphs and graph matching: when parts connect in complex ways, a graph is the natural description. In a face graph, nodes are eyes, nose and mouth with attributes such as size, and edges hold relations such as distance and angle. In a fingerprint, nodes are minutiae (ridge endings and bifurcations) and edges join neighbours. In chemistry, atoms are nodes and bonds are edges. Recognition means comparing the new graph with stored model graphs.

Exact and inexact matching: exact matching asks whether two graphs are isomorphic (the same up to renaming nodes), or whether one appears inside the other (subgraph isomorphism, which is NP-complete). Real data is noisy, so we use inexact matching: the graph edit distance counts node and edge insertions, deletions and substitutions, with costs. Worked: a triangle (3 nodes, 3 edges) and a path of 3 nodes (2 edges) have graph edit distance 1: delete one edge. Because exact graph edit distance is expensive, practical systems use approximations, such as assignment-based matching, spectral methods, or graph neural networks.

Strengths and weaknesses: structural methods describe patterns in a human-readable way, generalise to sizes they have not seen (the staircase grammar accepts 50 steps after seeing 3), and capture relationships directly. But primitives must be extracted reliably, which is hard in noisy images; grammars are usually written by hand and are difficult to learn from data; and matching can be slow. Statistical methods learn from data easily but ignore explicit structure. Many real systems are hybrids: statistical classifiers detect primitives, and structural rules combine them.

Real-life example 1, recognising Bangla compound letters: Bangla has many juktakkhor (conjuncts) like "ক্ষ" or "ন্ত", built from simpler letters. A structural recogniser detects strokes, loops and the matra (headline), then checks how they connect: which parts hang below the headline, which are attached left or right. Describing a conjunct as a combination of known parts means the system can handle a conjunct it has seen only a few times, as long as its parts are familiar.

Real-life example 2, checking electrical circuit diagrams: an engineering firm in Dhaka digitises old hand-drawn circuit diagrams. A detector finds symbols (resistors, capacitors, transistors) as primitives, and the wires become edges, giving a graph. Graph matching against a library of standard sub-circuits identifies amplifiers and power supplies, and a grammar of valid connections flags drawing errors, such as a transistor with an unconnected terminal.

Common mistakes: forgetting that chain codes depend on the starting point and orientation; computing differences without going around the loop; confusing edit distance with DTW; assuming a grammar can handle noise without error-correcting rules; and assuming graph isomorphism is easy (subgraph isomorphism is NP-complete). Exams ask for a chain code and its first difference, a small grammar and a parse, an edit distance table, and a comparison of statistical and structural approaches.

Recap: structural pattern recognition describes patterns by primitives and relations, as strings, trees or graphs. Chain codes turn boundaries into strings (a square gives 00224466, difference code 20202020). Grammars define classes as languages, recognised by parsing (S -> abS | ab for staircases); attributed and stochastic grammars handle real data. Edit distance (GATE to GOAT is 2) and graph edit distance compare noisy structures. Hybrids of structure and statistics work best in practice.
key_points: Structural recognition describes patterns by primitives and relations as strings, trees or graphs.
Freeman chain code: 8 directions; a 2 by 2 square traced anticlockwise gives 00224466.
First difference (mod 8) removes rotation: 2, 0, 2, 0, 2, 0, 2, 0; the shape number also removes the start point.
Syntactic recognition: each class is a language; S -> abS | ab accepts ababab but not abba.
Edit distance: D(i, j) = min(delete + 1, insert + 1, substitute + 0 or 1); GATE to GOAT is 2.
Graph edit distance compares noisy graphs; a triangle and a 3-node path differ by 1.
Attributed and stochastic grammars handle real, noisy data; hybrid systems combine structure and statistics.
lessons.tip: For chain code questions, draw the boundary on squared paper with arrows, write the digit beside each arrow, and always say which corner you started at and which direction you went round. Most lost marks come from a different starting point.
lessons.task: Draw a simple house shape (a square with a triangle roof) on squared paper. Write its Freeman chain code starting from the bottom-left corner, then its first difference. Now draw a slightly different house and compute the edit distance between the two chain codes.

quiz.q: What is the Freeman chain code of a 2 by 2 square traced anticlockwise from its bottom-left corner?
quiz.explain: Two steps east (0), two north (2), two west (4) and two south (6).

quiz.q: Why use the first difference of a chain code?
options: It makes the code independent of rotation
quiz.explain: Differences record turns rather than absolute directions, so rotating the shape does not change them.

quiz.q: Which string can be generated by the grammar S -> abS | ab?
quiz.explain: S -> abS -> ababS -> ababab; the other strings do not follow the repeated ab pattern.

quiz.q: What is the edit distance between GATE and GOAT?
quiz.explain: Insert O after G and delete the final E: two edits.

quiz.q: What is a main weakness of purely syntactic pattern recognition?
options: A single noisy primitive can make a strict grammar reject a valid pattern, and grammars are hard to learn
It always needs fixed-length feature vectors
quiz.explain: Real data is noisy, which is why stochastic and error-correcting grammars and hybrid systems are used.

lessons.title: Estimating and Comparing Classifier Error
lessons.content:
Imagine a student who practises the same 20 maths questions every day for a month and then scores 100 percent on exactly those 20 questions. Does that prove she knows maths? No. The real test is new questions she has never seen. Classifiers have the same problem: a classifier tested on the data it was trained on will look far better than it really is. This lesson is about measuring how well a pattern recogniser will really do on new data, how sure we can be about that number, how to measure errors in verification systems like fingerprint scanners, and how to tell whether one classifier is truly better than another or just lucky.

Why error estimation matters: every design decision in this course, such as which features to keep (lesson 17), how many neighbours k to use (lesson 11), how many mixture components (lesson 22), or which kernel (lesson 15), depends on estimating error. If the estimate is biased, we choose wrongly. And a system deployed in a hospital or bank needs an honest statement like "93 percent accurate, give or take 2 percent", not an optimistic guess.

Training error is optimistic: the error on the training set is called the resubstitution or apparent error. It is almost always lower than the true error, because the classifier has adapted to the training samples, including their noise. A 1-nearest-neighbour classifier has zero training error by definition, since every training point is its own nearest neighbour, whatever its true accuracy. So we must measure error on data not used for training.

The holdout method: split the data randomly into a training set (say 70 percent) and a test set (30 percent). Train on one, test on the other. It is simple and honest, but has two problems: we waste 30 percent of the data for training, and the estimate depends on the lucky or unlucky split, especially for small data sets. When choosing settings, we need three parts: training, validation (for choosing settings) and test (touched only once at the end).

How precise is a test estimate: if a classifier makes independent errors with true error p, the number of errors on n test samples follows a binomial distribution. Worked: 450 correct out of 500 gives accuracy 0.90. The standard error is the square root of (0.9 x 0.1 / 500) = 0.0134, so a 95 percent confidence interval is 0.90 plus or minus 1.96 x 0.0134 = plus or minus 0.026, roughly 87.4 to 92.6 percent. With only 100 test samples at the same accuracy, the margin grows to plus or minus 0.059. Small test sets give wide intervals.

k-fold cross-validation: split the data into k equal folds, typically k = 5 or 10. Train on k - 1 folds and test on the remaining one, rotating so that every fold is the test fold exactly once. Average the k error rates. Every sample is used for testing once and for training k - 1 times. Worked: with 1,000 samples and k = 10, each round trains on 900 and tests on 100; if the ten fold errors are 0.08, 0.10, 0.07, 0.09, 0.11, 0.08, 0.09, 0.10, 0.06 and 0.12, the estimate is their mean, 0.09.

Stratification and repetition: in stratified cross-validation, each fold keeps the same class proportions as the whole data set, which matters when one class is rare (for example 2 percent fraud). Repeating k-fold several times with different random splits and averaging reduces the variance of the estimate further.

Leave-one-out (LOO): the extreme case k = n: train on all samples but one, test on that one, and repeat n times. It wastes almost no data and is nearly unbiased, but needs n trainings, which is slow for large n, and its estimate can have high variance. For some classifiers, like k-NN, LOO is cheap because "training" is just storing the data.

The bootstrap: draw n samples from the data with replacement, so some samples appear twice and others not at all. Train on this bootstrap sample and test on the left-out samples (out-of-bag). The chance that a given sample is never drawn is (1 - 1/n)^n, which approaches 1/e = 0.368 for large n; for n = 1,000 it is 0.368. So about 63.2 percent of distinct samples are used for training. The out-of-bag error is slightly pessimistic, because training sets are smaller; the .632 bootstrap corrects it.

.632 bootstrap worked: the estimate is 0.368 x training error + 0.632 x out-of-bag error. If a classifier has training error 0.02 and out-of-bag error 0.15, the .632 estimate is 0.368 x 0.02 + 0.632 x 0.15 = 0.0074 + 0.0948 = 0.102. It sits between the optimistic training error and the pessimistic out-of-bag error. Random forests (lesson 25) use out-of-bag error as a built-in estimate.

Confusion matrix recap: for two classes, count true positives (TP), false positives (FP), true negatives (TN) and false negatives (FN). Accuracy = (TP + TN) / total; precision = TP / (TP + FP); recall or sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN); specificity = TN / (TN + FP). With imbalanced classes, accuracy misleads: a fraud detector that says "never fraud" is 98 percent accurate when fraud is 2 percent, yet catches nothing. Machine Learning (deep-cse-6-1) covered these, plus ROC curves and area under the curve (AUC).

Confusion matrix worked: a fraud detector checks 1,000 transactions, of which 60 are fraud. It flags 50: 40 real frauds (TP) and 10 honest ones (FP). It misses 20 frauds (FN), and 930 honest transactions pass correctly (TN). Accuracy is 970 / 1,000 = 0.97, which sounds excellent. But precision is 40 / 50 = 0.80 and recall is 40 / 60 = 0.67: a third of the frauds slip through. Their harmonic mean, the F1 score, is 0.73. Precision and recall tell the bank far more than accuracy does.

Verification and its two errors: many pattern recognition systems verify a claim rather than choose among classes: "is this really Rahim's fingerprint?" The system compares a score with a threshold. Two errors are possible: false accept (an impostor is accepted) and false reject (the genuine user is rejected). The false accept rate (FAR) is the fraction of impostor attempts accepted; the false reject rate (FRR) is the fraction of genuine attempts rejected.

FAR and FRR worked: five genuine attempts score 0.90, 0.80, 0.75, 0.60 and 0.55; five impostor attempts score 0.70, 0.50, 0.40, 0.30 and 0.20. Accept when score is at least t. At t = 0.75: FRR = 2/5 = 0.4 (0.60 and 0.55 rejected), FAR = 0/5 = 0. At t = 0.50: FRR = 0, FAR = 2/5 = 0.4 (0.70 and 0.50 accepted). At t = 0.60: FRR = 1/5 = 0.2 and FAR = 1/5 = 0.2.

The equal error rate: raising the threshold lowers FAR but raises FRR, and lowering it does the opposite. The point where FAR equals FRR is the equal error rate (EER), a single number for comparing systems; in our example EER = 0.2 at t = 0.60. A lower EER means a better system. In practice the operating threshold is chosen by cost: a bank vault wants very low FAR even if FRR rises, while a phone unlock wants low FRR so users are not annoyed.

DET curves: a detection error trade-off (DET) curve plots FRR against FAR for all thresholds, usually on scales that stretch small error rates so that good systems are easy to compare. It shows the same information as an ROC curve (FRR = 1 - true positive rate, FAR = false positive rate) but is the standard in biometrics and speaker verification.

Comparing two classifiers, McNemar's test: classifier A scores 85 percent and B 88 percent on the same test set. Is B really better, or is this luck? McNemar's test looks only at disagreements: n01 = samples A got wrong but B got right, and n10 = samples A got right but B got wrong. The statistic is (|n01 - n10| - 1)^2 / (n01 + n10), compared with 3.84 (the chi-squared value for 5 percent significance with 1 degree of freedom).

McNemar worked: on 200 test samples, n01 = 25 and n10 = 10. The statistic is (|25 - 10| - 1)^2 / 35 = 14^2 / 35 = 196 / 35 = 5.6. Since 5.6 > 3.84, the difference is significant at the 5 percent level: B really is better on this kind of data. If instead n01 = 15 and n10 = 10, the statistic would be (5 - 1)^2 / 25 = 0.64, far below 3.84, so we could not claim B is better.

Other pitfalls: test sets that are not like real use (all training and test photos taken in one lab); leakage, where information from the test set enters training, for example through feature selection or normalisation done on all data (lesson 17); testing many models on one test set and reporting the best (the test set becomes a validation set); and duplicates or the same person appearing in both training and test sets. For person-related data, split by person, not by sample.

Real-life example 1, evaluating a national ID fingerprint matcher: a government agency compares two fingerprint matching systems for a national identity database. Both are tested on the same 10,000 genuine and 100,000 impostor comparisons, collected from enrolment centres in different districts. System 1 has EER 0.8 percent and System 2 has EER 1.2 percent. At the agency's chosen FAR of 0.01 percent, System 1 has FRR 3 percent and System 2 has 5 percent. A McNemar test on paired decisions confirms the difference is significant, so System 1 is chosen.

Real-life example 2, honest accuracy for a crop disease app: an app diagnoses leaf disease from photos. The developers first report 99 percent accuracy, but their test photos came from the same fields and same days as the training photos. A reviewer insists on a test set from new farms in a different season. Accuracy drops to 86 percent, with a 95 percent interval of plus or minus 3 percent. The honest number guides farmers to treat the app as advice, not certainty, and tells the developers where to collect more data.

Common mistakes: reporting training accuracy; tuning on the test set; forgetting stratification with rare classes; ignoring confidence intervals; calling a small difference "better" without a significance test; using accuracy with imbalanced classes; and mixing up FAR and FRR. Exams ask for k-fold procedure, LOO vs bootstrap, the 0.368 and .632 numbers, a confidence interval, FAR and FRR at given thresholds and the EER, and a McNemar test.

Recap: training error is optimistic, so estimate error on unseen data with holdout, k-fold, leave-one-out or the bootstrap (0.368 of samples left out; .632 estimate 0.102 in our example). Report a confidence interval: 0.90 plus or minus 0.026 for 500 samples. Verification uses FAR and FRR, traded off by the threshold, summarised by the EER (0.2 in our example) and DET curves. Compare classifiers with McNemar's test: 5.6 > 3.84 means significant.
key_points: Training (resubstitution) error is optimistic; 1-NN always has zero training error.
Holdout, k-fold (k = 5 or 10), stratified and leave-one-out cross-validation estimate true error.
95 percent interval: 450 of 500 correct gives 0.90 plus or minus 0.026.
Bootstrap leaves out about 36.8 percent; .632 estimate = 0.368 x 0.02 + 0.632 x 0.15 = 0.102.
FAR = impostors accepted, FRR = genuine rejected; EER where they meet: 0.2 at t = 0.60 in the example.
McNemar: (|n01 - n10| - 1)^2 / (n01 + n10); 25 vs 10 gives 5.6 > 3.84, significant.
Avoid leakage, tuning on the test set and splitting the same person across train and test.
lessons.tip: For FAR and FRR questions, sort the genuine and impostor scores in two columns. For each threshold, count genuine scores below it (FRR) and impostor scores at or above it (FAR). Writing both columns side by side makes the EER jump out.
lessons.task: Ask 5 friends to sign their name 3 times each. Pick one friend's first signature as the reference. Score every other signature from 0 to 10 for similarity to the reference by eye. Compute FAR and FRR at thresholds 5, 7 and 9. Where is your equal error rate?

quiz.q: Why is training error a poor estimate of true error?
options: It is computed on the data the classifier adapted to, so it is optimistic
It uses too many test samples
quiz.explain: The classifier has fitted the training data, including its noise, so new data usually gives more errors.

quiz.q: In the bootstrap with large n, what fraction of samples is left out of each bootstrap sample on average?
quiz.explain: (1 - 1/n)^n approaches 1/e = 0.368.

quiz.q: Genuine scores are 0.90, 0.80, 0.75, 0.60, 0.55 and impostor scores 0.70, 0.50, 0.40, 0.30, 0.20. At threshold 0.60, what are FAR and FRR?
quiz.explain: One impostor (0.70) is accepted and one genuine (0.55) rejected, out of five each.

quiz.q: In McNemar's test, n01 = 25 and n10 = 10. What is the statistic and conclusion at 5 percent?
For person-related data like faces or signatures, how should training and test sets be split?
options: By person, so nobody appears in both sets
Put everyone's best samples in the test set
Use the same data for both
quiz.explain: If the same person is in both sets, the test measures memory of that person rather than generalisation.

lessons.title: Combining Classifiers: Voting, Fusion Rules and Cascades
lessons.content:
When a patient in a district hospital has a confusing set of symptoms, the doctors hold a medical board: three or four specialists each give an opinion, and the final decision combines them. Each doctor alone makes mistakes, but they rarely make the same mistake at the same time, so the board is usually right more often than any single member. Pattern recognition uses the same idea: train several classifiers and combine their outputs. This is called a multiple classifier system or ensemble. This lesson shows why combining helps, with worked numbers; the main fusion rules (voting, sum, product, max); bagging and boosting as ways to create diverse classifiers; the Viola-Jones cascade for fast face detection; and multimodal biometrics.

Why combine: no single classifier is best for every problem, and even the best one makes errors. Different classifiers, or the same classifier trained on different data or features, make different errors. If the errors are not all on the same samples, combining can correct some of them. Combining also reduces variance: averaging several unstable classifiers (like deep decision trees) gives a steadier result, the same reason an average of several measurements is more reliable than one.

Majority voting worked: suppose three classifiers each have accuracy 0.7 and make independent errors. The majority vote is correct when at least 2 of 3 are correct: P = 0.7^3 + 3 x 0.7^2 x 0.3 = 0.343 + 0.441 = 0.784. With 5 such classifiers, accuracy rises to 0.837; with 11, to 0.922; with 21, to 0.974. This result goes back to Condorcet's jury theorem from 1785: a large group of independent voters, each better than chance, is very likely to reach the right answer.

The two conditions: the voting result needs two things. First, each classifier must be better than chance: three independent classifiers with accuracy 0.4 give a majority vote accuracy of only 0.352, worse than each one alone. Second, errors must be diverse. If all three classifiers make exactly the same mistakes, voting changes nothing. In practice errors are correlated, so the real gain is smaller than the independent-case numbers, but still useful.

Measuring diversity, worked: two classifiers are each 70 percent correct on 10 test samples, so each gets 3 wrong. Case 1: both are wrong on the same 3 samples. They never disagree (disagreement 0), and the best any combiner could do, called the oracle accuracy (correct if at least one member is correct), is still 70 percent. Case 2: their mistakes never overlap, so the 3 plus 3 errors fall on 6 different samples. They disagree on 6 of 10 samples (disagreement 0.6), and the oracle accuracy is 100 percent, because on every sample at least one of them is right. Same individual accuracy, very different potential: diversity is what gives a combiner something to work with.

Creating diversity: diversity can come from different algorithms (k-NN, SVM, naive Bayes), different feature sets (one classifier uses shape features, another texture), different training samples (bagging), reweighting hard examples (boosting), or different random choices (random subspaces, random forests). The art of ensembles is to make classifiers that are individually good but disagree on hard cases.

Levels of output: a classifier can output just a label (abstract level), a ranking of classes (rank level), or a score or posterior probability for each class (measurement level). Voting uses labels. Fusion rules such as sum and product use scores, which carry more information: a classifier that says "A with 0.51" is much less sure than one saying "A with 0.99", and score-based fusion can use that difference.

Fusion rules: given posteriors P_j(class | x) from classifiers j = 1, ..., L, the sum (or mean) rule picks the class with the largest sum of posteriors. The product rule picks the largest product. The max rule picks the class with the single highest posterior anywhere. The min rule picks the class whose lowest posterior is highest. Kittler and colleagues derived these from Bayes' theorem under different assumptions: product is right when classifiers use independent features and estimates are accurate, while sum is more robust when estimates are noisy.

Fusion rules worked: two classes A and B. Classifier 1 says (A 0.6, B 0.4), classifier 2 says (A 0.7, B 0.3), classifier 3 says (A 0.1, B 0.9). Majority vote: two say A, one says B, so A. Sum rule: A = 0.6 + 0.7 + 0.1 = 1.4 and B = 0.4 + 0.3 + 0.9 = 1.6, so B. Product rule: A = 0.6 x 0.7 x 0.1 = 0.042 and B = 0.4 x 0.3 x 0.9 = 0.108, so B. Max rule: A's highest is 0.7 and B's is 0.9, so B. Min rule: A's lowest is 0.1 and B's is 0.3, so B.

What the example teaches: voting chose A because two classifiers mildly preferred it, but the score rules chose B because classifier 3 was very confident and the other two only mildly against. Which is right depends on how trustworthy those confidences are. The product rule is also fragile: a single classifier outputting 0 for the true class vetoes it completely, which is why sum is often safer in practice.

Weighted voting: not all voters are equally good. If classifier j has accuracy p_j and errors are independent, the optimal weight for its vote is log(p_j / (1 - p_j)). Worked: one classifier with accuracy 0.9 gets weight ln 9 = 2.20; two with accuracy 0.7 get ln(7/3) = 0.85 each. If the strong one says A and both weak ones say B, A scores 2.20 and B scores 1.69, so A wins: one expert outweighs two mediocre voters. This is exactly the weight formula used inside AdaBoost.

Stacking: instead of a fixed rule, train a second-level classifier (a meta-learner) that takes the base classifiers' outputs as its input features and learns how to combine them. To avoid overfitting, the meta-learner must be trained on outputs the base classifiers produced for data they were not trained on, usually via cross-validation (lesson 24). Stacking can learn, for example, that classifier 3 is very reliable for class B but not for A.

Bagging recap: bootstrap aggregating trains each classifier on a bootstrap sample of the training data (lesson 24) and combines them by voting or averaging. It reduces variance and helps most with unstable classifiers, such as unpruned decision trees. Random forests add random feature subsets at each split to increase diversity. Their out-of-bag error gives a free accuracy estimate.

Boosting recap: AdaBoost trains classifiers one after another. After each round, the samples it got wrong get larger weights, so the next classifier focuses on them. The final decision is a weighted vote with weights from each classifier's error, as above. Boosting reduces bias and can turn weak classifiers, only a little better than chance, into a strong one. It is more sensitive to label noise than bagging, because mislabelled points keep getting heavier weights. Gradient boosting generalises the idea and is a top choice for tabular data.

Cascades for speed, Viola-Jones: sometimes the aim of combining is speed, not just accuracy. In face detection, a camera image has hundreds of thousands of windows, and almost all of them contain no face. Viola and Jones (2001) arranged boosted classifiers in a cascade: the first stage uses only a couple of simple rectangle features and quickly rejects most non-face windows; windows that pass go to the next, more complex stage, and so on. Only windows that pass every stage are reported as faces.

Cascade worked: suppose each of 10 stages keeps 99 percent of real faces and passes 50 percent of non-faces. The overall detection rate is 0.99^10 = 0.904, about 90 percent, and the overall false positive rate is 0.5^10 = 0.00098, about 1 in 1,000. Because most windows are rejected in the first one or two stages, the average cost per window is tiny, which allowed real-time face detection on 2001 computers and later on cheap cameras.

Multimodal biometrics: a fingerprint scanner can fail on worn fingers (common among farm and construction workers), and a face system can fail in poor light. Multimodal systems combine two or more traits, such as face plus fingerprint, or fingerprint plus iris. Fusion can happen at the score level, using the sum rule after normalising each matcher's scores to a common range, or at the decision level, using AND (both must accept, lowering FAR) or OR (either can accept, lowering FRR). Score-level fusion usually gives the lowest EER.

Score normalisation, worked: a face matcher gives scores from 20 to 100 and a fingerprint matcher from 0.1 to 0.9. Adding them raw would let the face score dominate. Min-max normalisation maps each to 0 to 1: a face score of 70 becomes (70 - 20) / 80 = 0.625, and a fingerprint score of 0.4 becomes (0.4 - 0.1) / 0.8 = 0.375. The fused score is their mean, 0.5, compared with a threshold chosen on validation data. Other choices are z-score normalisation (subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation) and converting scores to probabilities.

Real-life example 1, mobile banking registration: a mobile financial service in Bangladesh verifies new customers against the national ID database. A face match alone fails for some users because of old ID photos, and fingerprint alone fails for labourers with worn fingerprints. The service fuses normalised face and fingerprint scores with a weighted sum rule. The combined EER is much lower than either alone, so fewer genuine customers are turned away and fewer fraudsters get through.

Real-life example 2, handwritten Bangla digit recognition: a postal sorting project trains three different classifiers for Bangla postcode digits: an SVM on pixel features, a k-NN on chain-code features and a small neural network. Each reaches about 96 to 97 percent. Their errors overlap only partly, because they use different features. A sum-rule combination of their posteriors reaches 98.5 percent, and samples where all three disagree are sent to a human operator.

Common mistakes: combining classifiers that make the same errors; assuming more classifiers always help, even if they are worse than chance; using the product rule when one classifier can output 0; training a stacking meta-learner on the same data the base classifiers saw; and forgetting to normalise scores before summing them. Exams ask for majority vote accuracy for independent classifiers, the sum, product, max and min rules on a small table, weighted voting weights, cascade detection and false positive rates, and bagging vs boosting.

Recap: combining classifiers works when each is better than chance and their errors are diverse: three independent 0.7 classifiers vote to 0.784, eleven to 0.922. Fusion rules use scores; in our table voting chose A but sum, product, max and min chose B. Weighted votes use log(p / (1 - p)). Bagging cuts variance, boosting cuts bias, stacking learns the combination. Cascades trade a little detection (0.904) for huge speed and few false positives (0.00098). Multimodal biometrics fuse traits for lower error.
key_points: Ensembles help when members are better than chance and make diverse errors.
Majority vote of three independent 0.7 classifiers gives 0.784; eleven give 0.922; three at 0.4 give only 0.352.
Sum, product, max and min rules fuse posteriors; in the example vote says A, all score rules say B.
Weighted voting with weight log(p / (1 - p)): 0.9 gives 2.20, 0.7 gives 0.85.
Bagging reduces variance; boosting reduces bias; stacking learns the combiner on held-out outputs.
Viola-Jones cascade: 10 stages at 0.99 and 0.5 give detection 0.904 and false positives 0.00098.
Multimodal biometrics fuse face, fingerprint or iris scores, usually with a normalised sum rule.
lessons.tip: For fusion-rule questions, make one table with classifiers as rows and classes as columns. Add a row for sum, product, max and min at the bottom. With everything in one grid, each rule is a single glance and you will see when rules disagree.
lessons.task: Ask three friends to guess the weight of a bag of rice (or any object) separately, without hearing each other. Compare each guess and their average with the true weight. Repeat with three objects. Was the average usually closer than the typical single guess?
