quiz.q: Three independent classifiers each have accuracy 0.7. What is the accuracy of their majority vote?
What happens when three independent classifiers each with accuracy 0.4 vote?
quiz.explain: Voting helps only when members are better than chance; here the majority is wrong more often.

quiz.q: Classifiers output (A 0.6, B 0.4), (A 0.7, B 0.3) and (A 0.1, B 0.9). Which class does the sum rule choose?
options: A, because two classifiers prefer it
quiz.explain: Sum for A is 1.4 and for B is 1.6, so B wins even though the majority vote picks A.

quiz.q: In a Viola-Jones cascade with 10 stages, each passing 50 percent of non-faces, what is the overall false positive rate?
quiz.explain: A non-face must pass every stage: 0.5^10 = 0.00098.

quiz.q: How does boosting differ from bagging?
options: Boosting trains classifiers in parallel on bootstrap samples
Boosting trains sequentially, increasing the weight of misclassified samples
quiz.explain: Boosting focuses each new classifier on earlier mistakes and mainly reduces bias; bagging trains independently to reduce variance.

lessons.title: Pattern Recognition in Practice: Applications and Course Capstone
lessons.content:
You now have a full toolbox: Bayes decision theory, density estimation, nearest neighbours, linear discriminants, kernels, PCA, feature selection, template matching, HMMs, clustering, mixtures, structural methods, error estimation and ensembles. A toolbox is useful only when you know which tool to pick for which job and how to join the tools into a working system. This final lesson walks through complete pattern recognition systems that matter in Bangladesh and around the world: handwritten Bangla digits, faces, fingerprints, speech and fraud. Then it looks at how deep learning changed the field, the ethical questions every designer must face, and where to go next.

The general pipeline: almost every system follows the chain from lesson 01: sensing (camera, microphone, scanner), preprocessing (cleaning and normalising), segmentation (finding the object), feature extraction, classification, and post-processing (using context, rejecting unsure cases). Evaluation runs alongside every design choice. Errors at an early stage are hard to fix later: a blurred scan or a wrongly cropped face hurts every later step, which is why practical engineers spend much of their time on sensing and preprocessing.

Case 1, Bangla handwritten digits, sensing and preprocessing: imagine reading handwritten digits on Bangla postal forms or exam answer sheets. A scanner captures the page at 300 dots per inch. Preprocessing converts it to grey, removes noise with a small median filter, and binarises with a threshold, such as Otsu's method, to separate ink from paper. Each digit box is cut out, the digit is centred by its centre of mass, scaled to fit a 28 by 28 grid while keeping its aspect ratio, and the slant is corrected. Now every digit is a 784-number vector in the same position and size.

Case 1, features and classifier: the raw 784 pixels can be used directly with k-NN or an SVM, but feature design helps classical classifiers: PCA to around 50 components (lesson 16), zoning features (ink density in each of 16 zones), chain-code direction histograms from the outline (lesson 23), and counts of loops and endpoints for structure. A reasonable design trains an SVM with an RBF kernel (lesson 15) on PCA plus direction features, with C and gamma chosen by 5-fold cross-validation (lesson 24).

Case 1, evaluation and post-processing: test on 2,000 digits written by people not in the training set (split by writer, lesson 24). Suppose 1,940 are correct: accuracy 97 percent, with a 95 percent interval of plus or minus 0.75 percent. The confusion matrix shows the common mistakes, such as Bangla 1 and 9, which have similar shapes. Post-processing uses context: a Bangladeshi postcode has four digits and must be in the list of valid codes, so an impossible reading is replaced by the closest valid one. Digits whose top posterior is below 0.6 are rejected and sent to a human (reject option, lesson 04).

Case 2, face recognition: the steps are detection (find faces, for example with the Viola-Jones cascade of lesson 25 or a modern neural detector), alignment (rotate and scale so the eyes are at fixed positions), feature extraction (eigenfaces and Fisherfaces in the classical era, lessons 16 and 14; deep embeddings today), and matching (nearest neighbour with a threshold for verification). Verification is measured with FAR, FRR and EER (lesson 24); identification among many people with rank-1 accuracy, the share of searches where the correct person is the top match.

Case 3, fingerprint minutiae matching: a fingerprint is described structurally (lesson 23) by its minutiae: ridge endings and bifurcations, each with position and direction. A good print has about 40 to 100. Matching aligns the two sets (rotation and translation) and counts minutiae that pair up within small distance and angle tolerances. Worked: a probe print has 40 minutiae, the stored print has 45, and 30 pair up after alignment. A common score is 2 x 30 / (40 + 45) = 0.71. The threshold on this score sets the FAR and FRR trade-off, chosen very low on FAR for national ID and border control.

Case 4, speaker and speech recognition: the sound is cut into overlapping frames of about 25 milliseconds every 10 milliseconds, and each frame becomes a feature vector of spectral features, such as mel-frequency cepstral coefficients. For speaker verification, a GMM per speaker against a background GMM (lesson 22) was the classical method. For word recognition, left-to-right HMMs per phoneme or word (lessons 19 and 20) were standard, decoded with Viterbi. Today neural networks handle both, but the frame-based feature pipeline and sequence decoding remain.

Case 5, fraud detection: a mobile financial service sees millions of transactions daily, and only a tiny fraction are fraud. Features include amount, time of day, number of transactions in the last hour, new device or new recipient, and distance from usual location. Classifiers include boosted trees (lesson 25) and anomaly detection based on density (lessons 10 and 22): transactions in low-density regions of normal behaviour are suspicious.

Fraud worked, the base rate: suppose 1 in 1,000 transactions is fraud. Out of 1,000,000, that is 1,000 frauds and 999,000 honest. A detector catches 90 percent of fraud (900) and wrongly flags 1 percent of honest ones (9,990). It flags 10,890 transactions, of which only 900 are fraud: precision 8.3 percent. Even a good-looking detector mostly flags honest people when the class is rare. This is Bayes' rule again (lesson 03), and it is why fraud systems use a second stage, human review or a verification call, rather than blocking accounts automatically.

The deep learning shift: in classical pattern recognition, humans designed features and machines learned classifiers. From about 2012, deep neural networks began learning the features too, directly from pixels or sound, given large labelled data sets and fast GPUs. Convolutional networks overtook hand-designed features on image recognition, and learned embeddings replaced eigenfaces and MFCC-GMM systems. Handwritten digit recognition, for instance, reaches above 99 percent with convolutional networks on standard benchmarks.

What still matters from this course: deep learning did not make these ideas obsolete. Bayes decision theory still decides thresholds and reject options; error estimation, cross-validation and significance tests still judge every model; PCA and clustering still explore data; nearest neighbour search on learned embeddings powers face and image search; HMM-style dynamic programming lives on in sequence decoding; ensembles still win competitions. And when data is small, explainability is required, or hardware is weak, classical methods are often the right choice.

Choosing a method, a quick guide: with very little labelled data, prefer simple models (nearest neighbour, naive Bayes, LDA) or templates. With sequences, think DTW for a few templates and HMMs or neural sequence models for many examples. With no labels, cluster first. With structured patterns like diagrams or molecules, consider structural methods. With many features and few samples, select or extract features first. With large labelled data sets of images or sound, deep networks usually win. In every case, compare against a simple baseline: a fancy method that does not beat k-NN is not worth its complexity.

Deployment and maintenance: a system does not end at a test score. Real data drifts: new handwriting styles, new phone cameras, new fraud tricks. Monitor accuracy on fresh labelled samples, track the rate of rejected cases, and retrain when performance drops. Keep the training data, code and settings versioned so that any result can be reproduced. Measure speed and memory on the actual device, because a recogniser that is accurate but takes five seconds per digit is useless for sorting mail.

Ethics: bias: a recogniser is only as fair as its data. In 2018, Buolamwini and Gebru's Gender Shades study found that commercial gender classifiers had error rates as high as 34.7 percent for darker-skinned women, compared with 0.8 percent for lighter-skinned men, because training data was unbalanced. A face or voice system trained mostly on one group can fail another. Designers must test error rates separately for each group (age, gender, skin tone, region, accent) and fix gaps before deployment.

Ethics: privacy and consent: faces, fingerprints and voices are personal data that cannot be changed like a password if stolen. Collecting them needs consent, secure storage (store templates, not raw images, and protect them), and clear limits on use. Mass surveillance with face recognition raises serious questions about freedom. Laws such as data protection rules, and the ethics covered in Professional Ethics and Cyber Law (deep-cse-6-6), apply directly to pattern recognition engineers.

Ethics: errors have victims: every system has FAR and FRR. A false match in a criminal database can put an innocent person under suspicion; a false reject at a social benefit distribution point can deny an old woman her allowance because her fingerprints are worn. Responsible design means choosing thresholds with these costs in mind, offering a human fallback, keeping a way to appeal, and being honest about accuracy, with confidence intervals, not a single optimistic number.

Course recap, part 1: pattern recognition maps measurements to decisions. Bayes decision theory gives the optimal rule when probabilities are known; parametric (maximum likelihood, Bayesian) and non-parametric (Parzen windows, k-NN) methods estimate them. Discriminant functions, the perceptron, Fisher's LDA and SVMs with kernels build decision boundaries directly. PCA extracts features and feature selection chooses among them, fighting the curse of dimensionality.

Course recap, part 2: template matching and DTW compare raw patterns; HMMs model sequences with forward, Viterbi and Baum-Welch. Clustering, fuzzy c-means, k-medoids and GMMs with EM find structure without labels. Structural methods use chain codes, grammars, edit distance and graphs. Error estimation (cross-validation, bootstrap, FAR, FRR, EER, McNemar) keeps us honest, and ensembles combine strengths.

What to study next: Data Mining (deep-cse-7-6) applies clustering, classification and association rules to large databases. Neural Networks and Fuzzy Systems (deep-cse-7-8) builds the neural and fuzzy ideas we touched on. Deep Learning (deep-cse-8-1) teaches learned features, convolutional and recurrent networks and transformers. Natural Language Processing (deep-cse-8-2) applies sequence models to text and speech. Computer Vision (deep-cse-8-3) takes images from pixels to understanding. All of them build on what you learned here.

Real-life example, a capstone project idea: build a Bangla digit reader for your own handwriting and your friends'. Collect 50 samples of each digit from at least 10 writers; preprocess to 28 by 28; extract PCA and direction features; compare k-NN, SVM and a small ensemble with 5-fold cross-validation split by writer; report accuracy with a confidence interval, a confusion matrix and a McNemar test between the top two methods; and add a reject option. This one project uses almost every lesson of the course.

Common mistakes in real projects: rushing past data collection and preprocessing; testing on data from the same writers or sessions; reporting one accuracy number without an interval; ignoring class imbalance and base rates; never checking error rates by group; and assuming a deep network is always needed. Exams on applications ask you to design a full pipeline for a given problem, justify each choice, choose evaluation measures, and discuss ethical risks.

Final recap: real systems chain sensing, preprocessing, segmentation, features, classification and post-processing, and evaluation steers every step. Bangla digits reached 97 plus or minus 0.75 percent in our example; fingerprints scored 0.71 from 30 paired minutiae; fraud detection showed precision of only 8.3 percent at a 1-in-1,000 base rate. Deep learning learns features, but the decision theory and evaluation of this course remain essential. Build fair, private and honest systems, and keep learning.
key_points: Systems chain sensing, preprocessing, segmentation, features, classification and post-processing, with evaluation throughout.
Bangla digits: binarise, centre, size-normalise to 28 by 28, PCA plus direction features, SVM; 1,940 of 2,000 gives 97 percent plus or minus 0.75.
Faces: detect, align, extract, match; verification uses FAR, FRR and EER, identification uses rank-1 accuracy.
Fingerprints: minutiae matching; 30 paired out of 40 and 45 gives score 2 x 30 / 85 = 0.71.
Fraud base rate: 90 percent recall and 1 percent false alarms at 1-in-1,000 fraud gives precision of only 8.3 percent.
Deep learning learns features, but Bayes decisions, evaluation, PCA, clustering and ensembles still matter.
Ethics: test error rates per group, protect biometric data, plan for the victims of errors; next courses deep-cse-7-6, 7-8, 8-1, 8-2, 8-3.
lessons.tip: When an exam asks you to design a system, write the pipeline stages as headings and give one concrete choice with one reason under each, plus how you will evaluate it. A clear, justified pipeline scores better than a long list of algorithm names.
lessons.task: Choose one problem in your area, such as recognising rickshaw licence plates, identifying ripe tomatoes, or detecting fake mobile recharge messages. Write a one-page design: sensor, preprocessing, features, classifier, how you will evaluate it, and one ethical risk with a mitigation.

quiz.q: Why do fraud systems usually send flagged transactions for review instead of blocking them automatically?
options: When fraud is rare, most flagged transactions are honest even for a good detector
quiz.explain: With a 1-in-1,000 base rate, 90 percent recall and 1 percent false alarms, only 8.3 percent of flagged cases are fraud.

quiz.q: A probe fingerprint has 40 minutiae, the stored one 45, and 30 pair up. What is the score 2 x paired / (n1 + n2)?
What did the deep learning shift mainly change in pattern recognition?
options: It removed the need for any evaluation
Features are learned from data instead of designed by hand
Classifiers no longer need training data
quiz.explain: Deep networks learn features from raw input; decision theory and evaluation remain essential.

quiz.q: Which practice best addresses bias in a face recognition system?
options: Measuring error rates separately for each demographic group and fixing gaps before deployment
quiz.explain: Overall accuracy can hide much higher error rates for some groups, as the Gender Shades study showed.

quiz.q: Why should test digits come from writers not in the training set?
options: To measure how well the system generalises to new people's handwriting
Because writers are not allowed in training
To reduce the number of classes
quiz.explain: Splitting by writer prevents the test from rewarding memory of particular people's styles.
